THE WRITER OF OUR NEXT "SPECIAL."

Sir Robert Reid, K.C., M.P., who will contribute an article next week tolour columns on "The Bonds of Empire," may well be described as one of the most popular personalities on the Frcnt Bench of the Liberal party in the House of Commons. Sir Robert is a son of Sir James Reid, of Dumfries, and went to school at CheltenhamCollege. From there he became an Undergraduate at Oxford University, and had a very distinguished career, being one of the many brilliant scholars of Balliol College. He graduated with first-class honours, and carried off the Ireland University Scholarship in 1868. Three years laterhe was called to the Bar, and in 1880, when the country returned an overwhelming majority for Mr. Gladstone's policy, Sir Robert Reid became member of Parliament for Hereford.

His personal popularity and his wonderful grasp of political questions attracted the attention of Mr. Glad- stone,who always had a leaning to Oxford 'men. In 1894 he became Solicitor-General, and later in the same year Attorney-General. It will be remembered that Sir Robert Reid was selected by the British Government to represent England at the Veaezuelan Boundary Arbitration Commission in Paris. So well did he advocate our claims that England won all along the line: and in 1889 Queen Victoria &In- ferred upon him the distinction of the Grand Cross of the Order of St. Michael and St. George. Sir Robert Reid is also an ardent sportsman. He played cricket fer Oxford against Cambridge three years, and also represented Oxford against Cambridge at the annual racquet tournament for three years in succession.

Mr. J. Bell presided at an open meeting of the Buckley-street P.S.A. Society held in the schoolroom, on Sunday. Mr. E. W. Jones was the speaker and the lesson was read by Mr. Andrew Scriven. Mr. A. Bates gave two violin selections, and Mrs. Colley Tendered :two solos.; Miss 11. Plinston, A.L.C.M., and Mr. George Colley were the accompanists. There was a good attendance. A meeting of the Warrington P.S.A. was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- atreet,on Sunday, when Mr. E. S. Taylor occupied the chair. MT's. Hannan sang " The Lost Chord "and 41 0 rest in the Lord," in a very creditable manner. Mr. J. C. Brocklehurst gave an admirable address.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Hospital Shopping Day Scheme.—The drapers trade association have taken an adverse view of the Shopping Day Scheme,iwhich is being organised by Lord Duncannon's committee on • behalf of King Edward's Hospital Fund. The proposal that they should con- tribute a percentage of their takings on November 3rd to the Fund., has been favourably received by the greater part of the shepkeeping community in London, but the drapers object, among 'other reas ' ops that it will establish an undesirable precedent, and 'that any extra trade gained on November 3rd, would be at the expense of their ordinary business on other days. No doubt there is some truth in this, but the scheme has been devised to help the hospitals, and not the drapers, and it is certain that a great many purchases would be made by the public over and above ordinary require- ments, in order to support the hospitals, and all this would be extra trade gained. The Pulpit and Dress Reform.—The rector of St. Stephen's Bristol, evidently thinks the pulpit should be used to advocate a more sober style of dress for women. It has been suggested that on certain Sundays all the pulpits should be handed over to the doctors for them to discourse and educate the people upon questions of health, and the Bristol rector seems to think that the same means might be adopted to spread the idea of a national dress for women. At the harvest thanksgiving service, he launched out against the follies of fashion, and told his "sisters" that some of the unnecessary material used for sleeves might vesy well go to "lengthen the little waistcoats they seem to have outgrown. The rector would have a national dress, which studied only utility, such as that of the hospital nurse, but it is to be feared that his preaching will be in vain. No one will deny that the eccentricities of fashion are sometimes trying, bat it would be a dull world without them. Winter Fashions.—lntending purchasers of winter toilettes would do well to wait another two or three weeks—longer if possible—before giving their orders. New fashions are appearing every day, but it is impos- sible to tell which among them will be taken up, and which discarded, and until November is with us, there is no certainty in the matter. Even then, the woman who has little to spend upon her clothes should carefully avoid anything in the nature of extremes, anything that dates. Her range of colours should be a limited one, and nothing striking, such as the bright red so modish this autumn, should be considered for a moment. Revivals.—Two notable revivals are, the "dress im- prover," and the floating veil. The former is composed of two pads, which boast springs, the whole being stiffened with a substance made of the fibres of the turkey's quills. Leading dressmakers and tailors pro- fess to be unable to fit a skirt successfully without an "improver "and are stitching them into all the newest creations. With regard to the floating veil, it is pic- turesque, but Scarcely comfortable wear, at this season of the year when gusty days must be expected. it may be of gauze or lace, and should cover the entire hat. About thebrim it is loosely arranged, and falls in grace- ful folds about the shoulders, where it is again slightly gathered together. Such a veil has a graceful,old world air, and Fs easily thrown back but so far our Parisienne and American sisters are the only women who look really at home in such an accessory. _ - . .

-- -- Evening Dress Fabrics.—tarlatan is another revival, and figures largely among the fabrics set aside for evening wear. Such gowns have round skirts gathered into the waist, broad belts, and fichus of the pelerine persuasion, and are being generally trimmed with the old-fashioned blonde lace. Book muslin too is being favoured by some modistes for evening wear, but toilettes built of this aro not a success. Theysavour too much of summer afternoon gowns, which the climate did not permit us to wear to a„ finish.

Hand-made Lace.—The demand for hand-made lace is very limited, but the .Association, which was formed in 1897 under the patronage of the late Queen, gives some encouraging accounts of the revival of the industry in Buckinghamshire. That county, and also Bedfordshire, and Devonshire, have long been the principal centres of rural lace making in England, but machine lace and the Board Schools have gradually reduced the number of workers. Children instead of being taught lace making, go to school, and when old enough go into service, or into the dressmaking. ot some other business. The industry has also suffered for want of being organised upon business lines, but this is being remedied by the North Bucks Lace Association. It furnishes patterns, provides the workers with regular employment, and buys their productions for cash. The "middleman" is thus eliminated, and one or two shops have been taken in London, specially for the sale of hand-made lace, which can he purchased at very reasonable prices. To Cheer the Cheerless.—Those people who hanker after everything that is bright and pleasant in life, generally succeed in making friends and enjoying them- selves. Bub there are many of more reserved disposi- tion who lead lives of dreary isolation for the want (sf friends and acquaintances. It has consequently oecurred to a lady in London to start a Guild of Social Intercourse, with a view to provide the dull and lonely with the opportunity of agreeable and social entertain- ment. As a rule, if people cannot or will not make these opportunities for themselves, it is not likely that they will be much assisted by such a guild, but a stranger is nowhere so lonely as in the heart of a great, city, and possibly it may be the moans of bringing sun- shine to same who, for some or other reason, have fallen into dull and friendless ways of existence.

Cheap Music.—Composers and publishers of songs and music seem to have at last recognised that their true interests will be served by issuing, cheap editions of popular compositions. There is 3 large public demand for cheap music. which cannot be met with copyright editions published at 2s. and not obtainablaunder Is. 4d. It is upon this state of things that the "pirates" have flourished, and the fact that they have sold hundreds of thousands of copies of popular pieces at a penny or two- pence each shows how large must be the profit on the sale of the printed copies. The Act of last year has by no means suppressed the "pirates," but with sixpenny nausic there will be less scope for their illegitimate enterprise. The public will readily pay sixpence for a piece of music that it wants, and it is impossible to doubt that the reduction in price and consequent increased sale will greatly add to the profits of com- poser and publisher. . New Books. Among the many books lately given to the wOrld by women, four uniformly bound works of fiction recently published by Messrs. Methuen deserves special attention. " Resurgam "by Mrs. L. T. Meade. is a spirited melodrama, with a strong religions thread in its plot, Miss Mary Findlater's " Rase of Joy" has strength and is eminently readable, Mrs. E. tNesbit's book of short stories "The Literary Sense," is bright and interesting, while "The Truthful Liar" by Mrs. David G. Ritchie shows us the conditions of polite life in a cathedral city which the author has closely and humorously observed. The dialogue is brilliant, and the characters out of the ordinary run.
MADGE.

div.head: CONTRITE TRAMP.
div.p: THE CONTRITE TRAMP.

Mr. Robert Kerr, (passenger traffic manager of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, has received the following letter from an anonymous correspondent Enclosed please find note for 10 dollars to pay for rides which T stole on your trains while a tramp, for I was a tramp, and " hobbed "almost from Maine to California largely on C.P.R. trains. Now I amaChristian,brought to know the love of God, and I must pay all my bills. I will pay them all in time. Hoping to get a reply from you. God bless you. Mr. Kerr.

div.head: Examiner Saturday, October 10, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner Saturday, October 10, 1903.
FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

We have to blame the unpleasant weather for the dulness of affairs in the sartorial World, although there is always little to note in the demi-saison. Modes generally speak- ing are never very decided until October it well on its way, although one cannot but observe the way the fashions are tending, and thereby wisely take advantage of the reduced prices that most of the best firms are offering and get a really well made dress whose cut and fit will always ensure its success, however severely plain the style. One cannot do better than invest three to five guineas out of a dress allowance in a neat tailor-made costume, even although at the first glance this may appear a piece of extravagance. I have generally found
A NEAT COATS

that if you go to a well-known tailor of good standing, you will there obtain good material and a good out which this season is all the more necessary, as cloth gowns show every sign of marked simplicity of style. During the busy season the usual price asked for a tailor-made, turned out by a first-class house, places, it beyond the means of many girls, but more in order to keep their hands in work during the slack season prices are really reasonable. Of late years the tailor - made costume had rather lost its original character for simplicity and severity, and it became a much strapped, tucked, and gauged garment, This year, however, there is every prospect that. it will be more upon the lines of the old severe type! The neat coat depicted Sets the figure of the wearer closely and has a high storm collar and deep pointed revers of fura It fastens down the front with invisible hooks and eyes, although half-a- dozen ornamental buttons give a finish to the front: The material employed is dull
'A DEMI-SAISON TOQUEi surfaced black cloth of a firm make, such as can always be relied , upon to keeps its fit welb

We are again to see in our midst the close-fitting long basqued Newmarket coat, trimmed in some instances with heavy soutache braid. The time is already close at hand when the woman with a good natural figure will no longer conceal its graceful curves and lines beneath the some- what shapeless if convenient bolero, but will triumph in a plain tight-fitting coat and smartly .ut skirt of walking length. The true admirer of the tailor-made (amongst whom we may safely reckon the majority of our masculine friends) could not honestly express any satisfaction at the elaborate trailing gowns which usurped the name and Were not nearly so comfortable as the original mode.

div.head: DIRECT LABOUR REPRESENTATION.
div.p: DIRECT LABOUR REPRESENTATION.
BIG DEMONSTRATION AT WARRINGTON.
Speeches by Messrs. D. J. shackleton, M.P., and A. Henderson M.P.
THE FISCAL QUESTION.
Workingmen mustered in strong force in the Parr

Hall Warrington, on Tuesday eyeing when a labour demonstration promoted by the Trades and Labour Council and Labour Representation Committee was held. The hall was comfortably filled and the speeches by labour leaders and local speakers were followed with interest. Mr. Edwin Plinston (Train- waymen's,Union) presided and was supported on the platform kyn.lr..D. J. Shackleton., M.P. for Clitheroe, Mr. A. Henderson, M.P. for Barnard Castle, the Rev. J. F. Matthews, Messrs. S. Wright J.P., J. Edwardson F. Stott (secretary of the Trades Council), Jolley, E. Malone, J. A. Seddon (St. Helens) and others. Before the meeting commenced the Firth Glee Party rendered selections in admirable style. THE CHAIRMAN AND THE FISCAL QUESTION. TheICHAinmAN read a telegram from Mr. J. Hodge, labour candidate for Gorton, regretting that he could not attend as he was delayed in Glasgow. He wished the meeting success. Continuing, Mr. Plinston said he did not think there over was an occasion in the history of trades unionism that demanded unity and enthusiasm more than the present time. During the past two years they had had a very important change affecting the vital interests of trade unionism. He referred to the juggling by the law lords of the country in reference to the Trades Union Act. That Act, passed some thirty years ago' was held at the time to safeguard the inter- ests and the cash of trades union organisations. With- out any alteration of the Act a wrong interpretation-- to their mind—had been placed upon it, and their funds to-day wereat the mercy of the employers who were not always straightforward in their conduct towards worliingnien. They had at the present time before the country a matter which affected every working- man in the country, and that night be sup- posed that great man from Birmingham would be telling the citizens of Glasgow what he was going to do with regard to the fiscal policy. So far as they were concerned, he thought they had made up their minds what they were going to do with an Act that was going tolinterfere with the price of bread-stuffs and raw material of every description. (Applause.) They had had from Birmingham in the past three acres and a cow. (Laughter.) Theyhad had promises of old age pen- sions, but had they got them? Now they were told that the price of bread was going to be raised with a promise of increased wages. He ventured to say that the workingmen of this city were not going to close their eyes and open their mouths and take what Joseph Chamberlain had a mind to give them. They knew something of him. They knew that he had left the Cabinet, that he had led the country at times on the strength of khakiism to a matter of politics which was never before the electorate. He was certain that in face of the fact that after many years of Free Trade this country was the most prosper- ons in the world, there was no real reason why we should change from that s 5 stem to one that was likely to turn it from the most prosperous to something els*. At no distant date they might have an election. They might or might not have a labour candidate fer Warrington. (Applause.) He hoped and trusted that they would have a labour candidate. (Applause.) Tilde Union law could not be put right until they had a fair representation of workingmen in the House of Commons. The men they sent to represent:them now, whether Tory or Radical, were mostly capitalists. Their interests in some matters were not identical with those of the working classes. The only way to remedy their griev- ances was to send workingmen representatives to the House of Commons. (Applause.) Mr. Henderson had come to them fresh from the Barnard Castle victory, andhe (the speaker) hoped he would arouse theenthusi- asm of Warrington!poople so that they would bear in mind that when there was an election their duty was to vote for the candidate who was in favour of the workingmen of the country. (Applause). TRADE UNION LAW.

pMr. J. EDWARDSON (wiredrawers) moved "That in the opinion of this meeting legislation is necessary to define our Trade Union rights and to secure absolute protection for the funds of the various trade orponiza- tions." The Trade Union movement, he said, was in a most serious position. He contended that the capital- ists were striking a blow to reduce men to the level of free labour. As workingmen they could do nothing unless they combined and they must send labour repre- sentatives to Parliament. (Hear, hear.) Some men said that Trade Unionism was nothing but agitation, but they should bear in mind that Mr. Chamberlain stated in his recent pamphlet that he felt sure.] that Trade Unions would uphold the wages of this country. It appeared to him that if workingmen were going to receive increased wages as a result of a new fiscal policy they would have to fight the capitalist, and that was most awkward. They did not want to fight unless they were absolutely compelled. (Applause.) Mr. MALONE seconded. F,MR. SHACKLETON, ALP., AND TRADE DISPUTES.

Mr. D. J. SHACKLETON, M.P., supported the motion. It was quite true, he said, that the law as affecting Trade Unions was in a very awkward position and certainly required defining. Those who had had work to .do in commotion with unions as secretaries and members of executives knew how diffi- cult it was to steer clear of the network of legal decisions which had been given against them dur- ing the past five or six years. He appreciated to the Lull the importance of the questions raised by Mr. Chamberlain but it was not his intention to trespass beyond the scope of the resolution. Mr. Shackleton proceeded to deal with sections of trade union law affecting picketing, conspiracy, and the responsibility of a trade union for the action of its members and officials. Trade Unionists, he contended, were not anxious to rush into strikes, but when they were forced to resort to them they wanted to be placed on a fair and equal basis with their employers in the fight. I(Applause.) In regard to the picketing question, an . Act was passed by the Hoese of Commons in 1875. In placing the measure before the house Mr. Cross,—now Lord Cross—the Home Secretary of that day stated in clear terms what his intentioni was and quoted the judgment given by Mr. Russell Gurney, Q.C., the Recorder of London in which it was held that trade unionists on strike had a perfect right to persuade others not to work, so long as it was done peacefully. Mr. ; Cross so far agreed with that decision that he caused it to be printed and seat to the magistrates and judges as a guide to what the law was. Further, the Attorney • General, not two years ago, in a debate in the House of Commons said he defied any man to show that peaceful persuasion by itself imposed any liability, either civil or criminal. Mr. Justice Kay had now decided to the contrary and held that it was illegal to picket the works or place of •business of an employer by sending parsons to try and induce men not to work there. That deci- sion was the law of the land to-day. In a dispute in his own twice which lasted for twelve mouths, the em- ployers sent out advertisements offering inducements of wages in eecess of what the strikers required in order to get people to work for them, but if Trade Unionists induced a man, by offering to pay his wages, to go back home, that was illegal. Surely if the employers could offer inducements like he had mentioned, Trade Unionists ought to be permitted to pay railway fares for a.man who had conic to work at a place where he did not know a strike ex- isted (Loud applause). Company and their servants. Tili) question was raised by the Company, taken to a Court of law, and there decided first one way and then the other, but finally against the trade unionists.. The Amalga- mated Railway Servants had to pay something like £30,000. What was their remedy,? They could accept the judgment as it stood, they could fight for anti-Taff Vale, er, they could have something between the two. Let those who sought to maintain the present position show why the law as interpreted by the House of Lords should be maintained. Up to within very recent years they had managed their trade unions with- out the responsibility which the decision cast upon them. They had tried to conduct strikes in a fair and equitable manner. If the points with regard to picket- ing and conspiracy were fairly settled there was no reason whyj their disputes should not be carried on with the same good feeling as in the past. He believed the decisions on picketing and conspiracy made it impossible to conduct a strike and keep within the four corners of the law. If those paints were settled the other was not of such great importance as had been attached to it. He was not prepared to say that they had a right to give in- structions to their man to do illegal thing's when those illegal things were unfair; He believed that if the points mentioaed were decided as clearly as they were before the recent decision and acted upon, the unions would be prepared to take the responsibility for the conduct of their officials at all events. But theylwould not be responsible for every Dick, Tom, and Harry in a union, who might do things altogether at variance with the wishes of the officials and against reason and common sense. Hew were they going to bring these reforms about ;? In Warrington they were not represented by a geatleman who supported him (Laughter and Applause). When he endeavoured during the last session to put two points straight, Mr. Pierpoint voted the other way or did not vote at all. He was not on his (the speaker's)list (Liughter). They had to consider seriously whether Warrington was a suitable constituency for a labour man to come forward with a fair show of success, and whether working men, Liberal, Tory, 1.L.P., and Socialist, sinking all their little differences, would endeavour to put the catsestions 4of which he had been speaking on an equitable basis. They must send men to the House of Commons who were willing to vote in the direction they desired, and if they could not find a Labour candidate they mast do the neat best thing. "I do not believe," Mr. Shackleton said, "in the policy of not doing anythingat all because I cannot get my man—(Applause.) I am speaking feel- ingly now. I know that if the Labour men alone had supported me in the House of Commons we should have had twelve votes, with my own vote making thirteen. But wo got more than that, and I want a few more who will go for labour, or who may be men who will be willing to support me or anybody else who is willing or hasthe good fortune to bring this matter again before Parliament.—(Applause.) We want Labour men first, as many as possible, but, failing them, we want men who are willing to support us in these or other matters closely affecting you." (Applause.) The resolution was then carried unanimously. REPRESENTATION ON THE TOWN COUNCIL.

The CHAIRMAN, remarked that at the present time the Warrington Town Council was without a Labour representative. Workingmen had a right to representa- tion in the Council Chamber and he thought that without saying anything detrimental to the members there might be some with Labour sympathies who would do quite as useful work for the town as some who were there at the present time. MR. STOTT AND DIRECT LABOUR REPRESENTA

div.head: TION
div.p: TION

Mr. F. STOTT (of the Amalgamated Engineers' Asso- ciation and Labour candidate for the Orford Ward) moved: "That this meeting pledges itself to promote the election of direct Labour representatives in Par- liament, and on all local governing bodies." Ha was very pleased, he said, to see tke. way in which they had received allusions to the question of direct representa- tives. Only by Herculean efforts were they able to work along inch by inch. What they required was am Independent Labour Party in Warrington. They were often told there was no need for an Independent Labour Party. He did not mean a party of isolation, as some of their weak-kneed leaders would like, but a party, which while acting independently, would be willing to co-operate with any party or to oppose any party as circumstances required. They were often told that there was no need fora Labour Party, and that what was good enough for our great fathers was good enough for us. In the old days they had no employers' federa- tions, no judges that gave trade union funds to employers,and new days demanded new methods. Those of them who had been interested in these questions had been disgusted to see the way in which their represen- tatives in Parliament had to go almost cap-in-hand to secure crumbs of legislation. Yet they had the power of reversing this, and securing legislation in their own hands. The workers had more than 70 per cent. of the votes, and their representation in the House of Commons was only 2 percent. (Hear, hear.) A few months ago a Labour Representative Committee was formed in Warrington, and though they had been well supported, he would urge them all to strengthen their hands. In the forthcoming niunicipal elections he had been asked to stand for the Orford Ward, but he had heard a statement to the effect that "no money was to be spared to keep Fred Stott off the Warrington Town Council," on the argument that it was the thin end of the wedge to get a Labour M.P. for Warrington. He did not say it was true, hut he did not deny it. He wanted the ratepayers to resent the suggestion that they could be]bribed by any money that colgd be spent in the Ward to induce them to vote in any Way but the way in which their convictions lay by sending a labour representative to the Town Council. If they were deter- mined to have a labour representative in Parliament they must work, vote and pay for it. (Applause.) Mr. JOLLEY (ironfounders) secondesl. He asked work- ingmen to dissociate themselves from political parties andl said that the labour movement would have to work out its salvation. There was now a chance for a group of labour members to hold the balance of power and 'secure the advantages which working:nen required. The workers had too long been content to be dragged at the heels of political parties and they would have to take an independent course. Everything was not fair and square in the Town Council, and they wanted to send Mr. Stott to keep his eye upon the questions which affected labour. (Applanse.) • MR. HENDERSON'S SPEECH. THE FISCAL QUESTION.

Mr. A. HITSDERSON, M.P., who was received with great cordiality, said he did not take theheartiness of their reception simply as a personal welcome but as a recognition of the splendid victory he was able to secure, as the iestrument of the labour party. in the Barnard Castle Division. (Applause.) When -he heard that in the municipal bodies in Warrington, they had not yet honoured themselves with a single representative he was somewhat annoyed, but perhaps that great gathering was an indication that at last Warrington was going to be merged in the flood tide of the rising of the industrial and independ- ent democracy, to assert its own right not only in the House of Commons but in their local public bodies. Alluding to the resolution he asked if they could ex- pect the present House of Commons, composed. Its it was of such a great majority of men whose inter- ests were not identical with theirs, to grant them the questions which so vitally affected their lives and the lives of their families. The House of Commons was com- posed of 670 representatives, and of that number only 14 could be claimed to directly represent the industrial part of the community. He was (pith prepared to be told that there were men belongiril to the great political parties who had a great amount of sympathy with much that they desired te obtain. But what was their ex- perience in the past? Whenever any question arose which vitally affected the interests of capital, where did they find many of those representatives who were so lavish with their sympathy when they were asking for votes? During the plot session an employers' Parliamentary Committee had been formed to watch the direct interests of those belonging to the employing classes. The members of that committee were drawn from both political parties, which clearly proved that, when it was neceissary there could be affected a power- ful combination of interests that were supposed to be .diometrically opposed and that they could agree to promote their own purposes. What an evidence this was of the necessity not only of voting for the resolution, but of carrying it into practi- cal effect. (Applause.) Before they could get what they wanted from Parliament they would have to con- siderably increase the number of direct labour repre- sentatives, and give those who might be sympathetic to them but hesitated to put their sympathy into practice, to understand that if they would have the votes of the working classes they would have to be prepared to give them something in return. (Applause.) What had been the past policy of the trade union move- ment, judged from a political standpoint? He ventured to say that most members of trades organizations would agree with him that they might have had written over the entrance of their lodge rooms" Nofpolitics admitted ' here" and they might have inscribed upon their banners " Wti know no politics.', That was their prolession,but what was their practice? Was he not right when he said that whilst collectively that might be true,individ- ually they could be found night after night spending their time, money, and strength in seeking to return a representative of one or other of the great political parties, who whenhe was sent to Palriatuent, they found to their sorrow, did little else than misrepresent, their position (Applause). In the past deputations had been sent, cap in hand, to plead on bonded knee, with their representatives—the representatives of the demo- cracy—that they would go into the right lobby and support questions which so vitally affected their interests. On perusing the division list they found that the very man whom they had sent to Parliament by their votes and appealed to by delegation had found his way, ,unfortunately for them, into the wrong lobby. (Laughter.) There were cases in which they could not get an opportunity Of appealing to members because they were conspicuous by their absence when matters affecting the interests of trade unionists were being discussed—as he believed the honourable member, for this borough was, when the Division was taken on the Trades Disputes Bill intro- duced by Mr. Shackleton last session. (Applause.) Yet, he supposed that because they called themselves Tory o r - were not entirely in sympathy with Liberalism, or they called themselvesiLiberal and were not entirely in sym- pathy with labour, when this good friend came down gain to Warrington and told them all the goody,goody

things he had done for them—(laughter)—they would again confer upon him the highest honour the borough could give—they would discharge their sacred duty at the ballot box by sending him to misrepresent them in the House of Commons. (Applause). At last there had been brought into their midst a unifying force which made it possible for the advanced socialist, the member of the Independent Labour Party; the old trade unionist nand theaton-trade unionist to meet on one common platform—the platform of direct labour repre- sentation. (Applause). They were determined to assert their right as workers to select candidates and if they selected satisfactory candidates from a progressive standpoint, what objection should there be, as far as one, at any rate, of the old political parties was con- cerned,to giving them a clear field? He would have theta remember that they were not selecting 670 candidates. He was delighted that one or two political leaders recognized that, and if local associations would have the wisdom and foresight displayed by the chief Liberal whip, they would get on better. (Applause.) As they had got to pay they were going to call the tune. He hoped that if at any time the progressive forces of this town determined to select a candidate of their own, one of the political parties which had been trying its hand for a number of years to win the seat and had not made much progress, would stand down and let someone else have a try. (Applause.) The presence of Mr. Shackleton and himself that even- ing was, he thought, an indication that so far the policy of selecting candidates under the auspices of labour organizations and the Labour Representation Committee had succeeded. (Applause.) The Labour Representa- tion Committee had focussed the scattered elements in the labour world. They were told that the policy of the committee was to "dump down" in a constituency a candidate irrespective of local wishes. Nothing could be farther from the truth. If they wanted a candidate in this town they would never get one front the Labour Representation Committee until, by a duly elected conference of the whole ot their trade organizations they had shown a unanim- ous desire to invite such a candidate. Then they would have to submit him to a public meeting before they could receive the endorsement of the Labour Repre- sentation Committee. Another objection was that they were endeavouring to promote class distinctions. That, he considered, was not worth replying to. How could they promote class distinctions when they formed three- quarters olthe population of the country They were, endeavouring to remove those distinctions. (Applause.) He denied that they were pursuing a policy of isolation because they sought the co-operation of those who were prepared to go with them—either Liberal or Tory. They were not undertaking the task of smashing one . of the political parties. In his electioneering he only tried to smash the party which opposed him. (Laughter.) Speaking of representation on municipal bodies, Mr. Henderson said that if they had had direct representatives on the Warrington Town Council they would never have been troubled with what was known as the non-trading policy (Applause.) If they got a few labour representatives on the council who had no axes to grind he would ven- ture to say that the man who was interested in contracts would see that as far as his firm was concerned he kept them out of their reach or at any rate out of the reach of the exposure of the direct labourirepresentativee They had gone on getting men returned who believed in the non-trading policy. They began to lock the stable door when the horse had gone. If they had got the men in before he ventured to say that they would have been saved all the worry and annoyance that the policy had brought in their midst. It was never to late to mend and as one f the results of that meeting he wanted them to return Mr. Stott to the Council in November. (Applause.) Alluding to the general political situation the speaker said they were in a crisis as far as general politics were concerned that he thought had had no parallel for the last twenty-five years. The crisis was of the greatest importance to the industrial population of the country. There was, he believed, no section of the community which had more to lose by the adoption of the policy that was advocated to-day than had the men who sat before him in that great audience. Some of the state- ments made in regard to the policy might be alluring to the unthinking mind but he believed he was right in saying that there were people in this particular district who had been seeking to persuade the workers to take a sympathetic interest in the proposals. He ventured to say that no labour leader came down and advised them to pursue that conduct, nor was he :a man who had been found fighting in the ranks with the workers in order to secure industrial amelioration. They had been told that this new fiscal policy was absolutely essential in order to draw our possessions over the sea closely to the mother country. That was what the statesman from Birmingham told them, but the Prime Minister told them something a little different at Sheffield. The statesman from Birmingham told them that the result of the policy would mean a tax upon food, but he was prepared to go into every workingman's home and prove that whilst .the price l of some things would be increased others would be reduced and the result of the whole thing would be higher. wages and old age pensions thrown in. Statistics proved that we did the greatest volume .of trade with foreign countries. If we gave a preference to the colonies and taxed our best customers, he contended that the foreigner would retaliate and increase still further the imports that we complained about so much ; or give up dealing with us if he could get another market. If we had not the import and export trade to-day some of our greatest industries in the country would beaffected.Dealing with the contention that wages would be increased he pointed out that employers regulated wages by the law of supply and demand. If there was not a demand wages went down; or at any rate they did not go up. (Laughter.) Mr. Henderson spoke of the failure of the Government to provide old age pensions which found such a prominent place in the 1895 programme. The Government had had more money passing through their hands than any previous Govern- ment, they had had a greater majority than any Govern- ment of recent times, and they had had time to deal with the matter, because they had monopolised more private members' time than any previous Government. What they lacked was the will. (Applause.) Even if they got old age pensions now he did not think there was much honour if they had to purchase them out of the starvation of so many people who were the least able to defend themselves. He .pointed out how the country had prospered under Free Trade. They wanted to defend and maintain the citadel of Free Trade but they wanted to go further. They believed starvation could be remedied or removed but not by the imposition of preferential tariffs. They should have a drastic scheme for the taxation of land values—(applause)—nationalise the royalty rents of the country—(applause)—and cripple the power of the brewer.- (Renewed applause.) Then there might be a possibility of there dawningupon this fair land of ours a brighter,nobler and better day for the industrial portion of the community.(Applause.) In conclusion he urged the workingmea to take a deeper interest in these questions, and said that what had been done at Woolwich,Barnard Castle,and other places could be done at Warrington. (Loud applause.) The resolution was carried unanimouslyaud the usual votes of thaVcs concluded the meeting.

div.head: ri R. HENDERSON ADDRESSES THE IRONFOUNDERS.
div.p: ri R. HENDERSON ADDRESSES THE IRONFOUNDERS.

Advantage was taken by the Local Branch of the Friendly Society of Ironfounders (England, Ireland and Wales), of the visit of Mr. Arthur Henderson, M.P., to Warrington and a gathering of a social character was held at the Winmarleigk Cafe, on Mondayevening. A Large number sat down to a splendid repast after which the Branch President (Mr. William Rowlands), occupied the chair. He expressed the great pleasure it gave him to have to introduce to them the Member for Barnard Castle, They were delighted that in Mr. Hender- son their Society had succeeded in securing a Labour Representative in the House of Commons Mr. HENDERSON, who received a hearty welcome, deliver6d a lengthy address on the present position of tha Trades Union movement. He referred to the great amount of misconception that still prevailed in certain quarters against their movement. It was said that the object of the Union or of certain leaders was to foster discontent and produce industrial warfare. Now this 'was not so. His experience proved that the leaders of , the movement would prefer to settle all their difficulties without resorting to a strike. (Applause). The move- ment to-day was in a satisfactory position numerically and financially; 400,000 had beeu added to the ranks during the past 10 years and during the past 5 years they had doubled their accumulated investments. (Applause.;Their Own Society had met every obligation and stood stronger to-day than ever it had done. (Ap- plause). A vote of thanks to Mr. Henderson concluded the pro- ceedings.

div.p: GRAPPENHALL

YOUNG MEN'S CM:B.—The gymnasium in connection with the above opened on Tuesday evening. A good number of members presented themselves and, under the tuition of Sergeant Sweeney, one of the gymnastic instructors at Orford Barracks, they put in a good and useful evening's work._ _

PARISH Ca/NCIT..—The Council met on Tuesday •to elect a representation to join the Day School Managers. Mr. W. H. Bradford was the nominee of the Council but had to resign. The next selection fell on Mr. William Long, who now becomes one of the managers of Grappeahall School.

div.head: Avother Drowning Mystery.
div.p: Avother Drowning Mystery.

Mr. S. Brighouse field-am in-quest on Monday niiat at the Red Lion Inn, Penketh, on • the body of Agnes Holden, aged sixty years, who lived at a lodging house at Warrington, and whose body was found float- ing in the Sankey and St. Helens Canal on Satur4ay The evidence shows that deceased had been to see her son, who "keeps the Alexandra Hotel, Widnes, on the 213th alt. She insisted in walking hack along the canal, although her son offered to pay her fare. It was quite dark at the time she left her son. She was not seen again alive, but her body was recovered on Saturday morning. A verdict of" Found drowned ." was returned.

Some of the most common are: All kinds of Skin Diseases (and they are many), all Blood Disorders (impure blood is the cause of ills too gu!merous to mention), Biliousness, Sick Headache, LLver and Kidney Complaints, ,Heartburn, Sickness, Sour Stomach, Acidity, Dyspepsia, Furred Tongue, Flatulence, Anwmia, Backache, Spasms, Dizziness, Black Specks before the Eyes,Waterbrash, Sleeplessness, Loss of Appetite, and that weak, nervous state of General 'Depression which sometimes lays hold of us, and, strive as we may, we cannot shake it off.

div.head: WEDDING OF THE WEEK.
div.p: THE WEDDING OF THE WEEK.

The marriage of Prince Andrew of Greece to Princess Alice of Battenberg, which haF been celebrated at Darmstadt, is a royal mar- riage for love. Despite the usual rumours of royal fascinations, it is very seldom that con- venience will permit the feelings of the heart to run away with the promptings of the head in the case of highly-placed members of ruling families. In this instance, however, though connected closely with our own and all the other royal families of Europe, Prince Andrew and Princess Alice are lucky enough just to fall short of political importance to the extent of being allowed to marry as their hearts wish. The young couple met first, it is said, at Coronation time last year, and at once an attachment sprang up between them. The marriage, however, is a very important func- tion socially, and many of the leading royal- ties in Europe are on their way to Darmstadt to be present at Wednesday's function. At Dne time it was said that the King, the Kaiser, and the Czar would all be present, but such an historic meeting has been ren- dered impossible for various reasons. Of the British royal family Princess Henry of Bat-
TAB PRINCE AND PRINCESS ANDREW 0

div.head: GREECE
div.p: GREECE

has made the tenber—s. journey, and Princess Christian . will also be there. The function promises to be a very brilliant one, and the presents are magnificent, though, possibly, falling short of a millionaire wedding in the States. The bride is very young and beauti- ful, and is popular both in London and Darmstadt. Both she and the bridegroom'are closely connected with oui- royal family, though on different sides, which makes the bond double. The latter is connected on the Queen's side through her brother, the .King ot Greece, and the former on the King's throu eh the much-loved Princess Alice, whose dea was such a grief to the nation. Thus thz young couple will carry with them the sincere good wishes of all in this country.
I'WE LAST OF FOTHERINCAY CASTLE.

Fothermgay Castle, near Peterborough, though only 'a stone remains, is the Mecca of the Jacobites and so-called legitimists, as the place of execution of Mary Queen of Scots, "dc jUIT hcreditario Queen of England, Wales and Ire- land, and Dowager-Queen of France, who for adherence to her faith and Royal prerogatives, was on this spot beheaded by vwrant of thc usurper Elizabeth on February Bth, 1587." Now it is feared that even this sole remain. ing trace may gradually disappear, and that

THE PROPOSED RAILING FOR PROTECTING THE REMAINING STONE OF FOTHERINGAY CASTLE. soon no single stone may mark the place "Where Richard dwelt, and where Queen Mary fell." This is due to the characteristic depre- dations of curiosity-seeking trippers ; and a committee under the presidency of Dr. Leonard Came and the auspices of the Archaeological Society of Peterborough has been formed for the purpose of erecting a protective railing on the lines shown in the illustration. 'When sufficient funds have been collected, this last trace of Fotheringay Castle will be guarded against eager Jacobite and common tripper alike for the sake of posterity. One of the former upon each anniversary makes a pilgrim- age to the spot, and lays a memorial wreath upon what remains of Fotheringay, and apart from this, it is one of the historical sights of the country, which attracts every Americar visitor.

div.head: NEW LORD MAYOR.
div.p: THE NEW LORD MAYOR.

The Lord Mayor of London is always the senior Alderman and the first name on the civic rota, but although everyone knows long beforehand who will be the Lord Mayor for any given year, so long as death does not intgfere with the reckoning, each Michael- mas - day the Court of Alder- men of the City of London solemnly goes through the farce of electing the fore-ordain- ed candidate to the civic chair of London. This is followed by the more sen- sible plan of a secret court of inquiry into his financial condi- tion, as the tenure of office, though only lasting one year,
usually entails ALDERMAN SIR J. T. RITCHI,E, the expenditure BROTHER OF THE Ex-CHAN- of ten thousand CELLOR OF THE 'EXCHEQUER. pounds over and

above the allow- ance. This must not be done to the impoverishment of his family, so the Lord Mayor-elect is required to 'produce proof of his financial state before this secret court, and to show by his books that he can afford to 'spend the sum requisite to the proper upkeep of this great office. The new Lord Mayor, who was duly elected with all the ancient ceremonial, is Sii James Ritchie, "Alderman and shipwright," the brother of the lately resigned Chancellm Df the Exchequer,. Born at Dundee in 1835, he is sixty-eight. years of age., and in 1897: during his year of office as a sheriff, he was knighted. He was the second son—the ex. Chancellor being the - fourth son—of Mr. W. Ritchie, a pioneer, jute - merchant of Dundee. In replying to a cordial vote of thanks acknow- ledging. the services of the presefit Lord Mayo' to the City Aldermen, Sir Marcus Samuel said the Lord Mayor had necessarily to exertise great caution, not only in what he said, but in what he did, but knowing well how the voice of the citizens had gone forth in times past in relief of those sufiering, and how it would be raised again to-day, he did not hesitate to express clearly his feelings of - horroi and disgust at the . treatment accorded to his, co-religionists in Roumania, • and nothing had made him feel more happy than the assurance he had that in doing so he should receive the support and sympathy of his fellow citizens. Sir James Thomson Ritchie is the head of the firm of W. Ritchie and Sons, jute spinners and merchants, of Lime Street J Be was 'elected Alderman for the Tower Warci b 189/1 /arid served as Sheriff in 18961 i

div.head: OUR THREATENED CONSUL.
div.p: OUR THREATENED CONSUL.

The state of affairs in the Balkans, instead of decreasing in horror and importance, seem; each day to grow more shameful and alarming and it is an anxious subject of discussion not only amongst all humanitarians, but alsc amongst all politicians. Bulgaria each week seems nearer to war on behalf
of its massacres and ill-treated relatives across the border ; and
now it is said

, that October i I 2 th will actu- ally see a ~-.-,., il declaration -of •Lfii, _ / war on behalf ....„.., af that State. Monastir an "'ii,, pears to be the ', •7f ' , centre of the , , ...; %,` troubled dis- r ~:'.. ~.":1;•:* / trict, and life there can hardly be pleasant for l- -. /-,-,/,;,::,;:,,z, the more civil .:,--•;;;> ..,- l'ed European
The Rus'sian MR. MACGREGOR, OUR CONSUI consul was AT MON AsTrR. murdered some
time back, and

it was announced th-it .the American repre- sentative had met with a similar fate, but fortunately the story turned out to be un- founded. Now comes the news that Mr. Macgregor, the British Consul at Monastir, has had his life threatened. Such an event could only precipitate our action as a nation in the matter, and it can hardly be worth the while of either party to bring down vengeance upon themselves by • such a deed. Mr. Reginald Wyon, a newspaper correspondent, has been ordered out of the country for letting us to much into the secrets of the situation; Mt lie, at- what may ultimately prove the risk of his life, has refused to go, and has been backed up by the British Embassy at the Porte. He points out that it is not the rebels who dislike correspondents, but the corrupt Turkish officials, and between the two the .Powers arc between the devil and the deep blue sea The only satisfactory point in the outlook is the fact that the Powers all appear to be in complete harmony on the subject, and ready to act in unison, or to support passively any joint action of Austria and Russia. This has been the political significance of the visits of King Edward, the Kaiser and the Tsar to Vienna. The state of the Balkans is a terrible blot on European civilisation, ,but the political exi- gencies of the situation demand careful action for fear of worse complications. The frightful condition of affairs in the north-eastern portion of Macedonia may be gauged from the huge numl-Ners of fugitives who are crowding over the frontier into Bulgaria. Two thousand of these wretched individuals, pursued by a squadron of Turkish 'cavalry, have crossed the frontier 'at Allen Kaviak. In cases of this kind the Turkish troopers fire on the mob just as the frontier is reached, and drive it into the wildest flight. Another fugitive group, composed of similar numbers, crossed the frontier of Samabof. These fugitives were protected by a rear guard formed by four revolutionary bands under the command of Lient.-Col. Zogarof. It may be safely stated that the hilly parts of the entire Razlog district are crowded with fugitives, nearly all the Bulgarian inhabited villages being burned down. Belitza, an important village near the frontier, has shared the fate of Mehomia and Betschewo. Seven hundred of its inhabitants were massacred by the Turks.

div.head: TRAIN FERRY.
div.p: THE TRAIN FERRY.

It is now possible to journey in the -same sleeping car between Berlin and Copenhagen. The new ferry for taking trains across the water was started last week. The name of the boat is the Friedrich 'Franz IV., and she is 265 ft. in length and 56ft. in breadth, The length of rails on her main deck is 216 ft. Above this main deck lies the promenade deck with cabins for the passengers. When the mail train, comprising locomotive and five sleeping cars, arrives at Warnemuende, in Schwerin, on the shores of the Baltic, it is run right on to the deck of the boat. The dis- tance on the land route saved by this short sea passage is nearly zoo miles. The speed of the steamei is 14 knots. The cost of the new piers at Warnemuende has amounted to 600,000. The two steamboats have cost 50,000 each. This system is that which the English railway engineers inspected a few months ago, with a view to the practicability

div.head: FRIEDRICH FRANZ IV.
div.p: THE FRIEDRICH FRANZ IV.

of a similar train ferry across the English Channel. According to the London corres- pondent of the "Petit Parisien," an Anglo- French combination with the title of the In t er- Con ti nen t al. Railway Company has taken the matter in hand, and among those inter- ested in the scheme are said to be some of the most powerful corporations in the railway and shipbuilding worlds. The ferryboats will take the trains and their contents on board at Dover, carry them across the Channel, and deposit them at Calais. There are several advantages of the ferryboat system, one of which is that time will be saved—an import- ant consideration in the case of flowers, fruit, vegetables, and dairy produce. France hopes that the markets of Newcastle, Edinburgh, and Glasgow, hitherto untouched, will be reached by the French producer, and it is hoped that much of the merchandise which at present passes by Ostend, Antwerp, Flushing, and Hamburg will be diverted to the ,ferryboats between Calais and Dover.

div.head: ISLE OF MAN AS A NAVAL BASE.
div.p: THE ISLE OF MAN AS A NAVAL BASE.

There are rumours of a proposal to establish an Admiralty station in the Isle of Man— It is said that the Coastguards have been required to furnish the authorities with full information with regard to Douglas and Ramsey, the chief ports, and details as to anchorage and landing accommodation for men and gun, postal and telegraphic facilities, engineering works and
THE TWO SUGGESTED PORTS.

foundries, water supply, and victualling have been supplied. Since those details were re- ceived, the Admiralty have commissioned Admiral Rice to inspect and report upon the two ports. Ramsey has the best anchorage of any Manx port, and is sheltered from all but north-east winds, while Douglas is the largest town, and is only exposed to south-east windsJ Douglas has also daily communication with England throughoutthe yeard

div.head: NORTHERN UNION LEAGUE.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION LEAGUE.
FIRST DIVISION.
WARRINGTON WIN AT BROUGHTON.

Warrington paid a visit to Broughton on Saturday and somewhat surprised everybody by defeating the Rangers on their own ground. The weather was excel- lent, and a very fast game was witnessed by 5,000 people. Warrington were short of Harris, Morrison, and Cook, and the Rangers missed Jewitt from the pack. Other- wise the teams were representative. Mr. J. H. Smith was the referee and the:players lined out in the following order:

Warrington—Hallam full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Foster, threenuarters ; Davies and Mahoney, half backs; Boardman, Lunt, Swift, Edmond- son, Jolly, Thomas, Harmer, and Naylor, forwards. Broughton Rangers—Poole, back; Widdeson, Harry Wilson, and Hogg, threequarter backs; W. James and Riley, half backs; Trotter, Beetham, Whitehead, Scott, Ruddick, Templeton, Winskill and Warwick, forwards. Dickenson started and after exchanges the Rangers obtained the advantage, Hogg racing down touch in the first few minutes. Hallam effected a fine tackle or the wing man would have scored. Davies relieved cleverly with the aid of touch and play landed at centre, where Dickenson was prominent, but failed to get clear. Mahoney got cleverly away and ran almost to the line where he passed, the ball being mulled by the forwards. Fish also missed a nice pass from the same source, and then Wilson and Hogg came down on the right with a rush, but found Fish too many for them. Warrington soon worked their way back notwithstanding a stiffish breeze, and Wilson attempting to reply screwed the ball to the centre, where Diokenson dashed up and ran clean through to score in nice position. Poole came across but was badly outpaced. Fish landed a goal. The re- verse aroused the home lot, who kept pegging away on Hogg's wing, but they never eluded Fish. Warrington attacked again, Harry relieving with a smart run and pass to Widdeson. The latter fielded neatly, got past Forsteriand finally ran in a clever try from his own half, W. James missing a :somewhat easy goal shot. Half- time : Warrington 5 points ; Rangers 3 points. On resuming play for a time was rather dull, until Willie James staved off an attack by the visitors, and giving Wilson possession, that player put in a good run to the Warrington "25 "flag. Here he was tackled by Hallam, who at full back played a brilliant game. Play was soon taken baok again into the Ranger's territory, where Davies made an attempt to drop at goal without sncoess. Willie James tried vainly to get past Hallam while Wilson had opportunities presented him, but he spoiled them by failing to pass to his wing man, Hogg. For Warrington, Hallam, Isherwood and Fish tackled splendidly, and were the means of keeping the home men out. Result:—Warrington 1 goal and 1 try (5 points), Broughton Rangers 1 try (3 points).

div.head: WIDNES v. SALFORD.
div.p: WIDNES v. SALFORD.

At Widnes, before 3,000 spectators. Salford won the toss, and Widnes had to face a strong wind and a brilliant sun. There was nothing of interest in the first few minutes, and then Thomas and Lomas got away, and the latter looked like scoring when he was brought down by Peacock. A long kick by Tilley and a mall by Red- ford gave Wailing a chance, and when a few yards from the line he was pushed into touch by Smith. When the play:was at centre Lomas received a pass, and beating all his opponents scored behind the posts. The same player kicked a goal. From the kick-out.Salford were soon on the attack again, and just before the interval Harter scored a second try. Lomas failed at the goal kick. Half-time score :—Salford, 1 goal and 1 tries (8 points). Widnes nil. Early on in the second half Widnes had the best 4of matters, and a neat bit of play by Lally (*enabled Wail- ing to get away, but Lomas was too speedy for him,and he was pushed into touch. After this the play was fast and exciting, but the home backs could not get going. It looked as if nothing further was going to be scored when the Salford forwards broke away from their own line, and Norris picked up the ball smartly and scored behind the posts. Lomas placed a goal. Result : Salford 2 goals and 3 tries (13 points). Widnes nil. Salford.—Smith, back,- Norris, Lomas, Thomas, and Bedford.threequarters ; Harter and Preston, half backs; Rhapps, Tunney, Heath, Williams, Buckler,Shore,Brown, and _Shaw forwards.

Widnes.—Tilley, back ; Aspey, Peacock, Taylor, and Wailing, three-quarters; Kennedy and Lally, half backs; Curtis, M'Cabe, Lynch, Leyshon, Power,Rigby,Webster, and McDonald, forwards. Referee, Mr. B. Ashton, Oldham. Touch judges, Messrs. J. H. Houghton,-.St. Helens, and T. Barnes, Warrington.

div.head: SWINTON v. RUNCORN.
div.p: SWINTON v. RUNCORN.

Although the weather was fine at Swinton, there was only a moderate attendance, numbering 3,000 people. Butterworth started for Runcorn, and Swinton attacked Houghton being brought down on the line. Richardson effected a clearance, and then off-side play by Tickle Jet in the visitors, and Jolley and Richardson put in a nice bout of passing, which Wallwork was successful in breaking up. Next Moran was prominent, but he lost the ball. Butterworth, however, a minute later got possession, and making for the line, looked all over a scorer. Chorley saved the situation just in the nick of time. Half-time araived with no score.

On resuming, Swintonsgained a footing in thevisitors' territory, and Evans from a penalty made a fruitless effort to land a goal. The forward work on both sides was fairly even, but Swinton appeared to get possession oftener from the scrummage than did Runcorn. Jolley eventually made a mark for Runcorn near the centre. Houghton kicked a goal. Swinton tried hard to score close to time, but failed. _ _
Result:—R7uneorn 1 goal (2 points), Swinton nil. Teams:—

Swinton—Chorloy, back; Oldfleld, Wallwork, DiXOR, and Hampson, three-quarter backs; Morgan mad Critch, half backs; Evans, Simister, Coletrup, Yates, Pomfret, Burrows, Tickie,and Cheethlm, forwards. Runcorn—Houghton, back; Moran, Butterworth, Price, and Jones, three-quarter backs; Rickardson and Jolley, half backs; Walker, Moulton, Langley, Tomlin- son;Richardson, Messenger, Woods and Poole,forwards. Referee, Mr. McCritcheon, Oldham. Touch-judgee, Messrs. R. Shaw, Tyldesley, and F. Little, St. Helens.

div.head: OLDHAM v. WIGAN.
div.p: OLDHAM v. WIGAN.

These teams met at Oldham, and a fast, bright game ended in an easy vi,ptory for the home team. There were about 5,000 spectators on the stands wheat Prater started against a strong breeze. Wigan attacked for a short time and forced a dead ball. Thexksome smart passing between Goodman, Dixon, and Civil ended in Goodman getting a short return pass and he scored, Ferguson failing at the kick. Spottiswoode, on the one wing, and Civil, on the other, each added another try before the intsrval. Olilhana were penalised for off-side soon after their first score, and Mason kicked a goal. The Wigan men pressed very hard during the third quer- •ter,but could not cross the line, and before the finish Spottiewoode again scored for Oldham, Frater adding the goal. Final :—Oldham, one goal and four tries (14 points); Wigan, one goal (two points).

div.head: KEIGHLEY v. BATLEY.
div.p: KEIGHLEY v. BATLEY.
At Keighley, before a goosl crowd. The game ended in a draw—two goals and one try (seven points). W. Davies scored all the points for Batley.
HUNSLET v. LEIGH.

At Hunslet, before 6,000 spectators. Hunslet were the first to attack, securing a minor point. Lees inter- cepted a pass and Hunslet had to defend. Ramage secured from a scrummage and rushed ever, scoring a try, which A. Goldthorpe converted. Play settled at centre for a short time, passing taking operations to the visitors' line. From the ensuing scrummage Goldthorpe dropped a goal. Result :—Hunslet, two goals and one try (seven points) ; Leigh, nothing.

div.head: HUDDERSFIELD v. HULL.
div.p: HUDDERSFIELD v. HULL.

The play in the first half of this match- at Hudders- field was of quite an interesting character. Harry ran in two tries for Hull,and Jackson also scored. Chambers scored an unconverted•try for Huddersfield, the interval arriving with Hull leading by 13 points to three. Final :—Hull, two goals and three tries (13 points); Huddersfield, one goal and two tries (eight points).

div.head: HULL KINGSTON ROVERS v. LEEDS.
div.p: HULL KINGSTON ROVERS v. LEEDS.
Leeds started strongly in this match at Hull, the backs doing fine work. Final :—Leeds, two goals and two tries (10 points) ; Rovers, one try (three points). HALIFAX v. BRADFORD,

At Halifax. Mosby kicked a penalty goa I for Bradford in the first half,and soon after change of end sMallinson scored a try for Halifax, which Wedgwood improved, following which Hadwen got over as the result of a fine rush, and Sinton obtained a try in the corner, this being the extent of the scoring. Halifax won by one goal and two tries (eight points) to one goal and one try (five points).

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
WARRINGTON "A" DEFEATED AT WILDERSPOOL. •

Warrington "A "sustained their first defeat of the season on Saturday when Broughton Rangers "A " visited the Wilderspool enclosure. There would be about 2,000 spectators present when Knight kicked off against the wind. In the opening stages Warrington pressed. The visitors were penalized but Knight made a very poor attempt at goal. Eventually Brooks broke away in fine style and passed to Watburton. This player transferred to Roberts and he in turn to Wat- kins who scored easily. Knight's kick at goal was unsuc- cessful. The visitors now became aggressive and Orarn made a plucky effort but was pulled up in time. Knight effected a capital save. Several smart passing move- ments were initiated but came to nothing. Warrington had a free kick but the visitors returned briskly and Worthington was unfortunate in not kick- ing a penalty goal. Bailey got possession and dashed away in grand style but stepped into touch when evading Jackson. Broughton continued to invade the home quarters, and Knight was injured in tackling, but was soon able to resume. Bailey again made an excellent attempt, but was tackled near the line. Soon afterwards Worthington kicked a penalty goal. Half-time: Warrington, one try (three points) ; Broughton Rangers, one goal (two points). In the second half, Knight failed in two penalty kicks, and Brooks tried hard to get over but was grassed. A fine passing movement resulted in Bails( scoring easily for the Rangers. Worthington added the extra points. The Rangers now carried all before them, and tries were scored by Bailey and Harris. Worthington kicked two goals. Final score: Broughton Rangers, 4 goals, 3 tries (17 points) ; Warrington, 1 try (3 points).
