div.head: • RUNCEN RURAL LESTRICT COUNCIL. .
div.p: • RUNCEN RURAL LESTRICT COUNCIL. .
The Water Question.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday morning under the • pre- sidency of Mr. S. Woodward. There were also pre- sent :—Admiral Jones-Parry,Messrs. G. Pilling, J. Dar- lington, T. Wright, T. Baxter, J. Moseley Williams, C. E. Liaaker, C. Roylance, J. Mounfleld, A. G. Guest, J. T. Collier, J. B. Chadwick, J. Edwards, T. Clarke, J. Spruce J. Stokes, with Dr. Adams (medical officer of health), Messrs. G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk),J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances), J. Swinton and W. Diggle (surveyors).

119.LT0N WELTER SUPPLY. At a meeting of Halton Parochial Committee it was resolved that the Clerk to the Rural Council be reques- ted to report to the Committee with reference to the proposed improved water supply, as early as practicable. The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: LIGHT WANTED,
div.p: LIGHT WANTED,
The Weston Parochial Committee resolved that a sub- committee be appointed to consider the advisability and practicability of lighting the parish. The Council approved the minutes. GIFT OF LAND.

It was reported that Messrs. White, Maclver and Co., had written on behalf of Sir Gilbert Greenall, stating that he failed to see anynecessity for reducing the bend in the road at Daresbury, but he would be prepared to give a little land to the road at the side of the old cottage, and also a strip of land a little to the oast. The Highways Committee recommended that the offer be accepted.

Mr. Darlington was under the impression that the Council would have to build a new wall, and he did not think it would be worth going to that expense to secure a strip of land about 18 inches wide. Mr. Swinton said the Council wouldnot have to incur any expense. The minutes were approved.

div.head: PRODSHA.M-DELAMERE ROAD.
div.p: THE PRODSHA.M-DELAMERE ROAD.

The Clerk reported that the sub-committee appointed to meet a sub-committee of the Northwich District Council with regard to the Frodsham to Delamere Station-road had met. They recommended the Council to join' the Northwich authority in an application to the County Council te take over the road if suitable terms could be arranged. Terms had been drawn up and it was resolved that the clerk make formal application to the County Council as suggested. This course was approved. _ PRECEPTS ON THE OVERSEERS.
The Clerk was instructed to sign precepts on the overseers for the ensuing half year.
THE WATER QUESTION.

The Clerk said he wished to present a report on certain negotiations which had passed between that Council and the Runcorn Urban District Council. They would remember that shortly after the County. Council inquiry at Runcorn, that Council called upon the Urban Council te sell their water mains in the parishes of Halton and Weston and to appoint an arbitrator for till:: purpose. The Urban Council replied making (certain suggestions that instead of selling the mains(they themves should supply the districts. The District Conncillitupointed a committee to negotilte with them to see if terms could be arrived at. Those negotiations fell through. The Urban Council were again called upon to appoint an arbitrator, and the District Council Committee laid further suggestions before thorn by which the Council should purchase the mains within the parishes and if their suggestions were accepted certain alterations might be made by which either the District Council should lay a main to Weston and Halton and supply the Urban Council or the Urban Council should lay a main and supply the Rural District Council. A letter con- taining the Council's suggestions was forwarded and that morning he received a reply from the Clerk te the Urban Council stating that that authority was prepared to enter into an agreement on the lines mentioned in sug- gestion number 1. The effect was that the Urban Coun- cil would lay the main to the Runcorn reservoir to supply Halton with waterat 7d. per 1,000 gallons at the Halton reservoir and Weston at a point near to the Runcorn sreservoir.
The Chairman remarked that he was appointed chair- man of the Water Committee and he had now pleasure in moving that the proposed agreement be approved by the Council.
Mr. Wright seconded, and:the proposition was agreed to.

THE INSPECTOR OF NUISANCES. The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the re-appointment of Mr. Farrington as inspector of nuisances, and also sanctioning the payment of £5 to the inspector for extra work in connection with the small-pox epidemic.
TUBERCULOSIS IN CATTLE. PROPOSED COMPENSATION SCHEME.

The Clerk reported the receipt of a letter from the Rural District Council of Wells asking the Council to consider a memorial to the Local Government Reardon the above question, and, if they could see their way, to support it or present a similar one. The memorial was as fellows :—" That in the opinion of this Council grave injustice is inflicted upon agriculturalists and others in the heavy losses sustained by the destroying of animals pronounced to be suffering from tuberculosis or other disease, when sold or bought for the purposes of human consumption. That in the experience of your m2morialists it often happens that in many cases animals are sent or received for slaughter in apparent health, and yet at the time of slaughter may be prontunced to be suffering from tuberculosis or other disease, the knowledge of which the sender er purchaser could not possibly be cognisant. That your memorialists feel that inasmuch as these animals are condemned in the interests of public health, the person upon whom such loss now falls (invariably the farmer as producer) should not be mulcted in such undue severity by being deprived of all compensation as at present. Your memorialists therefore consider that the Local Government Board should compensate those persons as described, when such meat is seized by the Government Inspector and found to be diseased, when satisfactory proof has been given that the person or personeso disposing of the said animal or animals are innocent of the existence of any such disease at the time of such disposal, and strongly urge the Local Government Board to7issue an order or promote legislation in the manner indicated." Mr. Antwiss moved that the council support the memorial.

Mr. Baxter seconded. He pointed out that many cattle had to be destroyed when they were net unfit for human food and gave very goad milk, jnst to please the fad of the public who thought they were likely to cause consumption. Farmers ought not to be expected to destroy cattle without receiving compensation. Mr. Stokes supported. He was of the opinion that if acompensation scheme could be arranged,it would do away with a very great deal of the selling of milk from unsound cows.

The Chairman was of the opinion that the memorial did not affect the farmers very much. He was entirely with the previous speakers on the matter but he thought they wanted something that went further. He sug- gested that the question be referred to the Parlia- mental,' Committee. Mr. haxt,..r : It seems to be a question for the butchers rather than for us. Continuing he said there had been cases at Warrington in particular where a butcher had given a good price for a cow which appeared to be healthy and had had to be destroyed because it wassuffering from tuberculosis. It was almost ruinous to small butchers not to receive compensation. After further discussion it was decided to support the memorial but only seven members voted on the matter—six for and one against.

div.head: PRESTON BROOK WATER 'PPLY.
div.p: PRESTON BROOK WATER 'PPLY.

The Clerk read a letter from Messrs. John White Maciver and Co., Warrington, stating that they were anxious that something should be done in connection with the water supply to Preston Brook and would be glad to know if the District Council intended taking any steps in the matter. Preston Brook was not in the Warrington Corporation area, but they believed the Corporation would give a supply if required. They sup- posed it was in the Liverpool CorpQration area, but they understood that body would not supply Preston Brook if they could possibly avoid it. The Warrington Corporation main extended as far as Daresbnry Vicar- age a,epresent, and they were making arrangements to continue it as far as" The Oaklands " from which place to Preston Brook was not a very great distance. Mr. Spruce said Warrington water was already being supplied to Daresbnry and it would not be a big under- taking to extend the main to Preston Brook. Mr. Linaker pointed out that one portion of the village was much nearer to the Sutton supply. He thought the matter should be deferred until it had been decided what to do in regard to the water supply to the new isolation hospital at Dutton. , It was decided that the matter should be considered , by the Isolation Hospital sub-committee with the addi- tion of Mr. Spruce.
STOCKTON HEAT If STREET-MAKING.

The following tenders for the making of Kimberley- drive and Dundonald-avenue, itockeon Heath, were opened :—Bennie and Thompson, Warrington, Kimber- ley-drive, £249 15s 9d • Dundonald-avenue, £376 4s. 6d.; William Owen'and Henry Garner, Latchford, Kimberley • Drive, £242 is. 7d.; Dtmdonald Avenue, £378 16s 4d.; Mitchell and Son, Manchegter, Kimberley Drive, £265; Dundonald Avenue, £380; Thomas Stringer, Warrington, Kimberley Drive, £244 is.; Dundonald Avenue, £375 13s. lid.; Frank Hayes, Stock- port, Kimberley Drive, £306 4s. 10d.; Dundonald Avenue, £465 us. Id.; .T. Dale, Northwich, Kimberley Drive, £268 ss. Bd. • Dundonald Avenue, £495 is. Id.; Frank Warburton, Stockton Heath, Kimberley Drive, £297 6s. Bd.; Dundonald Avenue, £444 18s.; F. W. Wright, Warrington, Kimberley Drive, £246; Dun- donald Avenue, £3Bl 10s. it was decided to accept Mr. Stringer's tender.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH__ NIGHTSOICCONTRACT.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH__ NIGHTSOICCONTRACT.
The seal of the Council was affixed to a contract entered into by Mr. Richard Miller for the removal of nightsoil at Stockton Heath.
WEASTE _LANE, THELWALL.

, Mr. Linaker reported that a sub-committee had met that morning and had considered the question of appor- tioning the expenditure on the works at Weaste-lane. The total cost of the works carried out was £362195. Bd. and the committee recommended the following appor-

1 . tionment:—Thelwall,£l4l Ils. Bd. ;Grappenhall £56 Ifs general district rate for highway improvements, £lO7 16s. ; Messrs. Lorin' or the trustees of the estate £56 15s. 1 An a meeting of Highways Committee the Clerk I reported that he had received several letters from Mr. • R. A. Naylor's solicitors with regard to the widening of Weaste Lane, Thelwall. The work had now been pro- ceeded with and they asked the Council to pay their ' costs. It was resolved that the clerk inform Mr. , Naylor's Solicitors that the council cannot accept i liability for costs incurred by him. This apportionment was agreed to. MEDICAL OFFICER AND DISINFECTION.

The Chairman said that the Medical Officer of Health *l presented a most excellent report on the subject of dMinfection and the matter had been carefully explained in committee. Dr. Adams practically told them that their present system of disinfecting rooms, while not altogether useless, was for all practical purposes, in dealing with some very severe forms of disease, not at all effective. He suggested systems which were much more efficient and ivhich would not of necessity be very much more costly. The report was adopted, and a copy will be sent to each member of the Council.
PROFESSOR DELEPINE'S REPORT.
Admiral Jones-Parry asked if the charge for Professor Delepine's report was included in the amount mentioned for the work at Weaste-lane.
Mr. Linaker replied in the negative. The Clerk said the cost of the report would be It general charge on the whole of the district. The County Council would pay half.

div.head: ALLEGED- BREACH OF EYE-LAWS.
div.p: THE ALLEGED- BREACH OF EYE-LAWS.

Mr. Linaker statAd that with regard to the conver- sion of the premises of Messrs. Lloyd, Church-street, Frodsham, from a shop into a dwelling-house, the Parochial Committee had decided to leave:it to the Dis- trict Council to pass the plans or otherwise. He con- tended that the plans were still contrary to the bye- Jaws.

It was decided that a sub-committee should inspect the premises, Mr. Williams remarking that the bye-laws had frequently been disobeyed at Frodsham. STOCKTON HEATH'S REPRESENTATION. Mr. Piling informed the Council that the sub-com- mittee appointed to consider this question recommen- ded that steps be taken to secure an additional Coun- cillor for Stockton Heath, the reasons that influenced them being the increased population and ratable value. There was at present a population of 3,326, with an assessment of £11,033. He proposed that the decision be confirmed.
Mr. Meunfield seconded, and said Stockton Heath was growing very rapidly. Between 30 and 40 houses were now in course of erection.

Admiral Jones-Parry said he understood from the newspapers that the Stockton Heath Committee had said they would leave that Council unless the application was granted. The Chairman said no such threat had been made to the Council.

Admiral Parry moved that the application be refused. He contended that Stockton Heath gave the Council too much work, and roads were being ruined because tho Surveyor could not attend to them in addition to Stockton Heath property. There was no seconder to the motion.

Mr. Pilling remarked that when the committee was sitting one of the overseers and one of the members of the Parochial Committee said that no such remarks as had been mentioned had ever fallen from thoir lips. The committee's decision was approved. FINANCE.
Mr.'Wright-reported that a balance of £1790 18s 3d was brought forward from the September accouut and the cheques drawn that day amounted to £392 12s 10d, making a total of £2183 us id.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE. DISTRICT.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE. DISTRICT.

Dr. Adams reported CMOs of scarlet fever at Dares- bury, Hatton, Newton by Daresbury, and Latchford and a case of diphtheria at„lialton. The schools at Kinsley had been closed for three weeks in consequence of an epidemic of whooping cough. This was all the businms of public interest.

div.head: 6,000 CHRISTIANS MASSACRED.
div.p: 6,000 CHRISTIANS MASSACRED.

The recent atrocities in the East remind one forcibly of the "year of terror," in which over 6,000 Christians were massacred. While in or Western countries we escape such horrors, thousands of lives are sacrificed annually through preventible diseases. Charles Forde'n bile beans are a preventive as well as a cure of indiges- tion, yet in many quarters they are not yet used; and every year over a million people die of indigestion and allied ailments. Mr. J. B. Egerton, of Booker Hill, Lymm, Cheshire, might have been one of these victims, had it not been-for bile beans.

Here is his experience:—"For five years I was a great sufferer from indigestion, biliousness, and the many ailments which arise from those terrible complaints. The pain I have gone through from. sifting and irregu- larity of the bowels, I can never describe, nor ever forget. I had doctors to 'attend me; I took many medicines, but all to no purpose. Three of my doctors gave'me a little relief,but it was not at all lasting. The last doctor said there was'no chance for me except to go away for complete rest.. Well, bile beans cured me completely, however, without going away. I found there was no necessity to incur expense and lose my business as well, in order to be cured. I heard of bile beans from a friend who had suffered from indigestion, and had been cured by them. "That was six months ago. I got a supply, and com- menced to take them at once. Candidly, at first I was in doubt as to whether they would do me good or not, but when I was well into the second box there was no longerany doubt. They put my system into order, sad my general health improved from day to day. I con- tinued improving in condition. The indigestion, biliousness, and all the pains ceased, and some months ago now I found myself cured." Bile beans which worked this great core, are obtainable fromall Chemists at one-and-three-halfpence and two-and-nine per box. Avoid all substitutes and preparations which are offered as being "just as good."
General Hunter and Warrington Recruits.

The following is an extract from the evidence of General Hunter before the Royal Commission on the war :—At the present time, from what classes are the recruits mostly got in Scotland? DJ they come from the scum of the few big towns ?—We get the worst class of recruit, physically, from Dundee. I cannot tell you why. I have ask.ed ministers ; I have asked missionaries ; and I have asked the local medical authorities in Dundee, and all the magistrates, and so on, but whether it is water or not I cannot tell you. Anyhow, the people who live in Warrington in Lancashire (I belong to a Lancashire regiment, and all our recruits in the regiment were either miners or mill hands) and work in the mills under the same conditions of life exactly as the people who live in Dundee, were of nothing like the inferior quality that these Dundee boys are. Whether it is from early marriages, or whether, as some people say, it is be- cause they no longer sup their porridge, but live on bread and butter and the tea-pot ; whether it is the want of milk, or the want of meal, or the want of lime in the water, or what it is, I cannot tell you, but the fact remains that they are the worst.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
OCTOBER 10th 1903.

THE reception accor- THE MORAL OF ded to Mr. CHAMBER- GLASGOW. LAIN'S proposals can scarcelybe called encour- aging. Some confusion in the telegraphic summary on Tuesday night made his figures at first seem more eccentric than they actually were, but they are eccentric enough. The magician who said he could summon spirits from the vasty deep was not more confident than Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. There is no reason to suppose that the spirits came when they were called, and none to suppose that figures will obey Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S command SO IS to furnish the beautiful surplus which is to banish dull care from the home of the taxpayer. With a moderation which astonishes Mr. ALFRED HARMS- WORTH our new wizard proposes to levy only a 10 per* cent. duty on foreign manufactured goods. Whether such partially-manufactured articles as serve the uses of raw material for our own pro- ducers are to be exempted we are not yet per- mitted to know. But 10 per cent. is to yield £9,000,000, and when the loss entailed by the reduction of duties on tea and so forth, is made good, there will be a balance of nearly £6,250,000, wherewith Mr. AUSTIN CHAMBERLAIN, glowing with the paternal ardour for the general weal, is to gladden all our hearts by taking off taxes. Des anybody except the wizard himself really believe in all this? Does the taxpayer look forward impatiently to the time when he will sit under his roof-tree sipping Australian wine and watching the figures of his household expenditure grow small by degrees and beautifully less ? Mr. CHAMBERLAIN says nothing about wool, but it appears tnat he hopes to conciliate Australia , by giving her a preference on her wines. We would not for worlds cast an aspersion on those robust and potent liauors. But the taxpayer who takes, like TIMOTHY, a little wine for the sake of the organ which Mr. BARRIE calls his "Little Mary" has been taught to prefer the lighter vint- ages of France and the Mine. He may not feel Nual to the Imperial task of drinking for the sake of Australia; and if foreign wines are made even dearer than they are he may give up wine-bibbing 6altogether. The Austealian grape, flourishes on a foil which has the properties of iron—but that is ‘o sufficient reason why the iron should enter into he taxpayer's soul! The Commonwealth may reflect seriously upon this before it consents to give a preference to British manufactures. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is certain, of course, that he can persuade the Colonies to reduce their duties on Our goods, and thus enable us to oust the foreign competitor, and convince the Colonial com- petitor that he is a very lucky man. We cannot discern the slightest indication of any such disposi- tion in the Australian mind. The Canadian manu- facturer has made it pretty plain that the preference already accorded;to us in his market,and not very stimulating to our trade, as compared with the American trade, is as far as he will go. Why the Colonial Protectionist should embrace the opportunity offered him by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN to let in a flood of British goods, and seriously check the development of his own mono- polies, we are unable to define. The Colonial Protectionist is not in our judgment a very sound economist, but he has hitherto maintained the definite principle that his own business is of the highest importance to the com- merce Of his Colony. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN • ECM seeks to prove to him that Imperial unity is of the highest importance, and that it must be achieved by an operation from which his particular business will suffer. What ground is there in human nature for the expectation that this coun- sel will prevail? The danger is that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S zeal will multiply the obstacles in the way of Imperial unity instead of dispersing them. He tells our working men that his plan will create employment and good wages for up- wards of 400,000 more of them than are earning wages now. A more audacious pledge was never given. It rests upon a hypothesis so visionary that no trade-unionist can really believe that it possesses any substance. Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN assumes that his 10 per cent. duty on foreign manufactures will give an immediate stimulus to our home industries, and set employers clamouring for more labour. He does not propose this duty as a palliative for the mischief of foreign competition ;he sees in it a positive and permanent benefit. It is suggested that if the duty should have the effect of lowering foreign tariffs Mr. CHAMBERLAIN will be compelled to repeal it,and the revenue will suffer accordingly But that is not his idea at all. He is now frankly a Protectionist ; and if the duty,which is so trivial that it pains the economic soul of Mr.TIARMSWOUTH should not stir our employers to call for 400,000 willing conscripts for heir factories, Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN will give the screw anether turn. The duty will be increased, and the country will be invited to resort to all the devices of the Protectionist gamblers, who are always trying to throw double- sixes with the dice-box. With the consequences of such an enterprise so clearly before them ,the working classes will not let themselves be c ajoled. TN) DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE has better reason than ever for thinking himself 'well out ofia Cabinet, the head of which is bound by the closest political and personal ties to the spirit of the Glasgow speech.
YESTERDAY was pub MR. MORLEY'S lished Mr. MoßLEy's " GLADSTONE." Biography of Glad-

stone—such a monu- ment, we "believe, as literature has never raised before to the memory of a great statesman. Readers who remember his monograph on Burke know how peculiarly fitted Mr. MORLEY is for any work which demands fine appreciation of political issues and a large philosophical grasp. His study of CROMWELL is a masterpiece of judicial temper,con- trasting eminently in that regard with the lyrical frenzy of Carlyle. But in many ways it was easie

to write about CROMWELL and BURKE than to write about GLADSTONE. Consider the sheer physical magnitude of the task. It is not too much to say that for upwards of forty years Mr. GLAD- stone was the political history of England, a com- manding figure in its religions history, and an in- fluence and a presence inseparable from all manner of national questions and social interests. The very name of GLADSTONE filled the world. He was the fcremost champion of ideals to which not his own countrymen alone, but all the civilised people, vibrated with passionate emotion. "The grand eternal commonplaces of liberty and self-government," Mr. MORLEY tells us, possessed GLADSTONE'S soul with as great intensity as his religious faith. There is an aneedote,known to but few people, which brings out this character- istic with startling force. "If I had to choose," said GLADSTONE on one occasion, " between Divine revelation and human freedom, I should choose human freedom." It was his love of freedom which made his name beloved in all the dark places of oppression wherever men, struggling for common human rights, waited for that clarion voice to give them the word of hope. In his own country his plume waved trium- phantly in all the battles of reform for half a century. There was one great department of thought that was closed to him—the constitution of his mind turned him away from science. But in all else he was in constant and active sympathy with the spirit of his time. His personality wasp% stimulus to toilers in many fields. We are not surprised to learn that his biographer has had to consult between two and three thousand docu- ments bearing upon the multiform energies of this wonderful career. The marvel of Mr. MORLEY'S book is that it handles this huge mass of material with such consummate skill that the story is unfolded without apparent effort ; nothing is overwrought or overlooked ; and we see the life of this great man in admirable proportion and perspective.

It is curious that an illustrious personage should have thought it necessary to warn Mr. MonLEY at the outset of his enterprise. Queen VICTORIA sent him a message impressing upon him strongly that he should not handle the work "in the narrow way of party." "This injunction," says Mr. MORLEY "represents my own clear view of the spirit in which the history 9f a career so memorable as Mr. GLADSTONE'S should be composed. That, to be sure, is not at all inconsistent with our regarding party feeling in its honourable sense, as entirely the reverse of an infirmity." Mr. MORLEY does not strike his political flag at any crisis: but never have the maturity and breadth of his mind, and the fine dignity and restraint of his style, been more conspicuously manifested than in his treatment of the stormiest passages of political controversy. When he comes to the period in which he was GLADSTONE'S most intimate associate in a policy which broke so many personal ties, and inflamed animosities to the highest pitch, he is more than ever the grave and temperate historian, alive to the errors and miscalculations on his own side,and yet abating no jot of allegiance to the cause. In dramatic interest his story of the first Home Rule Bill could easily be surpassed. We are taken behind the scenes of the great conflict, and shown the multiplicity of secret difficulties with which GLADSTONE'S genius and daring had to cope. Two memorable interviews between the great English and the great Irish Parliamentarians give us a sensation of the nervous tension of that excitlng time. PARNELL strove to convert Mr. GLADSTONE sto his view of the financial relations between England and Ireland; and at the end of a keen de- bate, in which neither would give way,the Minister left Mr. MoaLEY's room muttering, "Very clever, very clever !" He had met a disputant whom he could not conquer. The bill, says Mr. MORLEY, even had it reached the Committee stage woull have been wrecked on this issue by a will which was as strong as GLADSTONE'S. The book abounds in:episodes equally dramatic and moment- ous. The failures are recorded as impartially as the triumphs. What Mr. MORLEY calls the "unedifying ",chapter which ended with the death of GORDON is analysed as frankly as the psycho- logical weakness which led GLADSTONE to uphold his consistency in all his changes of opinion. But when all deductions have been made, the man and his achievements shine out of this biography with nndimned splendour. He ennobled political life: he left transcendant deeds on the Statute-book ; he was the mightiest personal force that ever stitred the mind and heart of his country. What men may come after him to rival his genius we have yet to learn ; but when we think of him laying the foundations of that financial prosperity which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and MT. BALFOUR are now pre- suming to dismiss as "a vain farce," the contrast is between the beneficent giant and the meddle- some pigmies.

The Mayoralty of the Borough is still an open question. Councillor Pierpoint declined the in- vitation extended to him by a deputation from the Town Council on Tuesday afternoon, and courteously gave his reasons. The most important of these was that he did not think it desirable the new Mayor should be selected until after the November elections. One in almost involuntarily compelled to exclaim "hear, hear." This view of the matter is honest and manly, and does Coun- cillor Pierpoint infinite credit. He could not have emphasized it more effectively had he spoken for a year on the subject, and we are sure the rate- payers will appreciate the sacrifice Mr. Pierpoint has made in their interests. It is only common fairness that the newly-elected members,possessing a direct mandate from the burgesses, should have a voice in the selection of the Chief Magistrate of the Borough. In consequence of Councillor Pier- point's action, the Mayoralty will probably remain undecided until after November Ist, when we cordially hope a second equally unanimous invita- tion will be extended to him ; and that, though "a busy man," he may then see his way clear to accept the office.

Direct labour representation was the text round which several interesting and significant speeches I were woven at the labour demonstration in Parr Hall on Tuesday. The local men were well backed up by Mr. Shackleton, and Mr. A. Hendersou M.P., the recent victor at the Barnard Castle bye- election, and an excellent case was made out for the object in view. We are strongly in favour of direct labour representation ourselves, believing, that it will tend very largely to the up- lifting, and educating of the working-classes. There is not a single argument worth the description why labour should hot have a voice on the administrative bodies of the country. The awakening of interest in their own affairs and the affairs of their country is to be heartily welcomed among the democracy, and there is no more strik- ing sign of the times than the activity among working-class organisations. Tuesday's demon stration was a credit to the Labour cause in War rington and we believe it will have the best results. Reference was made not only to labour representa- tion on our Town Council, but in the House of Commons. Why should not Warrington have a labour candidate P was a question voiced by Mr. Henderson, M.P., and it is one that

may have to be seriously considered in the near future, judging by present-day indica— tions. We believe, l-aoreover, that Mr. A. IL Crosfield, the prospective Liberal candidate, would be the first to take a broad view of the matter, because he has decided democratic sympathies. Mr. Shackleton, M.P, advised his hearers, if they could not get a labour candidate pure and simple, to do the next best thing. and that is, we .take it, to support the Liberal candi- date if his views affecting labour are, in the main, acceptable to Labour men. This is sound advice, which we have pleasure in endorsing. The future of Liberalism appears to us to be inseparably associated with the onward march of Labour. A fusion of the two forces is necessary if either is to succeed, though, perhaps, Labour could get along without Liberalism. We are certain, however, that Liberalism cannot afford to ignore Labour, and there is no reason why there should not be a genuine rappochement between the two. Their interests are in the main indentical, and it will be a happy day for all but our Conser- vativa friends when the two parties come to a workable understanding. In the meantime vm wish Mr. F. Stott well in his candidature for Orford Ward.

In a little more than three weeks the municipal election, will be over. In Warrington we are promised a contest in every ward so that it is time we knew the selected candidates. Rumours are as plentiful as blackberries respecting the prospective candidates but very little of a definite character has been divulged. The first candidate to enter the field with his election address is Mr. James Povey, who is opposing the return of Councillor Hulse in Fairfield Ward. Mr. Povey comes before the electors as a man of experience in municipal matters, he having been a member of the St. Helens Town Council prior to his removal to Warrington for business purposes. Five Liberals retire from the Council, and two of them have already informed their ward committees that they do not intend to seek re-election. These two gentlemen are Councillor William Roberts,who retires from the representa- tion of St. Austin's ward, and Councillor F. R. Roberts, who for six years has sat as one of the representatives of St. John's Ward. The St. Austin's Ward Committee approached Mr. Ewart with the view to his becoming the candidate, but on his refusal, Mr. Arthur Browne was asked to stand, and he has promised to give his decision within a few days. Last evening the St. John's Ward Committee discussed the situation, but decided to take no action for the present. The Non-Trading committee have a host of candidates but it is improbable that they will oppose the return of Councillor Barton in Whitecross ward or Councillor Pierpoint in Bewsey ward. As an indication of the trend of events the remarks of Alderman Sutton at the meeting of the Conservative Association are worth noting. "All Conservatives are now Non-Traders," says the Alderman in effect, and if a Non-Trading candidate happens to be a Conservative;thenConservatives are at liberty to support him. Evidently the designation ",Non-Trader '' has come to be worth something, even in the eyes of a true Conservative like Alderman Sutton.

Tuesday's meeting of the Town Council was neither very interesting nor very exciting. Prob— ably an unbiassed observer would describe the proceedings as prosy, for the business which occupied two hours and a half to transact was, 10 the main, of a humdrum nature. Still there were points of int3rest, such as the form of conscription obtaining on the ship "Clio," and condemned by Councillor James Evans. He asserts that two Warrington boys have been shipped to the West Indies without the knowledge of their parents. This is rather cool conduct on the part of the" Clio's " captain or some other respon- sible person,and an explanation is to be demanded. We don't dump boys down on the "Cho "with the idea that they are finished with so far as War- rington is concerned, and may ultimately he dis- posed of like so many job lots. Later on in the meeting we were treated to some fascinating facts and figures from the depot at Longford. Preferential tariffs do lot seem to he requisite here, for the trade is 10481 men and machinery being fully employed. In isel about £2,000 worth of new plant is called for, will, we suppose have to be supplied. There mighli otherwise be a scarcity of what a contemporarY once called "consecrated " manure! Councillor Lord worried the Water Committee with another batch of questions, which the chairman carefully replied to. We fancy this committee must be about tired of facing the inquisition once a month Such,however,is the penalty for straying from the path of virtue.

There is a serious split in the camp of the Inquiry Commissioners, for which each side blames the other, and in consequence of which the inquiry is for the time being at an end. Two very interesting letters are (provided for the reading public this week, one signed by the Council's representatives at the Inquiry, and the other by Mr. S. Norbury Williams, the chief spokesman of the Non-Trading three, The first of these import- ant documents descended upon the Town Council on Tuesday evening like a thunderbolt, and after being read by the Mayor it was handed over to the General Purposes Committee, who are called upon to recommend a course of action. So far nothing has apparently been done at the five meetings of the Commissioners but indulge in "desultory discussion," and all because an agreement cannot be come to on the question of reporting. The Council's representatives are wishful to carry out Rule 10 to the letter. This clause specifies "that a shorthand report of the proceedings shall be taken by such persons as the Commissioners may appoint,- and the Corpor- ation three insist upon a verbatim note of each and every day's proceedings at £2.5 per day, or whatever it may cost. They are strictly right 10 their demand, but Rule 10—as it stands—appears to allow a little latitude, and there is some reason in the Non-Trading view that such an expenditure in the early stages of the inquiry is unnecessary and wasteful. Mr. Norbury Williams contends that "the proceed- ings " does not mean the preliminaries to the in- quiry proper, which may consist of weeks spent in wading through minute books, invoices, con- tracts, ledgers, and the like, but the hearing of evidence. Then he would have verbatim note. As some concession the Non Traders are agreeable to the appointment of a clerk who would note any im- portant discussion during the preliminary investigations, at a salary very fe.r below the £24 a day required by an official notetaker. This is, roughly, the status quo. Mr. Noe-Airy Williams has had more experience of inquiries than anY man we could mention offhand, and when he says that this has been the custom in Manchester and elsewhere his view is entitled to very serious con- sideration, particularly as a considerable economy seems practicable. Vie Non-Traders will hold a meeting on Thursday evening when their views will be fully stated, and an expression of opinion from the public asked for. We should be sorry to see the inquiry wrecked and especially so on such a minor detail as the method of reporting For the sake of ultimate peace we sincerely hope the difficulty will be removed, and we venture to counsel both sides in the iuterests of the town to cultivate, as far as possible, a conciliatory spirit-

No question has agitated and divided the Council more, of late, than the proposal to make new street from Sankey-street to Rylands-street• Two months ago such a scheme was rejected, ana a 20 foot passage in place of the old Trinity Wynn decided upon. On Tuesday the new street scheme came up again on a proposal by Mr. R. • Garnett offering further concessions. It W.e9 asserted that a 40 foot street could be made in place of the 20 foot passage at less en.„4 to the town. Though this point was not n 16.1 sufficiently clear, the scheme passed through with the aid of the Mayor's casting vote, after 11 vete° for and against had been given. His Worship el" ercised his right to vote twice, and on such a all" cial question, we think he was ill-advised 31! deliberately committing the town to a scheme °I such magnitude. There is no doubt that the towns" people are looking very much askance at

the proposal,which is far from being under- stood thoroughly and the fear is moreover openly expressed that the job will be an 'expensive one in the long run. We cannot see how it is going to be otherwise. The give and take arrangement with Mr. Garnett may appear mutu- ally beneficial, but then he is by no means the only individual to be dealt with. A pretty problem the Council appear to have embarked upon, with the wideniug of Bridge-street still very much in the air! The policy of hastening slowly could not have been better employed than in this case, and We are sorry the scheme has been rushed through in the manner it has. Anything like a unanimous vote by the Council would have carried weight .with the ratepayers, but they can never be ex- pected to look with any other than a distrustful eye on a proposal which only scrapes through by the assistance of a casting vote.

Captain G. R. Crosfield takes us to task for criti- cising,last week, the objects of the National Service League, and in another column he endeavours to convince us that the salvation and safety of this country depend upon conscription. This is,in plain • language, what his arguments mean. We are sorry we cannot agree with him. There is less need in this country for compulsory military service than there is even for fiscal reform, and not evAn a Chamberlain could convince a British audience that the time'has now arrived for the freedom of the individual to be taken from him and handed over—temporarily may be—to the War office. The idea of conscription is abhorrent to the Britisher; we are inclined, moreover to believe that it is also an insult to his patriotism and sense of individual responsibility. What has the freeborn Briton done, or left undone, that he should be told compulsory measures are nedessary in order to make him take an interest in the preservation of his hearth and home? If the late war proved anything it proved that the Britisher is the readiest man on the face of the globe to voluntarily take up arms in the service of his sovereign. England was not menaced in the slightest degree,yet thousands of fine young fellows threw up good situations and severed home ties in order to assist the regular troops in bringing a troublesome, ill-managed cam- paign to a successful issue. Would they, and many times their number, not do even more in defence of old England herself? But, we can imagine Captain Crosfield saying: they would be raw re- cruits of problematical value as a fighting force. Under present conditions they would, admittedly. To compAl on pain of penalty, every one of these . young men to qualify himself in the use of arms and military drill, as the National Service League auggests is not,we maintain, the best remedy. We do not believe it to be even a practical remedy. The lesson of the war, in this direction, is directed to a development of the voluntary system, and not to conscription. The youth of the country are willing enough to voluntarily undergo a certain amount of military training under reasonable con- ditions. It is to those conditions that military men should address themselves. At present the Auxiliary forces are treated with scant courtesy, though their value is occasionally recognised.Make the volunteer feel that he is really looked upon as the stand-by of the nation,lmake it more easy, less irksome, and less expensive for him to join the force, and there will always be a response suffici- iently adequal.e to reassure the most nervous an .do away with all talk of conscription. This, we believe, is the true remedy for any deficiency in military resources that is supposed to exist in this country. We have no patience with the compul- sory service advocates, and we are surprised that a Volunteer officer like Captain Crosfield does not address himself to the proper recognition and extension of the force to which he belongs before advocating any form of conscription.

Appreciation is always the more acceptable when expressed in practical form, and the congregation at Golborne-street Baptist Churzh have certainly chosen a practical way of assuring the Rev. H. Dannico of their esteem. He recently completed twelve months'successful pastorate at Warrington, and to mark the anniversary the church members decided to present him with a cheque for £2O. This gift, together with a handsome wedding present, was handed to Mr. Dunnico on Thursday evening. .Golborne-street Church appears to have pro- gressed by leaps and bounds since this militant minister took charge, and judging from the entimsiasm of the workers a further period of prosperity is in store.

The members of the Warrington Board of Guardians are now standing on their dignity. They have heard so much lately about their appoint- ment of a "handy man" that on Wednesday a communication from the secretary of the Warring- ton Trades and Labour Council respecting it, was treated with a lofty contempt. Lit was decided nem con to let the communication he onithe table. Such action as this lends colour to the suspicion that the Guardians are anxious to draw the veil over what is an unsatisfactory piece of business. Mr. Knowles objects to the Proceedings of the Guardians being interfered With by labour unions of any description. This . the old story. But in a question of this kind, 'where a "handy man "is appointed ostensibly to do ;work hitherto performed by artizans, surely they have a right to seek information through their trades union organization. The Guardians 'would have shown a much better spirit by frankly 'replying to Mr. Stott's communication.

As will be seen from our advertisement columns, the Warrington Caledonian Association have again 'hooked the famous Glasgow Select Choir to give a grand concert in Parr Hall on Tuesday, December Ist, -the programme to be a miscellaneous one consisting of English, Scotch, Irish and Welsh part-songs, glees ' and solos. Those who heard the choir in Warrington last year will not need to be told that it is composed of the most highly trained vocalists who at part- Singing cannot be excelled. We are informed that the proceeds of the concert are to he devoted to the War- .rington Infirmary and the Caledonian Association's ilenervolent Fund. The opening meeting of the session was held on Monday night, when Mr. W. H. Sherburn, of Stockton Heath, read a papd on "Joseph Priestley, scholar, scientist, and saint." Mr. Sherburn briefly traced Priestley's intellectual and spiritual development, and also dealt with his local connection and scientific discoveries.
RUNCORN POOR RITE REDUCED,

The magistrates at the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday signeda poor rateof lsld in the £ for Runcorn The land rate was 61d. The rate, which was presented by Mr. W. Sutton, assistant overseer, is estimated to realize £3,005 13s id. It is a reduction of 2d in the £ compared with the last half-year, and.. is the smallest rate since April 2nd, 1896, when it was is in the Z. A rate of is 4d in the Z, for Norton, estimated to produce £382 16s Bd., was also signed, THE MAYORALTY OF WIDNES. _

_ A deputation of the Widn.es Town Council appointed in the matter of the Mayoralty for the ensuing 12 months waited upon Alderman S. Quinn a few days ago and invited him to accept the position. We learn Alderman Quinn has accepted the invitation,. and his acceptance will bring pleasure to a very large section of the Widnes community, since he is one of the oldest members of the Council, and has for many years taken a very active andpractical interest in municipal matters

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WIDNES.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WIDNES.

Early on Tuesday morning, John Glover, an Army Reperve man, of Princess-street, Runcorn, attempted to cdmmit suicide by cutting his throat with a razor. Glover, who is a young man, lodges with a widow, who heard him stirring in his bedroom shortly after five o'clock. She thought he was preparing for work, but as he did not come downstairs she went to his bedroom and found him lying in a pool of blood with his throat cut, the windpipe being entirely severed. Sergeant Breeze and Police-Constable Oakes rendered first aid and afterwards Drs. M'Dougall and Delaney stitched up the wound. He was removed to the workhouse hospital. Last week Glover received his reserve money, and he has since been drinking heavily.

SIR J. T. BRUNNER AND PROTECTION. Speaking at a Liberal meeting at Birkenhead on Thursday Sir John Brunner said Protection had existed for a few centuries, and always in the interests of the landowners. At Glasgow the other night they saw three dukes and two marquises. Was there no bargain beforehand? He was sure there was a very clear understanding that the landowning aristocracy should not come out of the little end of the horn. (Laughter and cheers.) If they once introduced Pro- tection into their system they would have the most terrible corruption, and nothing would be left that was pure and holy. The corruption of bribery would per- meate the whole political and commercial life of the country, and he would say. "For God's sake keep the filth out of your life." (Loud applause). What had happened since the colonies helped us in South Africa that Mr. Chamberlain should fear them leaving us?

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
THEFT AT EARLESTOWN.

On Wednesday, at Warrington County Petty Sessions, Sarah Cain, of Burtonwood, was charged with stealing a girl's frock, value 3s. 6d. from the pawnshop of William Jones, 42, Market-street, Earlestown, on Sep- tember 26. Prisoner pleaded guilty. It appeared that the woman went into the shop to redeem some pledges' and after she had one the manager missed the frock. Imformation was given to the police, and the woman dropped it on seeing her theft was discovered. The magistrates decided to deal with her under the First Offenders' Act,and she was bound over. Defendant was ordered to pay the costs.

div.head: ST. PETER'S SALE OF WORK. Opening by Mrs Buckton.
div.p: ST. PETER'S SALE OF WORK. Opening by Mrs Buckton.

To meet the needs of a poor parish like St. Peter's an annual sale of work has become a necessity for, as can readily be understood, it is impossible to raise the whole of the funds required in the parish itself. This year's sale, on very similar lines to its predecessors, was opened in the schoolroom, John. street, on Thursday afternoon. The room pre- sented a bright appearance the stalls being laden with a variety of useful and 'fancy wares, flowers, and edibles. They were in charge of the following : Mrs. Percival's stall: Mesdames Percival, J. Taylor, Greaves, James, Heron, John Taylor, Heacock, Misses Worrall and Percival; flower stall, Mrs. Clayton and Miss Boardman; refreshment stalls, Mesdames Lingley, Bamforth, Yeomans and Webster ; Church Army captain's stall, Captain Langton, Mesdames Grounds, Blundell, Blundell jun., and Knox; advertisement stall (Messrs. Kay and Cowden, Mrs. John Cowdell, Mrs. F. P. Rathbone, Misses Mary, Annie,Jessie and Ethel Wilkinson and Eva Kay ; tea room, Mrs. Burdett and Mrs. Skelland, Miss Lingley and Miss Pownall ; sweet stall, Miss Hughes and Miss Ada Hughes. Despite the miserable weather there was a good attendance at the opening ceremony Unfortunately Lady Greenall, who had consented to open the sale, was unable to attend. Anadmirable sub- stitute was found in Mrs. Buckton. Amongst those present were :—Mrs. Parr, Miss Parr, the Revs. 8., Percival (vicar), D. R. James (curate), W. H. Lester, E. C. E. Carleton, and W. Pollock Hill. Colonel J. D. Buckton, and Councillor John Roberts. _

At the outset the vicar expressed great regret that Lady Greenall was unable to be with them, but said that fortunately the sale would not suffer financially by her absence, as Mrs. Buckton had very kindly consented to perform the opening ceremony. He wished to express sincere and hearty thanks to all present for attending, and to those who had in any way contributed to the sale. In a poor parish like that, although they tried to do something to raise the funds required, they were mostly dependent upon those who came from outside to help them. They were very much indebted to friends outside the parish for the assistance they had given. He would like to thank the stall holders for offering their services, and also. for spending their money for the success of the sale. Referring to the object for which money had to be raised the vicar pointed out that dur- ing the past year they had spent on repairs and altera- tions to the school alone something like £206. Then they had always their regular organisations to support and they were always responsible for £220 for the curate and lay workers' funds. A considerable sum was there- fore required even after the grants had been received from the Society which helped them. Then again £3O I had been spent on special repairs to the church. He appealed to all present to give liberally and in conclu- sion cordially thanked Mrs. Buckton for her great kind- ness in stepping into the gap. (Applause.) Before declaring the sale open, Mrs. BUCKTON expressed regret at Lady Greenall's absence. In such a poor parish, she continued, the objects mentioned by the Vicar were exceedingly worthy, and she hoped they would do their best to clear the stalls of their wares. She was very glad Mr. Percival seemed to be in so much better health. (Applause). He had told her that he was going toask for £l5O to be raised by the sale, but he added that they wanted all they could get. (Laugh- ter.) She hoped a substantial sum would be realised. (Applause). Councillor JOHN ROBERTS proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Buckton, and referred to the valuable assistance which St. Peter's parish had from time to time received from members of the Buckton family. If it were not for the people who came forward from outside the parish they at St. Peter's would find it difficult to keep their heads above water, and they were thankful for generous support received. (Applause). The Rev. D. R. JA.MES seconded the motion, which was heartily carried, and the business of the sale commenced. YESTERDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

Yesterday the sale was re-opened by Mrs. Rylands. Tfie VICAR announced that Thursday's proceeds amountedlto £BO 16s. He called attention to the fact that the Bishop had said that for a parish of 7,000 in- habitants there should beat least three curates, one lay worker, and a Bible woman. They at St. Peter's had only one curate and one lay worker and the population was something like 10,500. Only those who had to deal with large parishes knee how very difficult it was to keep in touch with so many people. Mrs. RYLAN'DS emphasized the necessity for Chris- tian work in poor parishes, but pointed out that it could not be carried on without organizations. She hoped that people would come forward to help poor parishes, and that all woulel do their best to make that sale a success. (Applause.) On the motion of the EcTo, seconded by Coun- R rt cillor JOHN ROBERTS, a vote of thanks was accordad to Mrs .Rylands.

div.head: Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-street.
div.p: Ebenezer Church, Buttermarket-street.

The interior of the above place of worship presented a pleasing appearance on Sunday last on the occasion of the harvest thanksgiving services. The preacher in the morning and evening was Councillor Thornton who gave eloquent addresses. The choir sang in the morn- ing " Consider the lilies." and in the evening Sir John Stainer's "Ye shall dwell in the Land" the bass solo being taken by Mr. C. J. Sheath. In the afternoon, a service of song, entitled " Full Bloom "was rendered, the soloists being Mrs. Dutton (soprano), Miss E. Lee (contralto) and Mr. R. W. Cook (tenor). Mr. W. Birch presided at the organ. On Monday evening, a tea party was held and at the concert held afterwards, the chair was taken by Councillor Thornton. The following pro- gramme was rendered:, Pianoforte solo, Miss E. York; song, "Flower girl" Miss G. Fry; ventriloquial sketch, Mr. G. C. Maidment ; song. " Marguerite "Mr. A. Eger- ton (encored) ; recitation, "Curfew shall not ring to-night" Miss J. Hughes; song, "The empty chair" Mr. G. C. Maidment ; recitation, Vaddv, you've killed me" Miss S. L. Sheath. The accompanist was 'Mr. W. Jackson. The flowers were afterwards sent to the sick members of the congregation.

div.head: MAYORALTY.
div.p: THE MAYORALTY.
COUNCILLOR PIERPOINT AND THE
DEPUTATION.
WILL HE ACCEPT AFTER NOVEMBER Ist P

Councillor T_CCNION reported at the meeting:of the "'Own Council on Tuesday, upon the result of the deputation which hadbeen appointed to wait upon Councillor William Pierpoint to ask him to accept the office of mayor for the ensuing year. Councillor TINNION said: The deputation consisted. of Alderman Smethurst and Councillor Craik and my- self. We met Mr. Pierpoint this evening at 5.30, and, after placing the matter very carefully before him, and urging him to accept office,he said that under all the eh! cumstances he could not see his way to do so. I don't know that I am called upon to give his reasons, but he did say that he had preached the &doctrine that it was not desirable that the Mayor should be selected before the first of November, or until the election has been held. Considering that he had preached that doctrine he thought it would be very unfair to accept office. He also said he was a very busy raan,and that he would not have in the immediate future sufficient time to devote to the office; therefore he did not think he was the proper man to accept the position, considering the some- what disturbed state of the Council and the town. We endeavoured to lay the matter before him as fairly and as honestly as we could, but for the present he declined to consider the proposal. Alderman SUTTON said he was very sorry but he was disposed to admire the wisdom of Councillor Pierpoint in refusing office for the present, because the Non. Traders thought they were going to carry everything before them in the forthcoming elections. If that was the case it was only right that the new members should have a voice in the election of Mayor. (Hear, hear). It was on that ground that he (the Alderman) refused to be one of the deputation. It was a mistake now to ask Councillor Pierpoint to accept office, as they did not know they would be able to carry him afterwards. He rather admired the spirit in which Councillor Pierpoint refused to accept office at present. The MAYOR said he was sure they would all very much regret the decision. (Hear, hear). Councillor PEMBERTON • did not think Alderman Sutton ought to have referred to the Non-Traders in the way he had referred to them. They did not pretend to be prophets. To say they were boasting they could carry the town was wrong; the matter was in the hands of the ratepayers. He did not think it was fair to cast such a slur upon them. Alderman SurroN : It is what they have said. Councillor PEMBERTON : I have not said it, and our party has not said it.i Alderman SurroN : You are not everybody. Councillor PEMBERTON : Neither are you.

div.head: NOVEMBER ELECTIONS. Liberal Ward Meetings.
div.p: THE NOVEMBER ELECTIONS. Liberal Ward Meetings.

With the near approach of the November elections there is much speculation as to the probable candidates The municipal Non-Trading committee have announced their intention of contesting many of the seats which will falll vacant and several gentlemen are mentioned as nominees of that organization. In the Town Hall Ward Councillor Lord's term of office expires, and he will have the support of the Con- servatives in his efforts to secure re-election. He is, of course, the nominee of the Non-Trading Committee. The Liberal Committee of Whitecrozs Ward have again selected Councillor Barton as their candidate, and the probability is that he will not be opposed. Councillor Pierpoint's term of office as the representative of Bewsey Ward also expires, but it is improbable that the Non-Traders will offer opposition to his return. C oun- cillor Peacock is the retiring Councillor for Orford Ward and owing to the passing of the Education Act Councillor Upson will sever his connection with the Council. Mr. Fred Stott is contesting the seat kn the interests of the Independent Labour Party and has already held numer- ous election meetings. Mr. W. Hickman has been men- tioned as a Non-Trading candidate, but we understand that he does not intend to cone forward. The Liberal committee has not met yet. At a meeting of the St. John's Ward Liberal Com- mittee last evening a letter was read from Councillor F. R.,Roberts declining to seek re-election. A resolu- tion thanking him for his past services was passed. It was decided that in view of the fact that Mr. Maginn was spoken of as the opponent of Mr. John Holden, the nominee of the Non-Trading party, not to select any candidate at present. Councillcr HuLsE is the retiring representative of Fairfield Ward, and his opponent will be Mr. James Povey, whose address is published in our advertising columns. Mr. Povey says he is not a member of any political organization, nor of the Non-Trading Associa- tion, but he is in full sympathy with the members of the latter in their effort to purge the Town Council of all that is legally 9r morally wrong, and he would sup- port them in their policy of economy or reform. Councillor JOHN EVANS has been asked by the Con- servative Committee of Howley Ward to again come before the electors. but he has not given his decision. Mr. W. Benson is spoken of as the Non-Trading candi- date.

A meeting of the Liberal Committee of St. Austin's Ward was held on Monday evening under the presidency of Councillor Tinnion. Councillor W. Roberts declined to stand again and a vote of thanks was accorded to him for his past services. A deputation consisting of Councillor Burton, Councillor 'Bunion, and Messrs. Elwell, Critchley and Croskill was appointed to wait upon Mr. J. A. Ewartand invite him to contest theseat. Mr. Ewart could not seek his way to accept the offer and Mr. Arthur Browne was waited upon and will give his reply in the course of a few days. Mr. T. H. Ashcroft will be the Non-Trading candidate. The Conservatives have not yet had a meeting in Latchford Ward where Councillor Sampson retires Mr. S. B. Stringer and Mr. Edwin Plinston have each been mentioned as the Non-Trading nominee. The Warrington Branch of the National Union of Gasworkers and General Labourers has passed the following resolution supporting Mr. F. Stott's candi- dature :--` That we heartily endorse the candidature of Mr. F. Stott for Orford Ward, and pledge ourselves to do everything in our power to secure his return to the Warrrington Town Council. We do hereby impress upon all workers of the necessity of being represented by men of their own class, believing that labour should be represented in the same proportion as the profes- sional and manufacturing classes."
ALDERMAN SUTTON AND THE TRADING QUESTION.

At a meeting of the Council of the Conservative Association on Thursday evening, Mr. John White was re-elected chairman of the Association. Mr. E. Draper was asked to accept the office of deputy-chairman, and Alderman Francomb was re-elected vice-chair- man. After some discussion it Nvis decided to leave the selection of candidates in the hands of the Ward Committees, and that the organisation of the party be at the disposal of Conservatives wishful to have tlieadvantage of it. In the course of the discus- sion, several gentlemen emphasized the fact that as Conservatives they were not opposed to the principles the Non-Traders were contending for. Alderman Sutton said he did not know why they should not all be.*:balled Non-Traders. He thought meetings should be held in the Wards with the object uf disabusing the minds of the people of the idea that the Conservatives were anything elie but Non-Traders. They were certainly as much opposed to any Councillor making anything out of his position, as it was poisble for anyone to be, and he thought this fact could not be too widely known. In reply to Councillor John Roberts, Alderman SurToN said Conservatives would be quite free to support a Non-Trading candidate provided he was a Conservative* NON-TRADERS' MEETING.

• A public meeting of ratepayers opposed- to all trading by members of the Council with the Corporation either direct or indirect or through limited companies will be held in the Parr Hall on Thursday evening. The speakers will include Mr. S. Norbury Williams who Nviil deal with the Council's Commissioners' letter to the Mayor with regard to the inquiry.
