The Examiner, Saturday October 10, 1903. THE NON-TRADING INQUIRY. A SPLIT IN THE CAMP. Withdrawal of the Non-Traders' Representatives. THE OPINION OF THE COUNCIL ASKED. At the Council meeting on Tuesday the Mayor said: I have received a letter with some surprise and regret as it appears to indicate a very unsatisfactory position of things with regard to the commission of inquiry at its recent meetings. It is probably such an important document that I thought all the gentlemen would like to have a copy of it and they have been prepared. It reads thus :
Warrington, sth October, 1903.

Dear Mr. Mayor —The conimiisioners appointed to make the Trading Inquiry have met on five days. At the first meeting on September 10th it was agreed to advertise for tenders for a report and print of each day's proceedings and that pending the acceptance of a tender the Town Clerk should make temporary arrange- ments for such work. There was a difference of opinion as to the fullness of the proposed reports and prints and even as to the need of any report except when witnesses were before the commission. At ,the second meeting on September 16th, all the Commissioners and a shorthand writer attended; but at the outset Mr. Pemberton asked that the reporter should retire for -a little time; desiring to be conciliatory we raised no objection. Mr. Pemberton then proceeded to state that he and his colleagues did not consider it necessary to have a reporter and that they would not consent to one being present until witnesses were before us. Upon our pointing out that this would be a violation of rule 10 which expressly states "that a shorthand report of the proceedings shall be taken by such persons as the Com- missioners may appoint" Mr. Pemberton informed us that they had consulted their legal adviser who told them that:they ought not to have a reporter present during the earlier stages of the Inquiry and that the Municipal Non-Trading Committee— our committee" as he re- peatedly called it—would not consent. We pointed out that Mr. Pemberton's statement was not only a demand that we should violate rule 16, but was in itself a viola- tion of the spirit, if not of the letter of rule 2 which provides that "neither side shall appoint a lawyer"; He and his colleagues seemed to realize this and thereafter based their avowed objection to the presence of a reporter on the grounds of expense. In the subsequent discussion Mr. Pemberton became suddenly ill which made further business at that sitting impracticable. At the three following meetings on September 22nd, 24th, and October 2nd, a shorthand writer was present, and full reports have been taken. On September 22nd, a letter from the Secretary of the Non-Trading Asso- ciation containing insulting and baseless insinuations against "one or two of the Commissioners" was read. On September 24th another letter over the same signa- ture and offering a. perfunctory apology was submitted. The objectionable nature of these letters will be suffi- ciently evident . when they are made public. We wish to carefully dissociate Mr. Norbury Williams from them as he resented and repudiated them as vigorously as ourselves and our personal relations with him, here and throughout, have been most satisfactory. We have endeavoured to meet the wishes of our colleagues in a conciliatory spirit throughout; we offered to consent to their appointing a substitute. temporary or permanent, for Mr. Pemberton, we gave way to them in respect of the days and hours of meet- ing; desiring to secure a prompt, full and honest inquiry into the matters referred to us, we offered to sit from day to day; they would not agree to sit on more than three half-days weekly. We are reluctantly compelled to believe that the action of our colleagues in not even adhering to their own offer, in constantly appealing to the Municipal Non-Trading Committee, through whose members as it would appear, garbled versions of our proceedings have been circulated, and in declining to sit whilst a reporter was present, has been due to motives and based on reasons other than those which they have evoked. Their argument that the employment of a shorthand writer under rule 10 involved an unnecessary expense is untenable; Mr. Pemberton himself proposed that we should employ a Clerk, the difference between whose wages and the remuneration of a reporter would only be, as he admitted about 10s. weekly; whilst we pointed out that, if each Commissioner avoided unnecessary talk, the reports 'during the earlier stages would be short and inexpensive, bht quite as important as the longer one at a later period. The necessity for a full and accurate report was made clear at our fourth and fifth sittings when differences of opinion arose as to matters dealt with at our second meeting during the absence of the reporter. In view of the possibility of legal proceedings as the i outcome of the Inquiry, it s imperative in the interests of justice and for the protection of individuals that au independent report by a competentshorthand writer should be taken of all the proceedings of the Commissioners. Acting upon a resolution of the Municipal Non-Trading Committee their representatives withdrew from our meeting on October 2nd, as soon as we proposed to com- mence the real work of the InquitT. , We regret that so much time has been wasted in de- sultory discussion; we decline to assent to so serious a violation of the rules as our Colleagues proposed; a violation which we cannot believe is urged merely to save the ratepayers of Warrington 10s. or even £1 a week;and we now ask whether it is the wish of.the Town Council that we should proceed with the Inquiry des- pite the absence of the Representatives of the Municipal Non-Trading Committee. We are, dear Mr. Mayor, Your obedient servants, (Signed) T. BIRCHALL. ALF. J. JOLLEY, LIN. GREENING.

Continuing, the MAYOR said :—The-letter has only passed into my hands this evening, and as each member is to receive a copy of it I propose to refer the matter to the next meeting of the General Purposes Committee to discuss before bringing it before the Council. It is never wise to come to a decision before both sides have been heard. (Hear, hear.) This course was agreed upon. MR. NORBURY WILLIAMS REPLIES.

the very beginning of this agitation. The burgesses will remember that, at one of our early meetings, I read , a letter which I had received from Councillor F. R, Roberts, in which this same blustering spirit of threat was shown. He told me in that letter that if I did so- and-so he would take legal proceedings. This spirit has dominated the Traders froifi the beginning, and now it has unfortunately taken hold of the three Council Commissioners. How is it possible to get along satis- factorily with men who tell you plainly that legal proceedings will probably be the outcome of the Ixiquiry ? It seems to me that, after this most offensive and hate- ful threat, they have put themselves out of court. Who can act with judges who tell you before a case opens that every witness who comes before them will run the risk of being ruined if he ventures to open his mouth? I say this hateful spirit of intimidation has too long prevailed in Warrington, and that the three gentlemen who have now, by a peculiar side-wind, revived that hateful spirit, have done as much as three men can do to destroy the confidence of the public in any inquiry in which they take a part.—Yours faithfully, NORBURY WILLIAMS. October 7th, 1903, Warrington.

div.head: "Spirit of Intimidation."
div.p: The "Spirit of Intimidation."

Mr. S. Norbury Williams writes to us as follows: Sir,—l have broken a railway journey this (Wednes- day) morning, and am spending an hour in Warrington with a view to reading the singular and unfortunate letter addressed by my three Council-nominated collea- gues to the Mayor, and read at the Borough Council meeting held last evening. As the contents of this document have gone to the Press and are now public, I am, I imagine, justified in making a brief comment upon the document in question. I have, from the beginnmg, striven to keep secret the proceedings of the Commis- sioners, but now feel that as my three colleagues have thought it right to make a public Statement my mouth is no longer closed. I shall only now trouble the burgesses with a brief word on the subject, as I have this morning been asked to speak at the Parr Hall, on Thursday, the 15th inst., and I hope then to fully explain the matters in dispute. For the present T therefore content myself by refer- ring to the three points mentioned in the letter of my colleagues. (1.) Our present dispute has arisen upon the inter- pretation of the two apparently simple words," the proceedings." Our instructions state that a shorthand note of" the proceedings" shall be taken. Now, we three who represent the great majority of the burgesses, say that this doesnot mean that the preliminaries to the Inquiry are to be reported verbatim. I have helped in many inquiries in my time. Some of them have prob- ably taken three months to prepare, but the inquiry proper has taken 'only three (lays. We have had a short hand report of the three days, but of course not of the three months. It is so in Warrington. The commis- sioners will be engaged for perhaps three or six months in wading laboriously through minute books, invoices, contracts, ledgers, and documents of all sorts. They do this in order to prepare for the Inquiry. We say it is not necessary, in fact would be a sheer waste of the ratepayers' money, to pay a shorthand man to report all these preparations or gettings ready," as I may call them. When the witnesses are called then comes the time for the verbatim note. Then we shall of course insist on the full report being taken. Now we decline to countenance what to us seems to be the proposed waste.

(2) Then we come to the statement in the letter to the effect that, if we employed . a clerk instead of al shorthand reporter,the difference would be only 10s.per ' week. This is really so absurd that I do not think it necessary to enter at length into the point. The ordin- ary burgess can tell for himself what the difference would be. We, who represent the burgesses, say that it will be time to employ a costly shorthand reporter at £2O to £25 per thy when the full Inquiry begins, but not until then. On this point, the six Commissioners are at present 'hopelessly divided, but I still indulge the hope that wiser Counsels will prevail, and that the Inquiry will not be wrecked by the Council's representatives. At any rate, if .no means can be devised at the moment to bring the Commissioners together again, I certainly hope that the Council, after November 2nd next, and when it will probably repre- sent more accurately than it now does (although even then still far from perfectly) the feelings and wishes of the burgesses, will agree to anlnquiry upon the lines above indicated. I believe those to be the lines which the people have had in their minds ever since the Non- Trading movement took shape two years ago. (3) The third point is, to my mind, the most serious. I will repeat it in full, as it deserves much considera- tion on the part of those most interested, namely the burgesses of this town. It is this : "In view of the possibility of legal proceedings as the outcome of the Inquiry, it is imperative in the interests of justice and for the protection of individuals, that an independent report by a com- petent shorthand writer should be taken of all the proceedings of the Commissioners." This passage seems to me to damn the whole document. It shows the dominant feeling of our three colleagues. ,It is the same hateful threat which has been used from

div.head: FISCAL PROBLEM. Mr. Chamberlain's Glasgow Speech.
div.p: THE FISCAL PROBLEM. Mr. Chamberlain's Glasgow Speech.
LETTER FROM MR. PARKER.
MC. E. PARKER writes :

Whatever we think of Mr. Chamberlain's proposals, no one can refrain from admiring the vigour, and lucidity, with which he gives expression to them. A statesman of advanced years, swho with eye and mind undimmed, with natural force unabated, proposes to reverse the entire fiscal policy of the nation, calls for our admiration however much we may differ as to the wisdom of the proposed change. Mr. Chamberlain makes an appeal to us to look at this question apart from party controversy. He says "For my part Ifdisclaim any imputation of motive, or evil and unworthy motive, upon those who may happen to disagree with me" and yet in a later part of his speech he deliberately charges those who dis- agree with him of dreading the responsibility of empire and of caring little about the possibility of its dissolution. This habit of believing the worst of those who venture to disagree with him, and not forgetting tfi tell them so in caustic terms, has ever been a feature which has gone far to mar the finer qualities of this statesman, and we fear the fault is too deeply seated to be eradicated even if he himself should desire it. The greatest dangerthat this controversy has of being poisoned with party bitterness, is in the biting tongue of Mr. Chamberlain himself, and if he can restrain his unruly member we may hope the conflict of words and reason may be waged with good humour and good feel- ing, even if we do not see eye to eye. Leaving the personal factor and passing on to the question, we note an important part of the argument rests on what Mr. Chamberlain conceives to be signs of decay in the prosperity of the country. He Isees "cracks and crevices in the wall of the great structure," and "knows that the foundations are not broad enough or deep enough to sustain it." In proof of this he proceeds to give evidence. He tells us, that since 1872 there has been an increase of our exports'of only twenty millions. But why does he select a special year and why 1872? Had he taken two years earlier 1870, the increase instead of 20 millions would have been 83 millions, or two years later it would also have been the 83 millions. The year 1872 was a boom year following the France. German war, and,it is quite unreliable as a basis of argument, and it is surprising that Mr. Chamberlain who ought to knew better should so use it.

Taking the average over the decade 1870 to 1850, the increase since 1872 would be 78 millions against the, German increase 56 millions, and the United States 110 millions. I may here say that I do not think Mr. Chamberlaia's figures for the United States are correct. This time it seems to mehe has understated the American figures as well as the British. The population of both these States is greater than our own. If my readers will work out the exports, per head (assuming Mr. Chamberlain's figures to be correct) they will find that the increase of our exports per, head has held its own, and this for the larger amount per head, with these two countries.
The total exports in 1900 were as follows :—Great Britain, £7 per head; Germany, £4; United States, £3 15s.

But it ought to be remembered, although Mr. Cham- berlain did not mention it, that a large proportion of our exports are not included in the Board of Trade returns. The figures are taken from the values given at the port of departure, and are always given as low as i possible, as the value given forms, n many cases, the basis of the tax in protected countries. Inasmuch as our goods are almost entirely,delivered by our own ships, the amount we get from the foreigner is not only the value of the goods in England, but the value at the foreign port; that is, the foreigner pays to our merchant fleet for the freight of the goods. Now in the Blue Book just published the amount paid to our fleet for service = carriers, is calculated at 90 millions per

div.head: annum.
div.p: annum.

This amount goes far to explain,what is a conundrum to many, why our tabulated imports appear so much more than ourexports. If therefore the amount paid in freight is now 90 millions, inlB7o it would be about 65 millions, a difference of 25 millions. Part of this is freight on imports; so roughly speaking we may take it that 10 millions belong to exports. The exports of Germany and the United States would be subject to additions for their shipping, but inasmuch as we have as much shipping as the whole of the world put to- gether the proportion would not be large. We not only carry our goods, but are general carriers for the world. Mr. Chamberlain also omits the growth in our exports arising from the continued progress of ourship- building. Our exports of ships built for foreigners has increased about 'six millions since 1872. Further, in the figures used by Mr. Chamberlain to indicate the slow growth of our commerte, he omits altogether the increase in our trade as merchants or exporters of im- ported produce. These re-exports now amount to about 65 millions. If to the 78 millions (being the increase of exports from 1872 to 1902, arriving at the figure of 1872 from the average of its decade) we add the 10 millions increase in freight earnings on the increased exports, and the six millions increase in exports of ships which Mr. Chamberlain altogether omits, we arrive at a total of 94 millions instead of 20 millions as stated by Mr. Chamberlain. The 94 millions on a population of 41 millions gives £2ss. Bd.per head of an increase in thirty years.

The German increaseoocording to Mr. Chamberlain, is 56 millions; add to this 4 millions earned in freight; and this 60 millions on a population of 56 millions gives an increase of £1 is. sd. per head. The United States increase according to Mr. Chamberlain, is 110 millions plus 3 millions for freight, and 'this gives 113 millions on It population of 76 millions, equal to an increase of £1 9s. 9d.per head. Thus instead of our exports dimin- ishing relatively with Germany and the United States, they have increased in proportion to our population as much or more than either of these countries. Mr. Chamberlain speaks of "cracks and crevices" in our industrial system. It appears to me there are cracks and crevices in the foundation of his argument which make it entirely unsafe to build upon. The misuse of figures in a vital question like this is inex- cusable. We are certainly all liable to make mistakes (and if lam wrong in any pf my figures, or in the use of them, I trust some of your correspondents will pnt me right) but in a matter which affects the prosperity of the country for years to come,such palpable careless- ness, or worse,on the part of a great statesman, on such a great issue is altogether unpardonable.
CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketh, October Bth 1903.

div.head: MR. EDWM WOODS AND IRON TRADE
div.p: MR. EDWM WOODS AND IRON TRADE
PROSPECTS.
MR. EDWIN WOODS writes :---

Sir,—l have lately been thinking how serious amatter it is to continue to buy steel rods from Germany, to be drawninto wire, as we at the Longford Wire Works have been doing for many years. rhe so-called Free- Traders, who might be better styled, "One-sided Traders," say what an advantage it is to the general public that we can buy 2s. 6d. or ss. per ton cheaper from the foreigner than from manufacturers of rods in ourown town. When I examine this statement, which I have only done closely during the last few weeks, I find that the facts are as follow:

If I buy 1,000 tons of rods from Germany, I am doing a great injustice to my country to the extent that T cause a loss of production in England of not only the 1,000 tons of rods which I buy, but also of the labour which would be reqiiired to produce the raw material for the manufacture cf the rods. It requires about, 3,000 tons of ore, and about 1,500 tons of coal, which is turned into coke to make the ore into pig iron, and about 450 tons of coal to turn the Rig iron into billets, and 'about 550 tons of coal to make the billets into rods; so that, to produce 1,000 tons of rods, I have shewn . you that it is a loss of labour in producing 5,500 tons of raw material. which, added to the loss of the rods, makes a total of 6,500 tons. I have come to the conclusion therefore that, instead of its being an advantage to the public to buy rods from Germany, lam doing a great injustice to this country, as, in preventing the production in England of ore, coal, pig iron. billets, and wire rods to the extent I have named, I am giving work to foreigners, while,in my own town, men are working one, two, and three days a week. I sincerely ask, not only the working man, but everybody, to give this matter, the most serious consideration, and vote for any candi- date who will help us to break down such unfair trad- ing. _ - -

admit that lam the greatest sinner in Warrington in this respect, as we at the Longford Wire Co. have no rolling mills, and to try to compete with the Germans and Americans in wire, with our present system, there has been no other course left open to us. If we can prevent other nations dumping their iron and steel in this country, by working with our colonies, I can soe great future for our ironworks,and leaving the question of manufacturers out of consideration altogether, the demand for steel, iron and wire would be so enormous that our working men would once more see bright times and, I think, a steady prosperity. The Longf ord Wire Co., Ltd. Warrington, October Bth, 1901,

div.head: LABOUR DEMONSTATION.
div.p: THE LABOUR DEMONSTATION.
An Impression.
'For a' that, for a' that, Its coming yet for a' that, That man to man the world o'er Shall brothers be for a' that."

I was present at the great labour demonstration in the Parr Hall .the other evening and listened with con- siderable interest to the very able speeches that were delivered in, favour of "Trade Union rights" and the election of "representatives in Parliament and on all local governing bodies." If we are to take the enthusiasm which permeated the meeting as the fore- runner of serious thought and determined work on behalf of the objects I have mentioned, we may look forward to having a united Labour Party in War- rington before many days. The CHAIRMAN (Mr. Edward Plinston) was supported by representatives of most, if not all, of the different Labour Societies of the _town. The Passive Resisters, too, were represented by a reverend gentleman Who, taking his seat on the platform rather late, mistook the applause intended for a remark of the Chairman as a special greeting to him and, of course, smiled and bowed and looked more than delighted at the.re- ception which he thought was accorded him. But we were pleased to see him all the same.
A CANDIDATE FOR TIIE BOROUGII,

I The CnAnnfAx soon got to his work and.he was _not long before he told us that "at no distant date we might have an election, and we might have a Labour ' Candidate for Warrington." His remark, expressed somewhat falteringly, was greeted with loud "applause. Although there has been a rumour in Warrington for some weeks that there "might be a Labour Candidate" yet we were of opinion, that Liberalism had never a better chance of retnrnini.a member than the present and we were inclined to think that, at last, success would crown the efforts of those who have striven so valiantly, but in vain' to see "their man" win. No name was mentioned, but I saw- Mr. James Dodds present.
TABOUR MAN PREFERRED.

...... Mr. J. EDWARDSON, president of the Trades Council,. and a representative of the Wiredrawers proposed the first resolution in a few welllchosen words and Mr. E. Malone of the Railway Servants,, formally seconded Our anxiety, Of course, was to hear the man from Clitheroe who sat on the right of the Chairman wait- ing to take his turn. Mr. Shackletm, M.P., is a tall, big man with whiskers and helmadeu very lucid speech. The only thing he lacked was a blackboard and a piece of chalk so that he might have put down a few dates to impress them on our memory. For instance- 1875—when it was held that "whatever was right for one man to do was right for one or more to do " ; 1871—when Mr. Bruce the then Home Secre- tary introduced his Bill; 1861—when the Trade Union Commission sat,and so on. When he had finished with the dates we began to learn something as to what "picketing," "conspiracy," and "responsibility for the conduct of every Tom, Dick, or Harry. in their 'ranks," meant. He also finished up his speech by stating that "they wanted in Parliament more mem- bers who would support labour interests. " Let them send someone, labour man preferred, but someone who would help the Labour Party."
A DIVERSION.

- After the first resolution had been un.anintouslv carried the members of the Firth Glee Party, all labour *men and Trade Unionists, favoured us with a delightful selection entitled "By Celia's Harbour." It was rather funny, the way they arranged themselves round the Chairman and the two members of Parlia- ment. I felt somewhat for poor Mr. Henderson who 'stroked his forehead from time to time and looked as if the sweet music was charming away his thoughts and he would have nothing left him but the notes in his hand. There is nearly always something funny about a Glee Party, somehow. Either you find a tall man beside a short man, a thin man squeezed in , between two unduly fat men, or the way they do their 'hair or turn their toes. But we had nothing to com- plain of on Tuesday evening. They looked well and sang batter and were the recipients of well-earned applanie.
FESTIN.I LENTE.

The second resolution pledging the meeting to pro- mote the election of Direct Labour Representatives in Parliament and on all governing bodies was moved by Mr. F. Stott, the Labour candidate for Orford Ward, who delighted in the compound 'appellation of "the young man in a hurry." He is a very-much-alive young man and for some minutes -held us under his sway. His remarks were received with considerable enthusiasm and he evidently stands well in the eyes of his labour friends. Perhaps the only discordant note of the meeting was sounded by him when re- ferring to the Labour Representation Committee which was formed in Warrington some mouths ago. It has not met with the success which he thinks it de- serves. There is not the unanimity he would have (perhaps" on account of the revolutionary character of the debates " held in the Trades Council) and he urged for closer union. He must not be in "too big a hurry" and it would be as well for him to remember that he can help the cause he has so much at heart by having for his motto " festina lente "—hasten slowly Mr. Jolley seconded in an exceedingLy neat little speech.
PITCK PERSONIFIED.

I must cordially admit that the gentleman "I went for to see" and hear was none other than the next speaker, Mr. Arthur Henderson, M.P., the victor of Barnard Castle, known for six or seven years as the wonderful Liberal agent for the division he now repre- sents in Parliament, a convert from Liberalism to Labour. He is not a great speaker, but he has remarkable tact and ability and, although he speaks with the voice of a preacher, yet he does not preach, at any rate so far as politics are concerned. He had a great reception. His recent success was evidently quite fresh in the minds of the audience. If there is one thing more than another that a working man admires it is pluck. And, in Mr. Henderson, pluck is personified. .He is a man of the people. Twenty-five years ago,, we are told, he was a foundry lid in New- castle, helping to support a poor family, and to-day he is in the British House of Commons. -We cannot but admire him. We know he will go a long way and we wish him success.
lABERALISM AND L

If Mr. Henderson is correct in his assertion that little, if any, good can come of an alliance with the Liberal Party, then the situation is certainly an un- fortunate one. Either Liberalism will have to take a , decided stand on the side of Labour or else Labour will sever its connection entirely from it. The opinion . of Mr. Henderson is worth having because he has seen the subject from both sides and should be in a position to judge to some extent as to what the result is likely to be. There is no gainsaying the fact, however, that the Liberal Party has very largely created the strife which is now simpering all over the'country. If—l say, if—the Liberal' Party will not help the Labour Party to gain its objects, and will altogether stand aloof, or vote in the wrong lobby when the:interests of labour are at stake, there can be nothing to inspire the workingman with confidence. But if, on the other hand, Labour will have its leaders at any price and will not listen to reason and sound argument then by severing its connection, it is only falling out of the frying-pan into the fire and the cure is likely to be far worse than the disease. The opinions of the Labour Leaders differ on this point. Some think Civil no good can come out of an alliance whilst others are in favour of a better understanding. Let the workingman himself decide.
TN CONCLUSION.

What are the signs of the times? We are told that few, if any, find their way to notoriety without excel- lence of some kind ; but of all merits, that of an enlarged and comprehensive mind is the rarest, and the wants of society raise to distinction infinitely more persons than nature has blessed with this quali- fication. Unfortunately, hitherto the wants of certain towns and districts have been but poorly represented in Parliament because the constituents have had an autocrat, or worse still an autocratic-democrat sup- plied them, ready-made so to say, and they have voted, for him because he was supposed to represent their interests. We are told that the times are changing. So far as the workingman is concerned, 1 , there can be no two opiniims. He is beginning to realize his strength and that his interest is of equal importance to the state and well-being of , society as the money'd. In future, he is not I going to sell his vote. He is ''(-ming to use it with discretion. Surely, it is quite time that some- thing was done for him. if the present political partiee will not help him he cannot be blamed for seeking other support. The error we ought to avoid is, that silly deference for great names, which gives such undue weight to mere authority, and restrains . men without a reputation from fair exercise of an I independent judgment. A man who has never worked I a day in his life, but rather looks down upon "his brother (?)" who does work, is not a fit and proper person to represent a worker. And yet, how many of the drones are day-by-day eating the honey that is
being gathered by the workers. For a time we have, stood it, but are. going to • stand it no longer. Democracy must and will eventually win. DIUUND OSBORNE.

div.head: Labour Prospects at Warrington.
div.p: Labour Prospects at Warrington.
Mr. Henderson's Opinion.

On Wednesday afternoon an" Examiner" reporter had a brief interview with Mr. A:Henderson, the mem- ber for Barnard Castle who expressed himself as being very pleased with the success of Tuesday even- ing's demonstration and thought it a happy augury for , the progress of the labour movement in Warrington "If there was so much enthusiasm at present, what" he asked" would the interest be at election time ?" Mr. HENDERSCK is very optimistic in regard to the prospects of, a labour candidate at the general election He has consulted election returns and found that for some years thb number of votes polled by the Liberals has varied very slightly: The probability, he. continued, was that -since • the last election there had been a considerable addition to the electorate of working class voters, and he was of the opinion that if the progressive forces would rally round a good labour candidate the seat might be "lifted." Had he not already contested the Barnard Castle division with success,. said Mr. Henderson, he would have been very pleased to have -fought an election at Warrington.. There were, many gentle- men of his acquaintance who would have been grati- fied to have had such a meeting as that on Tuesday evening to inaugurate their candidature.

Mr. lIENDERSO; thought it not unlikely that a labour candidate would be invited to contest Warrington at the next election. Our representative took leave-Of him as he was about to depart for Gorton to address a meeting in supplrt of the candidature for Hodge.

div.head: FANCY DRESS BALL PRETTY SCENE IN THE PARR HALL.
div.p: FANCY DRESS BALL PRETTY SCENE IN THE PARR HALL.

In striking contrast to the damp and depressing conditions outside on Thursday evening, the interior of the Parg Hall was bright and cheerful, and was the scene of a picturesque pageant in which local ladies and gentlemen masqueraded in costumes typical for the most part, of those worn under various climes and con- ditions in the present day, and also in byegone ages. A. few of the characterisations were historical, others mythical, and many dramatic and comical. As this living wealth of colour aud beauty tripped "the light, fantastic toe" the ensemble was pleasing in'the extreme. The occasion was the fancy dress ball in connection with the Warrington Lifeboat Saturday Fund, and was reminiscent of the reeent fancy dress parade of Sep- tember sth. About 125 guests assembled and they were received by the Mayoress, who was accompanied by Mr. Roger Parr and Miss Parr.

A- large number of the general public watched the proceedings from the galleries and by paying an admission fee of one shilling helped to swell the local funds of the lifeboat institution. A special feature of thet evening's proceedingswas an open cake-walk com- petition. Similar competitions have proved a great attraction in other towns and considerable interest seemed to be evinced in this item of Thursday's pro- ceedings. Many were delighted with the performances of the young couples who entered the competition, but speaking for ourselves we cannot say we like the "cake walk "as it wasprodueed. Instead of that grace- ful and sylph-like movement which should be the chief characteristic of dancing, the participants are thrown into the most preposterous positions and the attitude of the lady dancer;at times, borders on the extravagant. It is only fair to add that the performers were greeted with hearty applause. Mr. B. Browne was the judge and. heably led off the competition with a typical exhibi- tion with Miss Lilian Pairfax,of Sefton Park, Liverpool, as his partner. Awards weregra,nted as follows: Ist. prize' Mr. Harry Walker and Miss Thornton, of Liver- pool,22 and cake ; 2nd prize, £l, Mr. W. Sealey and Miss F. Brightmore, of New Brighton: 3rd prize, 10s., Mr. Monaghan and Miss Smith, of Birkenhead. Mr. Percy Randall's band provided the music and gave entire satisfaction. The catering WaS in the safe hands of Mr. and Mrs. Powys and Mr. W. Chalmers had charge of the refreshment bar. Mr. Chalmers has kindly consented to hand over the best part of the pro- ceeds to the committee. The arrangements were com- plete in every respect and creditiis due to all concerned, The onerous 'duties of hon secretaries fell upon Mr. Stanley Wilson and Mr. Ernest A. Sanders. The stewards were Messrs A. Booth, J. Podmore, jun, A. G. Robertson, J. Davenport, C. E. Houghton, W. Brow n,A. Fawcett and G. T. Bibby. Mr. D. Davies, who has taken such an active part on the committee had the misfortune to break his collar bone in a cycle accident , but happily he was able to be present and assisted the M.C's. Messrs E. Pickavance, S. Wilson, C. J. Newton and E. Morris. Mr. Ralph Johnson supplied free the furniture re- quired and many of the costumes were obtained front Messrs S. B. Watts and Company. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. ,• Warrington Borough Ponce Court.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. ,• Warrington Borough Ponce Court.
Minor Cases.

SATURDA.Y.—Before Messrs Birchall (in the chair) Hayward and R. T. Fairclough. and Dr. Fox. CONSTABLE ASSAULTED.—John O'Neil, 13, Garden- row, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Arpley-road, en Friday afternoon, and with assaulting Police-constable Cooper. Prisoner pleaded not guilty. The officer stated that he saw the prisoner, who was drunk, in company with some other men, standing on the footpath in Arpley-road. Witness went towards them, and some of theta stepped from the footpath. Prisoner used a foul expression to the officer, and "tupped" him in the face three times. Witness would have been further assaulted but for the prisoner's brother.—Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs. THEFT OF BOOTS —James Cattle and Mary Singleton, Ro.erson's lodging-house, Ship-yard, were charged with stealing from the washhouse at the rear of 24, Wilders- pool-road, two pairs of boots, valued at ss. the property of James Hallwood, on Thursday. The Chief Constable stated that the two prisoners had been living together in Warrington for about a week, and got their living ostensibly by selling lavender. They were thus able to enter the backyards of houses. The boots were seen in the wa,shhouse about two o'clock. and were missed about seven o'clock. They were next discovered by Superin- tendent Monoghan, who found that the prisoners had sold one pair to Mr. Leslie, secondhand dealer, and the, other pair was being worn by the female prisoner. The bench sent the prisoners to gaol for twenty-one days. MONDAY—Before Mr. F. Monks (in the chair) Alderman Smethurst, Councillor Thornton, Messrs. Birchall, . .

Hayward and S. Wright. MAINTENAIsTE.—Henry Chilton, 38, Catherine-street, was ordered to contribute is. 6d. per week towards the maintenance of his son at Ardwick-Green Industrial School. UNREGISTERED LODGING HOUSES.—EIiza Devlin, 6, Dolman's Yard, was summoned for keeping an unregis- tered lodging-house—lnspector Flood said he visited defendant's house during the night of September 30th. Two men, defendant and her child, and; another woman were sleeping there—Defendant, who pleaded poverty, was discharged on promising not to repeat the offence— Mary Jones, 15, Lower Ship Yard, and William Ward,l3, Lower Ship Yard, were each fined is. for similar offences. DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—Kate Johnson, 1, Chapel Court, was fined ss. for committing abreach of the peace by acting in a disorderly manner in Winwick-street on September 26th. TUESDAY.—Before Aldermen Sutton (in the chair) and Hutchinson, and Dr. Fax. THIEF SENTENCED.—James Lee, Glass House-square, was charged with stealing from Thomas Riley, a farm labourer, between seven o'clock and half-past leven on Monday, a silver watch and metal chain, valued 40s. He pleaded guilty, he said, to save trouble. Prisoner alleged that prosecutor had given him the watch and guard..--He was seat to gaol for a menbh. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. Hepherd (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillor J. Roberts, and Mr. Thornton. OBSCENE LANGUAGE ON A TRAMCAR.—John Turner, clerk, 123, Knutsferd-road, was summoned for making use of obscene language in a Corporation tramcar, in Knutsford-road on October 3rd.—Dafendant did not appear.—Mr. S. Wilson (deputy Town Clerk) prosecu- ted, and said that on being asked for his fare defendant refused to pay, and used obscene and abusive language to the conductor.—A fine of 15S. and costs was imposed. VIOLENT ASSAULT.—Da,vid Henry Guest, Water- street, was summoned for assaulting William Butler Smith, _painter and decorator, *Bewsey-road, on October 7th.—Mr. Browne appeared for the complainant and said defendant owed his client 15s. Although he had asked for payment several times complainant had not obtained the money. On Wednesdayinorning he was cycling along Winwick-road when he saw the defendant who signalled to him to stop. Complainant did so and Guest commenced to dispute about the account. At defendant's request complainaht went down Longford- street and defendant without provocation struck him on the nose with his fist. Complainant reeled and fell and the landlord of the "Star" Inn and several women came to his assistance. Subsequently he went to Dr. Curtis and it was found that his nose was fractured.— Complainant gave evidence and denied taking off his coat and striking the de fendaiat first.—Defendant alleged that complainant was the aggressor.—A fine of 40s. was inflicted with the option of a.month's imprisonment.

usA MoToßisr Lowe,carter, Bennett- street,was charged with stealing the contents of a tool bag attached to a motor cycle belonging to Charles Parkes, Standishgate, Wigan.—From the statement of the Chief Constable it appeared that prosecutor went into the Mersey Cycle Works, Bridge-street, leaving the machine outside. Oncoming out he saw prisoner leaning on the saddle and ordered him away. Prisoner took his departure and it was found that he had rifled the tool bag. He was subsequently arrested by Detective Memo& and P.C. Stewart with the articles in his pDssession.—Prisoner who had previously been imprisoned for theft, was sent to gaol for two months. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. J. Fa.irclough (in the chair)
and Mr. .T. R. Young:,

ALLEGED WIFE ASSAULT.—John -Golden, Thelwall- lane, was charged with assaulting his wife on Tuesday. He pleaded not guilty. Complainant said she was sew- ing in the house on Tuesday, when defendant commenced to curse and call her bad naraes. He then ran her out of the house, and threatened to "chuck her neck out." When she was going out he threw &bottle at her. Defendant frequently came home drunk and a fortnight ago gave her a black eye.—Defendant alleged that his wife provoked him with her drunken habits, and the case was dismissed.

THE BATTERED BELLEISLV. After lying at the bottom of Portsmouth harbour for upwards of a month, the hulk of the old battleship Belleisle was on Thursday refloated and brought into dock. She was sunk on September 4 by a torpedo, which was fired at her for the purpose of testing the value of celluloid corn pith, an American invention, which, it is claimed, will prevent the inrush of water when a ship's plates are perforated. In this case it did not do so, for a big hole was torn in the Belleisle's side by the torpedo, and the water rushed in at such a rate that the vessel was soon submerged. For the purposes of experiment a section representing part of an armoured battleship was constructed in the Belleisle. In this the Whitehead torpedo tore a hole several feet wide, starting the plates over a large area. The task fraisiUg her was entrusted to the Liverpool Salvage C ,mpany, who completed it on Thursday. In the aftern ,on the vessel was towed into dry dock at Portsmouth, where she will be thoroughly examined by experts.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 10 1903
A DEPUTATION.
The CLERK informed the Board that the annual meet- ing of the Association of Poor Law Unions would be lield in London in November.

Mr. GEORGE PILLING moved that Mr. A. J. Jolley and the Clerk attend the meeting as representatives of the Board. If they could reduce the expenses of the Vaccination Act it would repay the Board very well. That was one of the chief questions that was going to be discussed.
Mr. Mather seconded and the proposition was carried unanimously.

COST OF THE NEW POLICE BUILDINGS. At a meeting of the Watch Commttee, held on September 3rd, a letter was read from the secretary of the Grocers' and Provision Dealers' Association, com- plaining of the damage done to shopi fronts by persons striking matches on the paintiand stone-work, when it was resolved that the Town Clerk be instructed to pre- pare and submit to the committee, a bylaw dealing with the practice complained of. It wastalso resolved that the members of the Council be invited to inspect the central police office premises in accordance with the understanding arrived at at the last Council meeting.On the 17th September it was resolved that the 2ad class merit badge be granted to P.C. Dyson for meritorious condnct in stoppirv, a runaway horse, and that the Town Clerk and BoroughbTreasuror be requested to report on the contract and cost of the new police premises. The MaYoR proposed the confirmation of the minutes. The members had not come to any understanding with regard to the police premises. 'Alderman SUTTON seconded, and it was unanimously carried.

div.head: NEW COUNTY EDUCATION AUTHORITY.
div.p: THE NEW COUNTY EDUCATION AUTHORITY.

The Clerk reported the receipt of a communication from the Director of Education for Lancashire, trans- ferring the powers and responsibilities of the Union School Attendance Committee tO the Lancashire County Council.
The County Authority would be unable to avail them- selves of the Clerk's services after September 30th last. Books, papers and documents were left in charge of the district clerk, Mr. G. F. Clarke.

div.head: NEW RTE.
div.p: THE NEW RTE.

The Clerk presented a statement upon the estimates for half-year ending at Lady Day, 1904. The estimated particulars of common charges and of contributions required from the Union townships for the half-year ending at Lady Day, 1904, showed a total of £13,990 against an actual exp•nditure of £13,787 us. 9€l. in the corresponding half of last year. By former inclusion of the county rates with the receipt for common thud chargesicalculated upon the preceding c•unty rates, and by the continued variable increases of such county rates the township balances, as shown on the ledger accounts, became unequal and by one contribution for county rate made by the Borough, not required by reason of their becoming a County Borough, the'mequality be- came greater, the Auditor has at his recent audits advised removal of the inequality. It would not be practicable to effect absolute adjustment in one half- year. He (the Clerk) proposed as a step in that direction to make an equal call of sixpence in the £ upon the overseers of all townships, and when adding a small sum to cover outlay until the first call was due, to leave the Borough out of such calculation until the township balances are at about an equal rate in the £. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY moved that the estimates as read by the Clerk be approved and precepts in accordance there- with he issued and served upon the various rural town- ships of the Union, the township of Newton, Haydock and Warrington standing over until the approval of their new supplemental lists. Mr. PILLING seconded, and the resolution was carried. The effect of the resolution in the rural districts is that there is a rate of 6d. in the 2. for Union common charges, with a ppnny extra, which goes towards a bahnce in favour of each township at the end of the half year.

INCREASE OF RELIEVING OFFICERS' SALARIES. The Board went into committee to consider applica- tions from Mr. T. J. Garnett and Mr. F. H.Aukland for increases of salaries.—Mr. Garnett's application read as follows :—" In the year 1891 my predecessor as Relieving Officer of No. 1 District received £l6O per annum as salary. Since that time considerable altera- tion has taken place in the town and district. The population of the town has increased over 33 per cent., and'as No. 1 District comprises the greater portion of the town, it must have also the greater portion of such increase. The rateable value has also advanced over 50 per cent., and is another evidence of growth in the dis- trict. In 1891 there were 16 cases of lunacy dealt with it No. 1 District. In 1902 there were 49 cases. During the eleven years, since 1891, the total number of cases is 392, oran average of very nearly 36 per annum. This is a very great addition to an unpleasant and sometifnes dangerous duty, and as no special remuneration is pro- vided for this class of case it is only fair that it ought te be taken into account when an officer's salary is being considered. As a contrast. I atay point out that nay salary is £l7O per annum, or £lO more than was paid in 1891, equal to about 6} per cent., and I respectfully ask you for an advanoe so that it may be ie proper proportion to the greater responsibilities of the office."—Mr. F. H. Aukland wrote :—" I beg respectfully to make application for increase in my salary as Relieving Officer. My service with your board dates from 27th March, 1893 (over 10 years), and during this period I have had one increase, on the 31st October, 1894. My predecessor received as Relieving Officer a salary of £ll5 twelve years ago, my salary for same duties at present stands at £lO5. During last twelve years my district has increased considerably in rateable value and population, and during the last winter, through economic administration of out-relief no increase in my relief cheque was required.—Trusting my application will be received by you favourably." -The reporters were absent during the discussion, but we understand that it was decided to increase the two officers' salaries by £lO per annum. Mr. Garnett will tierefore get £lBO and Mr. Aukland £ll5 per annum. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: Church Society Anniversary.
div.p: Church Society Anniversary.

The anniversary service in connection with the Warrington Church Society was held at St. Paul's Church on Wednesday evening and was well-attended. The preacher was the Rev. W. E., Collins, professor of f,celesiastical history, King's College, London, who based his sermon on the words "A vision appeared unto Paul in the night" Aces xvi. 9. Instead of a visionary being an impractical person, said the preacher, the man who saw visions was the most practical of all. He saw things as they really were and that was the one source of doing anything at all that was worth doing. 'Vision was the source pf all progress. Addressing the members of the Church Society he said they were banded together to bear witness to the faith and to bring home to themselves and others the fact that they were More than members of isolated separate churches and Of certain parishes. They were the Church in 'Warrington. They were the members of that Catholic Church which existed throughbut. the world and they were banded together to present a picture of the unity of the church and to gain for themselves the strength that came from fellowship.—N collection was taken in aid of the Society's funds. •

div.head: OLD ACADEMY.
div.p: THE OLD ACADEMY.

At a meeting of the Finance and Estate Committee held on' the 21st September, it was resolved that the lease of the Old Academy be renewed fora terna of seven years at the rent of £4O per annum. Alderman BENNETT moved the adoption of the minutes. Councillor CRA EIC seconded. .

Councillor THORNTON asked a question with reference to the old Academy. It was suggested it be re-let for seven years at per annum. He did not know that he wanted to raise any discussion,. but he desired to know if it, was advertised or whetker at was renewed. He had heard a gentleman say he would like to take the premises and give £lOO a year. The MAYOR: lam advised it was let by tender to thefpresent occupiers with the option of renewing the tenancy unless it was required by the Corporation. Councillor PIERPOINT :, Are those conditions in the renewal lease? I think it would 'be better to let the tenancy be from year to year. Seven years is too long a lease on which to let Corporation property.

div.head: APOLLO PRIZE MALE CHOIR.
div.p: THE APOLLO PRIZE MALE CHOIR.
Annual Concert.

Warrington the advent of the winter musical season the Warrington Apollo Prize Male Choir has renewed its / Work with increased zest, and on Monday evening the members gave further evidence of their ability to cater for the music-loving public by holding their third annual concert in the Parr Hall. A large audience assembled, although the better-priced seats were not as well patronized as one might reasonably have expected. The programme was one of more than ordinary interest and was sub- mitted in a way that earned the unqualified approval of thefaudieriee. There was no lack of variety. At one moment the company might be listening to light,spark- hug opera music and at the next to the splendid chords of some stately chorus. Under the able conductorship Of Mr. T. Brough the Prize Male Choir was keard to -distinct advantage in the choruses "Hues of Day" (Jules Berleur) and "Pilgrims" (Parry) and the part songs" Spin, Spin "and "Wake, little Kate." The voices blended beautifully,and each piece was given With that careful attention to expression so essential to a successful interpretation. "Pilgrims" was rendered with particularly fine effect. Whilst the opening lines were solemn and subdued, the ooncluding passages, of a joyous and inspiring nature, brought out the full volume of tone. All the members of the choir, it is to be noted, Paid attention to the conductor and Mr. Brougla is to be congratulated upon the ability with which he piloted then through the intricacies of the various selections. The solos were admirably interpreted by Mr. Clayton and ltfr. Percy George. The Apollo Prize Mixed 'Choir also appears to be making encouraging headway and added not a little to the success of the entertainment. The choruses " Song of the vikings "(Eaton Faning) and" The storm" (Rowland Rogers) were rendered With taste and precision. In the last-named there was again what might be termed a study in contrasts. Commencing with the supplicating cry of the voyagers On the storm-tossed vessel—"Miserere Domino" --it ends with the triumphant strains of "Gloria tibi Domino" as the ship lies safely at anchor in the bay. Mr. T. Brough again occupied the Post of conductor and he and the members generally. • are to be congratulated upoa the high degree of pro- ficiency attained. The selections by the St. Helens • Opera Company, under the conductorship of Mr. H. Berrey, formed an enjoyable feature. Most of them were of a light, sprightly description, and on the whole, were well presented. The soloists were Miss Griffiths, Miss A. Dennett, Miss Tabernacle, and Messrs. It. Atherton, W. Milne, J. liVeddall, and R. Hamblett. Although choruses and part songs constituted the major *Portion of the programme there were some capital solos and duets. Miss Foster, who possesses a sweet 'voice of good compass, delighted the audience with an "Pressive rendering of "Dear Heart" (Mattel). In responding to an encore she sang the ever-popular Scenes that are brightest " from "Maritana." Messrs. R. Berrey and W. Milne scored a success with the duet "Our girls" and another pleasing duet was "The Ballad 6_iagers " by Messrs. H. Berrey and C. Rigby. Berrey had been announced to give a solo, but unfortunately he was seized with illness and to the regret of the audience, could not appear. Miss . A. Dennett stepped into the breach and sang in a, • !manner which earned high encomiums. A better humor- •lst than Mr. Whit Cunliffe it would have been hard to find. Hilarity reigned supreme when he was on the -platform, and again and again were encores accorded. Both as a mimic and vocalist Mr. Cnriliffe excels, and lie was distinbtly happy in his choice of items. Efficient accompanists were found in Messrs. E. Wilkes,.A.L.C.M., and A. Trow, who discharged their duties with taste and skill..

div.head: Police Court and Prison Cate Mission.
div.p: Police Court and Prison Cate Mission.

The work of the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission of the Diocesan Church of England Temper- ance Society for the month of September includes the following items :—During 261 visits to 26 police and petty sessional courts in Liverpool, Wigan,Warrington, St. Helens, Bootle, Widnes, &c., 1,090 persons were spoken to by the missionaries in the courts and cells, of whom 441 were subsequeattly visited in their abodes. Fifty-nine women, boys, and girls were provided with work, taken to refuges, or restored to friends. The magistrates sought and obtained the assista,nce of the missionaries on behalf of 70 persons, many of them first offenders, and the police and court officials had their help on behalf of 39 persons. At the Mission Room near Walton Prison—open every week-day morning-671 men and women were provided .with breakfast and were helped and advised in various ways. Thirty-five persons were visited in their abodes from the prisons. Twenty-three tickets for work at thelSociety's Firewood and Mat Factory, 78, Cedar- ,street, Bootle, were given to men from the courts and prisons. One hundred and twenty-eight persons visited the offices and the homes of the missionaries to be assisted in various ways. One hundred and fifty-nine letters were written by the missionaries With reference to persons in whom they were interest- ed. One hundred and fifty-six pledges of total abstinence were taken in connection with the work_ 18 meetings were addressed, &c., &c.

TIOLLANDERS CONSUME THE MOST TOBACCO. French statisics show that Holland consumes more smoking tobacco than any other country in the world. her quota per head approximates 9 lbs. The United States comes round with about 41bs. Belgium and Ger- IneaKare next, then Austria with about fa lbs. Norway and Denmark coma before Canada, and France is tenth with aboot 2 lbs. per head. Sweden and Russia are almost ajireast, then England and Italy, and Spain is lowest with 1 lb. Italy and Spain, however, are the greatest consumers. of cigarettes.

div.head: DOUBLE PROGRAMME.
div.p: A DOUBLE PROGRAMME.
A PARALLEL PLATFORM,

Tactics. • THE real purpose of the Chamberlain-Balfour policy becomes more obvious every day. It is all a matter of tactics. Mr. Chamberlain has left the Cabinet for several reasons, but no one of those reasons is because he disagrees with the Prime Minister. They are tactical reasons, and may be put down in the follow- ing order: (1) Because they wish to make it more difficult for the Unionist Free 'Traders to take a stand for Free Trade. (2) Because Mr. Chamberlain's continuance in the Cabinet would neesita,te ;In immediate declaration in favour of Protection, for which both Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Balfour agree the country is not yet ready. (3) Because the cause of Proteclion can be best advanced by Mr. Ciminherlain devoting his whole time to propagandist work. (4) Because Mr. nalfour'S Retaliation scheme and Mr. Chamberlain's Prefrrence scheme provide alternate policies, ei:her of which can be adopted or adapted according to the needs of each constituency. It is, fortunately, not necessary to prove that Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain are working on laiie i owards the same end. noir letters and th* friends proclaim that object to I.lie world. Art Sheffield on Oetober2nd Mr. Bafour said : "3:r. Chamber- lain's view, believe me. does not differ by a scintilla or by a hair's breadth from my view."

Electoral Reasons. SINCE the days when Mr. Chamberlain founded the Birmingham Caucus he has never been guilty of maliing electoral necessity subservient to patriotism or statesmanship. In judging his motives in any course of action we Must always keep this in view. He is the first election agent in tl:e land. What he is doing now is exactly what any astute election- eering hand would advise under similar circumstances. He will try to spike the guns of the Unionist Free Traders ty withdrawing from tilt; Government tile chief object of their attack. He will help Mr. Balfour to hold an open mind upon the food question until the time conies when settled convictions involve no electoral danger. He will devote himself unsparingly to this last campaign to place himself at the head of the British Govern- ment. And, as the best means of doing this, he will instruct each Unionist candidate to advocate just as much, eras little, Protec- tion as each candidate.'eparticuhir constituency requires.

I will say that he (Lord Salisbury) does intend, he and his friends, to put a duty on corn, although he does not think it convenient at the present moment to say so. And although he allows some members of his Government to agree in favour of it in one place, he enjoins upon other members the duty of repudiating it in another. Remember this is not a question upon which the Government can be allowed to have two voices.

In 1885 Mr. Chaplin was advocating a tax upon corn in the rural districts of Lincoln- shire, while Sir Howard Vincent was advocat- ing free food but a tax upon . manufactures at Sheffield. Other county and borough candidates took the same diverse lines. What was attempted by Lord Salisbury in 1885 will be attempted by Mr. Balfour at the next election. In 1885 the trick of a double pro- gramme and a pUrallel Protectionist platform, to suit all constituencies was exposed and defeated. We must see that the trick is once more as fully exposed, and then its defeat will be equally certain. As at Rochester.

THE success of the double programme was seen at Rochester. There the Unionist candi- date appealed for support as an opponent of the food tax, but an advocate of Protection for Rochester's chief manufacture—cement. Free Traders will be very much to blame if they allow the same tactics to meet with success in other districts. It should be more easily exposed than it was in 1885, because we have the definite assurance of Mr. Balfour, Mr. Chamberlain, and all their friends that they are working together along parallel lines towards the same end. They openly confess that the resignation of Mr. Chamberlain is purely a matter of tactics. The end they are both working for is Preferential and Retalia- tory Tariffs, a mere ephemism for Protection. Vainly is the net spread in the sight of any bird. As In 1885.

THE Liberal party has set itself to repeat their victory at the General Election of 1885. Mr. Chamberlain seems to have also adapted the methods of that election as the surest road to success; the only difference being that the late Colonial Secretary has adopted the methods of the Tory party in 'lBB5. Then, as now, the Tory party was playing with Protec- tion. It would not be correct to say they were more than playing with the question, or that they made it their policy. Then, as now, tire was no definite policy of Protec- tion before the country. Then, as now, a detailed scheme of Protection would be self- destructive. Then, as now, what would pro- tect one industry would destroy another; but a general promise of Protection can be made to suit all interests. Then, as now, Tory candidates advocated just as much Protection as their constituenc!es favoured, and Free Trade in everything else. Then, as now, in the boroughs they advocated Protection for' manufactures but Free Trade for food; while in the rural districts they supported a tax on corn and Free Trade in nlanufactures. Nobody censured this double-Need programme more strongly than Mr. Chamberlain. Speak- ing at Birmingham on :Novtinber 7th, 1885, he said:

BIBBY'S QuAtrEnLv.—The autumn number of this quarterl:, is an exceptionally good one and fully main- tains the high reputation which this illustrated journal of country and home life has gained both for the quality of its literary matter and the beauty of italletterpress and the reproductions of the various coloured and half- tone plates. A leading feature of this quarter's literary supi,lement is an illustrated article based on Mr. C. NV. Leadbetter's recent work entitled "Man—visible and invisible." The first group of pictures show what is called the astral body of the ordinary man under the influence of differing emotions. For instance there is a picture of the astral body of a man in intense anger and another whilst in love. Another series of pictures shows the mental body of a savage, of an ordinary man and of a developed man. The whole form an interesting collection and present some striking contrasts. In addition there are some well written articles on a variety of subjects and the coloured plates accompanying the number are alone well worth the price asked for the magazine.

The Examiner, Saturday October 10, 1903.

was to obscure the past, although this might have been the effect desired by one less renowned for political integrity, less famous for honourable scruple, than the late Colonial Secretary; and, whatever the motive, it is necessary to prevent the result. If we have not already forfeited for ever the esteem and srespect of other nations as a result of years of fatal inactivity,. alternating with blundering diplomacy and fool-hardy precipitation, it will require years of statesmanship to restore our former prestige. We have a Government which has lost every claimito popular respect—a Govern- ment which owes its very existence, not to the deliber- ate verdict of a thinking people, but to the excited votes of an electorate hysterical with war-fever, :a Government which would seem even to have lost the necessary strength of mind to abdicate. The special mandate asked for and obtained in 1900 was a dangerous and foolish electioneering artifice,and it will be nothing more than its perpetrators deserve, if the public that they temporarily duped shewthat it has profited by the experience of the past three years, and when called upon to give its verdict on the way its confidence, so readily I given, has been used (with the War Commission report to show how undeserved that confidence was), demands the banishment from-office of these so-called statesmen. _ _

_ The hope seems to be entertained by the still unrepentant Conservative party that, by diverting public/ attention they will escape the day of reckoning and so we see a party thoroughly cowed, paralysed with fear, watching, waiting, and praying, while the Colonial Secretary crashed through civilisation. Safe Conserva- tive seats are lost, and the Prime Minister, perched uncertainly on a rickety fence, mutters contemptuous platitudes. Mr —Chamberlain's scheme, buoyed up by specious appeals to isolated instances and carefully selected figures, changes in almost every detail from day to day, as each new suggestion is rent to pieces by carefully-considered and logical argument; while the champions of Conservatism tour their constituencies .or avoid them without daring the luxury of political speeches. So Liberalism has its opportunity, and occasion to undertake a nation's defence from the attacks of Conservatism gone mad, dominated by the atavistic tendencies of unimporta at pessimists. Before any programme of progressive legislation can be considered, many of the achievements of the past eight years will have to be re- paired and amplified, if not undone. The Workmen's Compensation Act must be extended, and the Education Act radically altered. No civil servant, be he Cabinet Minister or village schoolmaster, receiv- ing his salary from public funds, must be subjected to religious tests. Denominational teaching would seem only possible at the expense of the denomination re- quiring it, and religious strife must cease in order that national education, which depends on the co-operation of all sections, may be efficient. Thus only can we keep our position in the world and the loyalty and respect of our Colonies. The public, andparticularly those who have lost rela- tives and friends in South Africa, will demand the reorganisation of the War Office, and, indeed, of our military system generally. In 1900, when the Conser- vatives demanded the gratitude of this country for the conduct of a great war, there were many who sus- pected that our battles were being fought with accus- tomed bravery by our soldiery, hampered by an incap- able Administration. This suspicion is now on the evidence published by the War Commission shewn to have been only too well founded. Lord Lansdowne's carelessness and inefficient conduct of the War Office having been proved, his dismissal, and that of his col- leagues, would seem to be imperative, especially now that he has been promoted to wider fields and a position of greater importance. The foreign policy of our Government had earned European derision even before the Prime Minister had begun to make "esoteric statements" for the edification of the Sultan of Turkey. Our diplomacy in Venezuela only re- cently resulted in England becoming the catspaw of the German Government; while now we are seriously discussing methods of retaliating on Germany for a suggested insult to Canada. The Sugar Convention. Treaty has raised the price of sugar to an the inhabi- tants of this country, who are thus to be subjected to a tax controlled by a committee of foreigners on which England is represented only in a minority of one. It has raised the price of a raw material to our jam manufacturers and fruit preservers, while lowering the price of the same raw material to their competitors abroad. It has crippled fruit-farming, a youthful and i prosperous industry n England; while we are to spend in the increased cost of sugar about thirty-four times as much as we obtain by a higher price for the sugar they export to us for the West Indian sugar planter. These blunders are vitally important, but with the War Commission Report beforeus,we are induced to ask whether they do not become insignificant compared with what may be in store for us if Lord Lansdowne is permitted to conduct our foreign politics. But blame cannot be shifted from the Cabinet collectively to one mem- ber. Mr. Chamberlain, who knew and had com- municated to the War Office the insufficiency of our armaments in South Africa, "squeezed the sponge "and risked war when he was well aware that this country was totally unprepared for the task they might have to undertake. Mw. Brodrick, with his expensive bom- bastie, and useless Army Corps scheme and his love for i bugle-calls and buttons, s a luxury that can be dis- pensed with. A Cabinet which knowingly indulges in bluff and risks war for which, as they are aware, we are totally unprepared, is not to be tolerated. The lives of British soldiers are too valuableto be left at the dis- posal of Conservative gamblers, and Liberals must see that these gentlemen are not allowed exultantly and flippantly "to trip lightly amid all our dead." When a positive programme of reform comes to be considered, the Liberal party will have to turn to their country districts, whick demand urgent legislative attention. Some method must be found of keeping a healthy rural population properly heused,and if possible with some stake, however small, in the land 2f England under cultivation, independent of the personal character or financial position of any particular landlord. And the kind of cottage wanted in our villages must be let at a rent which does not permit of cottage building be- ing considered a remuneratiTe outlay of capital. We are driven, therefore, for a real solution of the problem partly, perhaps to some method of obtaining the profits of the drink trade for the public weal, but mainly to placing in the hands of local authorities revenue ob- tained by an equitable system of land taxation. Farmers should appreciate the suggestion that, were taxation on urban property sufficiently heavy, rates on agricultural land might well and fairly, in regard to its comparative value, be materially lowered. Indeed, the Liberal party must not neglect the farmer; and while demonstrating to him the meretricious character of Mr. Chamberlain's proposals, which are sometimes made to appear to benefit agriculture gener- ally, it must consider how the general prosperity of the rural parts of England may be increased by improving the condition of the tenant farmers. It must be remembered, however, that agricultural depression is never so acute as it as represented to be. The farmer , lives directly on the produce of his farm' and even the rent of his house i,s included in the cost of conduct- ing his business, and thus he is apt to grumble at the small amount of actual cash he is able to turn over.

But one is inclined to quarrel with the mere sugges- tion of raising the price of wheat for the doubtful benefit of the farmer, while so many less extreme and more certainly beneficial reforms, such as the tenant farmers' representative, Mr. Lumbert, has advocated in the House of Commons, amid a general chorus of dis- approval from the Tories, remain to be carried through To mention one subject in fuller detail, it will be undoubtedly necessary to devise some means of enforcing a Parliamentary rate for the carriage of our goods on our railways, just as it was found necessary and possible to enforce a Parliamentary rate for the carriage of pas- sengers. Every farmer knows the way in which heavy railway rates absorb profits ; every manufacturer realises how railway rates enforce the concentration of our industries in big towns, and so conspire to produce over-crowding. But the anomalies of a system regula- ted not by mileage but by traffic. Competition need not be discussed here. Most railway companies are, of course, much over-capitalised. Land was purchased at the top of the market, and now that all landowners are suffering from the depreciation in the value of their land railway companies have never reduced their sub- scribed capital to represent this loss. Thus it will be seen that housing and taxation, farm- ing and temperance, have all to receive the attention they merit, while there are still administrative depart- ments to reform and changes in the electoral law to bring about. Ample material exists for a programme of useful work, which will take years to carry through, and only the very sanguine amongst us can hope for much from the Conservative party. On the one hand there are the promises so readily given by Tory leaders at the election of 1895, and the tendency of these gentle- men to pass inoperative laws' in the hope of appeasing the popular demand for drastic reform; and on the other hand, we have the history and traditions of the Liberal party, and the frequent suggestions on these important subjects by its present leaders. The solitary legislative achievement of probable worth that can be directly attributed to the Conservative party is the Irish Land Act, granted to Ireland at a time when the Government were in sore need of Irish support, but in reality reflecting the efforts of generations of Liberal statesmen.

It is the existence of this constructive programme which demonstrates the impossibility of an alliance with the "Conservative Free Traders." (Many of these are merely striving to keep their seats in Parliament ; while, of the rest, some are unable to decide on a course of action,and others ore to be appeased by a com- promise—and a compromise on this subject is imposs- ible.) The Liberals cannot, with the Government . before them as an example, demand a special mandate for a negative policy—a policy of mere resistance. They must therefore proceed to win the country not only to sense of shame and indignation at the Conservative record, but further to a sense of confidence in their programme of reform and progress, of efficiency and modernity. For the rest they must hope, each to the extent of his own faith, that if ever the time comes for votitig on "Fair Trade," however disguised, in the House of Commons, they may obtain some assistance from the genuine Free Traders on the other side. 'the party that desires the confidence of the nation must cultivate the greatest attributes of the true re- former—infinita patience and tolerant sympathy for the laborious work of building up a consistent policy, ever adapt Able in its application to the changing needs of successive generations, but securely founded on incon- testable principles for the welfare of the majority. Now

that a new lease of life to this Government, with its past record and present intention, can mean nothing but further danger, and even irreparable harm to the Emptre,the price of failure becomes incalculably heavy. I It is incumbent, therefore on Liberals, by a careful and ' thoughtful preparation for an unflinching and uncom- promising fight, to win a victory for Liberty, Efficiency, and Honour.
EDWIN S. MONTAGU.

P.S.—Since the above article was put into type the political situation has been dramatically changed. The resignation of the Duke of Devonshire, Mr. Balfour's scolding letter, and Mr. Chamberlain's raging speech at Glasgow have swept the minor incidents of Cabinet' reconstruction into the shade. The moral for Liberals is to be prepared to meet the enemy, whether the General Election takes place before or after Christmas.
[This artical forms one of a series which we have arranged with leading members of the Eighty Club to contribute to our columns. Book copyright strictly reserved.]
