div.head: SOME NOTES ON
div.p: SOME NOTES ON
THE31.,111,13 AL SITUATION
BY EDWIN S. MONTAGU, Peospective Liberal Candidate for West Cambridgeshire.

The intention of this article is to lay before the reader certain propositions regarding the politics of the day rather than exhaustively to treat of any one item in the programme:of either party. The duty of the Liberal politician is to explain as patiently as be scan to the country that the present Government is unworthy of the confidence of the people; and furthenthat it is possible for the men who adhere to Liberal principles to :torn a Government capable of controlling the destinies of our empire. It may be that, in criticising the past eight years and the present plight of our Ministry and its supporters, the temptation to bitter language and even violent expressions of vituperation .will be irresistible but, to those who are following events as they occur with the proper amount of attention, the degradation of England as controlled by an inefficient Ministry is so depressing that language is apt to become unruly. Perhaps it will be said that, even granted the Government is bad, there is no evidence of the possibility of a better alternative. Were this pessimistic view correct, indeed our country were past salvation. But surely a Ministry composed of men who have profited by the experience of the long career of this Tory Government, who are actuated by a belief in cautious administration and legislation for the majority, rather than by a belief in close attention to details of temporary importance and of interest to small minorities only,would be preferable to a Ministry of discredited men. Even those who believe in Con- servative principles have every reason to blush for their present exponents. Perhaps it were as well to deal first with the question uppermost in men's minds—the blow dealt by the late Colonial Secretary at our confidence in Cabinet responsi- bility, by erecting his Fair-Trade bogey to harass political and commercial circles. At a time, however, when the newspapers are filled with figures from statis- tical returns and expositions of elementary economic truths I do not propose to argue the matter fully here. It ,will be necessary for those who undertake the defence of our Empire to repeatfagain and again, with all the proof that can be collected, such fundamental doctrines as—exports purchase imports; those who cannot sell will not buy; an import duty certainly affects the con- sumer, Ste. But there are one or two points in this con- nection which cannot be too often emphasised. (1) It is not sufficient, or of any importance at all, for Mr. Chamberlain to announce to the world what he will tax and what he does not intend to tax, what he desires to protect and what he does not " propose "to render more costly. It must be self-evident that once the foundation of the tariff wall has been laid, the archi- tecture of that wall will depend, not on one man or on one party, but on the efforts of successive financial ministers, influenced it is to be feared, by powerful commercial undertakinas. Free Trade can be so easilf undermined by continual unambitious attacks that the slightest sign of the approach of the thin end of a wedge must be recognised and met, particularly when it is seen that the wedge cannot be controlled for any length of time by the carpenter who inserts it. And although the Liberal party should be ready to consider any suggestion for change which may make for increased prosperity, Mr. Chamberlain should have learned from the apprenticeship he served to Liberalism that it must be averse to dangerous experi- menting with poisonous nostrums or changes for the sake of change. For instance, were he to suggest that Nonconformists should be publicly burnt at the stake as a penalty for resisting the payment of rates he must not be surprised to find that the suegested change does not receive the support of the Liberal party. (2) Further, even though one Colony, or, for that matter, all our Colonies, approve in the abstract of the idea of protection for their exports, it will be impos- sible to satisfy in the concrete the conflicting claims of a world-wide Empire, the component parts of which, at different distances from the home market, are all inter- ested in the production and sale of different commodi- ties. Moreover, in that a duty designed to give a pre- ference to a Colonial producer cannot be used for retaliationagainst the foreign manufacturer without disturbing the preference, Mr. Chamberlain's scheme is seen at once to consist of at least two conflicting ideas. Indeed, if it were possible to institute a system of Preferential Tariffs to the satisfaction of all our colonies and dependencies, the system must, if it is to serve its purpose of benefiting the colonies, be so rigid in detail that one hesitates to consider the conflicting feelings and possible enmityaroued between the home oonsumer and the Colonial producer in years of scarcity when prices are high. (3) In considering the condition of British trade,only a distorted and dangerous view can be obtained by the superficial consideration of isolated industries,and it is impossible to interfere with one industry without not ' only promoting inefficiency in that industry, but also interfering harmfully with innumerable interdependent occupations. Thus, to protect steel would result in harming, on the one hand, shipbuilding, and so our docks, our shipping, and our sailors; and on the other hand, agricultural implement making, and so, to a cer- tain extent, our farmers and our agricultural labourers. (4) Next, it must be remembered that a duty imposed upon an article is likely to raise its price, not only by the amount of the duty, but by more than the amount of the duty. This result is occasioned because, in determining retail prices, fractions of the smallest current coin' are necessarily regarded ;as whole coins; moreover (and this is more important), inbuying a taxed article a larger outlay of capital is needed and upon this outlay a return as naturally demanded. The importing merchant has consequently to raise his charges by the amount of the duty and by a certain sum representing the interest on his additional outlay. (5) It is obviously amistaken way of fighting foreign trusts to encourage the formation of similar combines, with the resultant increase in the cost of living, and the corruption of legislature and public service generally here at home. Even if Protection does not immediately lead to the formation of Trusts, by tariffs certainly it is possible to prevent foreign competition; and then, combinations thus freed from the stimulation of com- petition and nourished by this protective system, can produce inferior articles and raise prices while ruining the smaller tradesman who is hampered by lack of capital. Such a combination, ever growing at the ex- pense of the consumer, who as prevented by the tariff wall from buying elsewhere, becomes at last all-power-' ful to manipulate and influence the incidence' of the taxes, and to corrupt voters, legislators, Government, j and, indeed, the whole country. Mao is ready for the responsibility of risking so undesirable a result as the loss of honourable government for the benefit of the few shareholders in certain manufacturing companies? The situation is best summed up by veference to three quotations from Mr. Chamberlain's speeches: The effect of eight years of Conservative Government may be grave, but no Liberal can agree that we have arrived at a condition of things when "a system of ' Preferential Tariffs is the only means by which the Empire canibelkept together." Nor can we even agree that the proposed system would have the desired effect, while it is quite clear that" if you are to give a preference to the Colonies you must put a tax on food." ntlAnd therefore since "I can conceive it just possible; deceived by misrepresentations,that the working classes might be foolish enough to submit for a time to a pro- posal to tax the food of the country," Liberals must use their best endeavours to prevent this possible and disastrous contingency. Littleneed be said of the recent resignations of cer- tain of Mr. Balfour's Ministry. The Prime Minister has published, at a somewhat exorbitant price, a pam- phlet which consists of philosophic truisms and hypo- thetical considerations quite inapplicable to Great Britain. State interference with a trade to protect the workmen is confused with State interference with a trade to protect the trade, while moat-favoured-nation clauses and the efforts of other nations who have tried and are trying " retaliation " are - completely ignored. The questionable methods by which the Premier endeavoured to purge his Cabinet of Free Traders, and his skilful handling of the Chamberlain correspondence, may servo temporarily to keep the Conservative party from disruption, but are dangerous to the prestige and honour of England's system of Government. So also the arrangement by which Mr. Chamberlain as a free man and Mr. Balfour as Prime Minister are both to work for the consummation of the same policy, each as his position allows, should, by its subtlety and lack of straightforwardness, discredit the Government. Meanwhile, it must shew us that though Mr. Chamberlain has retired we have nevertheless to fear an attempt eventually to establish a preferential system of protective taxes; and so the situation, con- sidered politically rather than morally, is practically unaltered. Mr. Balfour's speech of ThOrsday night at Sheffield, with its temporary repudiation of Mr. Cham- berlain's Colonial scheme, and its request for a mandate to impose retaliatory duties, carries the situation but little further. Old arguments are repeated, and vague speculations are clothed in language still more vague; bet nothing is said to allay our fears of the Premier's "palliative," or to answer the doubts of questioning electors. How long will England suffer this contempt- ible effort to ignore the responsibility of the Govern- ment to the people, whosevenlict it fears? But the Conservative record cannot be'expiated by a speech from Highbury or Sheffield or a flood of leaflets from Birm;ngham. It must not be supposed that Mr. Chamberlain's motive for his unconstitutional conduct

Mr. Edwin Montagu has just completed a dis- tinguished career at Cambridge University, where he held the office of President of the Cambridge University Liberal Club, and after leaving the University was at once adopted Liberal candidate for West Cambridge- shire. .
Mr. Montagu is anexcellont platform speaker, and his friends confidently anticipate for him a successful career in the House of Commons.

div.head: National Service League.
div.p: National Service League.

Sir,—.As you have criticised adversely the object of the National Service League, I hope you will allow me the opportunity of replying to the objections raised. (1.) You say the more fact that it is to be carried out under compulsion is repulsive to the free-born Briton." I ,feel sure that when the average Briton learns to appreciate how insecure our position really is, lie will findnothing repulsive in having to undergo the i minimum amount of training necessary n order to ren- -*ler secure all that is most dear to him; rather will he, just as the Romans of old and the Swiss of ta-day, welcome itas the privilege of his nationality. •(2) You speak of the vast army of trained men. The probable number coming up for training annually would be 200,000, which with the proposed period of training gives us 800,000; this is none too manyfor the adequate .defence of these shores. You say that the needs of Switzerland for military defence are greater than ours. I cannot agree with this, seeing that the independence .of Switzerland is guaranteed by all the Great Powers. Do not. let us rely too much on our insular position: remember that during the Boer War an enemy of 50,000 trained men could have marched from one end of England to the other. (3) You say that compulsory service is no remedy. I maintain that this is the only true remedy. By this means only shall we be able to form' the great second 'line of defence: which is necessary if our navy is to be -really effective. By this means only shall we avoid the • necessity of• greatly increasing the regular Army 4.50 that it may be large enough for Home Defence as well as Imperial Defence. To go into the arguments for and against increasing the present auxiliary forces, would make this letter too long; I hope to have an opportunity of dealing with this question later. But apart from the military side of the queStion, -universal service has advantages which it is impossible •to deny. It would inculcate a sense of the responsibili- ties and duties of citizenship, badly needed. It would, by drawing the inhabitants of slums out into the coun- try, help to check the physical and moral degeneracy attendant on life in towns. It would cultivate that -spirit of .method which is so often replaced by that of muddle, thereby helping the race in the commercial struggle which is before it.' _

Let us therefore clear our minds of cant and face the .question like men. I ask those who appreciate the vital •necessity of this movement to do their share of helping it forward by joining the National Service League, which has been formed to educate public opinion until the nation sees the necessity of adopting some such -scheme as that proposed by the League.—l am, your Obedient Servant,
GEORGE R. CROSFIELD, Captain. (Hon. Secs.' Warrington Branch N.S.L.).

He concluded his remarks by expressing the hope that this Church would not be behind in itsfiervice of praise in connectionwith public • worship.

At the evening service the pastor spoke on the • words from The Revelation There was no more ;Sea." These words were not to be taken literally but • should be concidered in the light of what they repre- ..sented to the writer. To him the sea was a symbol of Limitation, ,Nystery and Separation. The preacher ..showed by various illustrations how in this life we were restrained by inany limitations, that life was a great and solemn mystery and full of separation and partings, but concluded by saying that we reed not therefore be -discouraged; fox one day these things would pass away and be no more. div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB.
DISTRIBUTION OF BOWLING PRIZES.
Captain Crosfield on the National Service League,
COUNCILLOR WILLIAM PIERPOINT HAS A HORROR OF CONSCRIPTION.

• Several interesting speeches were delivered at the Warrington Liberal Club on Saturday evening on the aims and objects of the National Service League. The subject was introduced by Captain Crosfield who attended to distribute the prizes in connection with the annual bowling main in the unavoidable absence of his brother Mr. A. H. Cresfleld. The proceedings were presided over by Mr. Thomas Locker, and amongst those present were :—Major F. Mc I. borne, Councillor William Pierpoint, Councillor Wilkinson, Mr. William Furness Mr. Arthur Browne, Mr. J. Critchley, Mr. W. Ford and others. At the outset, the Chairman said perhaps a little ex- planation was due as to the reason why Mr. Arthur Crosfield was not present, although they were very proud indeed to see a Crosfield amongst them. (Hear, hear.) It appeared that Mr. Pemberton dictated a letter to Mr. Arthur Crosfield, stating that the prize distribution would take place on October 3rd. Instead of giving that date the typist put October 31st, (Laughter.) Mr. Crosfield his arrangements to come on October 31st and could not be present that evening owing to a business engagement. The annual general meeting of the Club had been fixed for the 31st. They would there- fore have the pleasure of Mr. Crosfield's presence at that meeting. (Hear, hear.) A short musical programme was then submitted after

which The CHAIRMAN, in asking Captain Crosfield to dis- tribute the prizes, said the past bowling season had been greatly interfered with by bad weather. Nevertheless they had the usual outing to Winnington. where they were unfortunately beaten. They succeeded in beating I the Saracen's Head team in both home and away games, this being the first time they had won the double event since the Saracen's Head had been under the present management. Then they again succeeded in beating their Sankey-street friends. (Laughter.) He couldnot I recollect how many consecutive times the Liberal Club bowlers had beaten the Conservative Club bowlers, and if they (the Liberals) could not beatthem man electoral I contest, at all events they could beat them at bowls. (Laughter.) There was promise of the green being in still better condition next year than it had been for the 'last five or six years. (Applause.) Captain CROSFIELD, who had a hearty reception, said Ihe had to convey to the members his brother's regrets I at being unable to be present, and he sent his very best wishes. (Hear, hear.) Proceeding to refer to the sub- ject of national defence, Captain Crosflelcl said at the present moment we were in a very insecure position and it was not safe for us to remain in that position. It was necessary to take some action at once. He , spoke to them not as Liberals but as Britons. He need :only refer them to the statement of Colonel Lonsdale Hall, before the Commission of Inquiry into the war, in support of the statement he had made. Colonel Hall I stated that during the late war an enemy of 50,000 trained and well-equipped troops could march from one end of 'England to the the other and there would be ' nothing to stop them. Those remarks would be just as true to-day if we were engaged in a war of like magni- tude. During the Boer war practically all the regular troops were away with the exception of afew thousand recruits, and the defence of England was left to the Volunteers and about half the Militia. Lord Roberts stated before the War Commission that the Volunteers were unfit for home defence. He thought that made the position pretty plain, but in case there were any who were disposed to say" Well, we don't mind about the forces on land, we rely on the navy," he would repeat what had been so often said before, that if we were going to rely on the Navy alone, and have no second line of defence, we were going to tie the Navy down to play a defensive partalone ? (Hear, hear.) If the Navy had to do that, it was, of course, weakened enormously. It was absolutely necessary to have a second line of defence if wewere going to enable the Navy to act with a perfectly free hand and assume the offensive at any point necessary. He felt that our present position in regard to defence was a serious one. Ile put it before the fiscal policy or the education bill or anything else, because what was the value of ;thew if ,we had the enemy in the land. (Hear, hear.) The remedy for our present posibion was in his opinion, that recommended by the National Service League. Since his brother (Mr. Arthur Crosfield) had advocated I another course, which he (Captain Crosaeld) did not ; agree with—(laughter)---he would first of all reply to ; him. (Hear, hear,) His brother admitted just as I strongly as he did that the present position was a very I serious one and wanted a remedy..He went on to advocate lan increase of the auxiliary forces and better pay for the men- (Hear, hear.) If they were going to pay the men for doing the defence work of the empire they were going to foster a wrong spirit and he did not think he could explain that'spirit better than by relating the ' experience of a sergeant-major the other day. Whilst at the range the sergeant-major told somenrohinteers to pick up the 'empty cartridges. One of the Volunteers turned round and said "any drink on this job major." (Laughter.) If that spirit became rife the nation was doomed. That spirit was far too much abroad to-day, and he was strongly against , the encouragement of any policy that would tend to I foster it. In the second place the cost of paying the Volunteers on the lines suggested would be fabulous. If they were going to put the second line of defence in the hands of Volunteers a much longer term of service ' would be required of them to make them efficient and they must have at least half a million men. The mini- mum amount of pay would be £1 a week, and if they continued that for, say, two m9nths, they would easily see what a large sum wouldbe required. Then it would be impossible to find the numbers required, and it would not be conducive to discipline because the first time a man thought he was badly treated or was offended he would simply "chuck it.' Another objection was that we could not make use of it as a stimulant to education. In Germany any person who passed through a certain examination, instead of having to serve two years, only served one. That had had a great effect all through Germany, and had been a stimulus to young men to edutate themselves. He Quite believed it would be a splendid thing for this country if they put a value on education like that and said to these men who had educated themselves—and by educa- tion he meant mentally, .morally and physically—your term of service for purposes of defence will be reduced. The scheme he recommended was that proposed lby the National Service League. It was summed up in the few words—universal compulsory training. The training advocated:was two month's training in a camp of exercise under canvas in the first year, and 14 days' training In the second, third and fourth year. Captain Crosfleld pro- ceeded to read the programme of proposals and said he lad come there thdt night in the hope that they -Would give the matter their earnest consideration, Now was the time taact. He could not conclude better than by quoting Major Seeley who had said: "Not by spend- ing money on (slips, though the Navy of course must have our first care, not assuredly by shouting imperial greatness, but by personal self-sacrifice will this empire be maintained. Igo further, I believe if all these warn- ings fall on deaf ears then this mighty empire of which we are so proud will fall to pieces and this nation will be humbled to the ground." (Applause.) Captain CROSFIELD then distributed the prizes as follows:- 1, F. Jewkes, gold albert 2, J. Parr, clock, 3, W. Daintith, six-bottle cruet 4, J. Berry, four-bottle cruet 5, A. Mynekyme, silver teapot 6, W. Lawlor' flower stand 7, W. Patrick. case of carvers 8, W. Dainteth, sugar and cream bowl

div.head: Examiner, Saturday October 10 1903
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday October 10 1903

less trained, but all in various stages of training. The' was no continuous and self-contained whole. What they wanted was an army that had a certain training ; not quite so much training as the regular army, but suffi- mealy trained to defend the shores of England in case of any sudden declaration of war, or any landing with- out such declaration. Some said that we had muddled throuqh before and could muddle through again, but muddling through cost the 'lives of a great number of men and that should stop. Everybody who had really gone into the subject said there was no really volun- tary system—by which was meant citizens giving their services voluntarily to the nation—that would do for this particular home defence, because they had never really been able to get sufficient men for the purpose. They wanted men and not bov. They knew that youths of 17 and 18overe very willing but they could not stand the wear and tear of war. They went down in their thousands. They had now come to the question whether the whole of England's young manhood must not be made to serve. Some people said they had no objection to serving, provided everybody else did. In Switzerland every man who was physically capable of bearingarms did so gladly as anational defence,and felt it a disgrace if he was not passed into the service when the:calf came at the age of 20 years. He did not see that Englishmen were behind the Swiss at all in the matter of patriotism. That system would give them a sufficient number of men for all requirements, and, in his opinion, the amount of service advocated by the National Service League was the minimum which men should be called upon to do. They had to teach a soldier discipline. It was not a matter of teaching him how to handle a rifle, and shoot and drill, but he had to be so disciplined that in the hour of danger he would instinctively do what he was ordered to do, and feel that he would face all the pain and mutilation, and, possibly death, on coming under fire. They could not teach a man that in a week or two. The National Ser- vice League was not formed so much to lay down the law as to educate public opinion on these matters and make people think. It was a matter altogether outside politics' and should be taken up quickly by parties of all shades of opinion. The Liberal Club was one of -the very best places to open a propaganda of that kind in Warrington, and they knew that Liberals went further afield for their ideas than the Conserva- tives, and he hoped they would be supported by the Liberals of Warrington in the matter. (Applause.) He was an old Volunteer adjutant in Warrington, and had admired tremendously the spirit and the way the men had come forward as soldiers for their country, but he had always thought "Why should these men alone bear •the greater portion of the burden of home defence?" At present there was a vast amount of misdirected effort and wasted enthusiasm that would be avoided if they could get proper regulations and organisation on the lines he had advocated. He did not want anyone to think that, being an advocate of the National Service League, he did not look upon the Volunteers as a wonderful force. He was their adjutant for five and a half years, and knew what the Warrington Volunteers could do. (Applause.) He was always very proud of them, and should continue to be. (Applause.) He thought them a most excellent corps but at the same time he thought their efforts ought to 'be supplemented and helped by the whole nation. (Hear, hear.) COUNCILLOR PIERPOINT AND TILE SPIRIT

OF MILITARISM. Councillor William PIE RPOINT, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. A. H. Crosfield, the donor of the prizes audit° Captain Crosfield for his presence, said no words of his were necessary to commend for their apprecia- tion anyone who bore the honoured name of Crosfield. In all efforts that he (Councillor Pierpoint) had put forth On behalf of the Liberal party he had found an excellent example in the late Mr. John Crosfield and Mr. George Crosfield (Applause). Mr. Arthur Crosfield had been one ofithe mostiOnsistent members of the club and had done what he could to cultivate the social side of their political life. (Hear hear). His absence was due to a business engagement and to the little mistake which had been made with reference to the date. Still it gave him great pleasure to find that Captain Crosfield was taking so much interest in the Liberal party in Warrington. Proceeding to refer to the question of National defence, Councillor Pierpoint said he had not had time to study the speeches which had been made at Appleton Hall on the subject, but he must say he did not like the word compulsion. He did not like anybody to compel him to do anything, and he was a fair specimen of a Lancashire man. (Hear, hear.) He had a great horror of conscription. (Hear, hear.) Conscription was compulsory, and the suggestion made by Captain Crosfield in all good faith and with the most honest intentions, savoured somewhat of conscription or compulsory service. He had no great objection to military traming,for if it did nothing telse it set a man up, and gave him a spirit of reliance which was eminently desirable. (Hear, hear.) It made & man sub- ject to discipline which, he was bound to admit, as an old Volunteer himself, was a very good thing. (Hear, hear,) But he did not like the words compulsory ser- vice. Wherever he had gone in countries where there was compulsory military service, he did not find that thepeople hada, great fondness for it. There seemed to be a (spirit of militarism abroad, and if we oncelet in this system of compulsory service, it would be diffi- cult to control it afterwards.

Captain CROSFIELD pointed out that the proposed scheme was not based on the lines of the French or German military systems. It was based on the Swiss syst,em. Councillor PIERPOM said he had not been able to study the question, but he felt they ought to exhaust every means in their power of improving the present system of military service before they embarked on any form of compulsory service. (Hear, hear.) The vote was carried with acclamation. "r Captain CROSFIELOII acknowledging the compliment, said he would take two points raised by Councillor Pier- point. He (Captain (rosfield) used the word corn- pulaion, and he knew that it went against the grain, but he believed compulsion was the only remedy. He would ask them to remember that the liberty of the state was far more important than the liberty of the individual. Councillor Pier. point had said that they must look into their present system and see if it could be improved. The very fact that during the Boer war the country was left without regulars showed that the regular army could not per- form its imperial mission and defend these shores. The country needed something more for defence, and he believed the National Service League proposals would supply that want. A musical programme was submitted. The zEolian Glee Singers (Messrs. H. Bennett, W.Bennett, W. White and W. Knowles) contributed several glees; Mr. George Kendrick played several selections on the banjo and ,Mr. W. Whittaker very efficiently gave a whistling solo. Mr. E. A. Sanders was very successful in his recitations. The duties of accompanist were discharged by Mr.W. H. Kendrick, who also gave two pianoforte solos.
The proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman and the artistes.

I hear that Harris and Edmunds are both well again and will commence work on Monday, and in all probability be fit for play on the following Saturday. Cook, the forward, who has enlisted, did so somewhat hurriedly and is rather repentant now. There is a chance that he may be seen in the Warrington ranks again before long.

The " A " team, who received such a trouncing last Saturday, will not be dismayed by the visit to Pendle- bury, and points are expected. Ernest Ratcliffe is down on the list once more, and if his knee remains sound the three-quarter game should give him ample opportunities to shine.

I would just remind my readers of the County trial match on the Wilderspool ground on Monday next. The best exponents of the Rugby game in Lancashire are billed to appear,aud the 12 aside game in such capable hands should prove very attractive. Fish, Dickenson, and Boardman, of Warrington, will be included in the teams.
There has been a meeting of the Works League Committee this week, at which the offer of the War- rington F.C. to supply competing teams with jerseys, etc., was gratefully received.
The following matches in the Works League will be played next Saturday. Whitecross v. Rylands Bros, or Walker's,Lon.don and North-Western v. Crostield's Cable Works v. Naylor's.

div.head: PECULIAR STORY FROM LATCHFORD.
div.p: PECULIAR STORY FROM LATCHFORD.
Is It a Ruse?

I A peculiar story comes from Latchford. It appears I that one evening last week, the dwelling-house of Mr. J. B. Chappell, of 7, Wash-lane, was broken into by I some persons at present unknown. The intruders effected an entrance by the back window and after Ihelping themselves to a suit of clothes and a generous carving of a shoulder of mutton they made good their escape, leaving the back door open. The occupants of the house were .sleeping upstairs at the time and did not discover that they had had these unwelcome visi- tors until an early hour next morning: A peculiar feature of the affair is that a letter was subsequently written, which may or may not be a clever ruse to throw the police off the scent. The com- munication bears the initials of what are represented to be the names of three individuals, who describe themselves as "Catholics." Regret is expressed by I the writers at having made a serious mistake in visit- ing Mr. Chappell's house, and they proceed to state ; that it had been their intention to visit the house of I the Rev. J. F. Matthews, who lives next door. The 1 suggestion intended to be conveyed in the letter is that this visit to Mr. Matthews' house was to be paid as a sort of reprisal for his attitude towards Roman Catholics in the'Education controversy. It is hardly conceivable that such was the motive of the intruders , and their action savours too much of that indicated by the series of petty larcenies from dwelling-houses which have taken place in Warrington recently. The police are in possessisn of the facts and we hope they may soon lay hands, on the depredator or depredators

Fifty-nine women, boys, and girls were provided with work,. taken to refuges, or restored to. friends. The magistrates sought and obtained the assistance of the,: ' missionaries on behalf of 70 persons, many of then( first offenders, and the police and court officials had their help on behalf of 39 persons. ' At the giSsion ; Room near Walton Prison—open eyery week-day morning-671 men and women were provided with breakfast and were helped and advised ,in various ways. Thirty-five persons were Visited in their abodes. from the prisons. Twenty-three tickets for work, at. the'Society's Firewood and Mat Factory, 78, Cedar- street, Bootle, were given to men from the courts and prisons. One hundred mid twenty-eight .persons visited the offices and the homes of the missionaries to he assisted in various Ways. One hundred and fifty-six pledges of total abstinence were taken in connection with the work- -18 meetings were addressed, &c., &e.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
By " Ovalist."

The habitues of Wheater's Field, Lower Broughton, metlwith a shock during the course otSaturday afternoon such as they had never expected when on their way to the ground. Warrington might have been doing well, but they could hardly be considered a match for the Rangers at home, especially as the latter had shown indications of having come back to fruln. A valuable two points were looked upon as certain assets of the Broughton Club before the commencement of the match, but by the call of time those assets had been transformed into additional liabilities, and all through Warrington's unlooked-for skill and determination. We have won at Wheater's Field previously, and in fact divided the points there last season, while the match before only resulted in a one point win for the Rangers, but they nevertheless venture to count the " wirepullers " as prospective victims. Fe .v teams probably push the Rangers harder on their own ground, and by now they will perhaps be ready to recognize that the wearers of the modest looking primrose and blue jersey are a force to be reckoned with. War- rington's victory on Saturday was only narrow, five points to three, but the visitors were certainly the better side.

On paper, no one could reasonably have expected Warrington to win the match, because the Rangers appeared to have a stronger and more representative team. The Warringtomans were somewhat like a bird with only one wing, whereas the Rangers had their best attacking combination at threequarter. For all that they were no better off than the visitors, because one wing was so entirely ignored that it might almost as well never have existed. The match somewhat reminded me of a boxing contest between two one-armed men, in -which. Warrington had the stronger arm. Fish and Isherwood were always more than a match for Wilson'and Hogg, while Dickenson gave the middle men a particularly warm time,and in fact it was his individual dash which earned Warring- ton the kudos. He looks like getting a good few tries this season, but I would counsel him against that be- setting sin of the centre threequarter, selfishness. He has already developed a tmdency to forget the existence of his wing-threequarter, and such forget- fulness does not conduce to the success of the side. Perhaps, when Harris takes the field again, we may see the lengthy centre making the;openings we expect from him.

The spectators, and there was a fair number from Warrington got good value for their money. There have not been many more interesting games at Broughton, and except for a short spell just after the interval, there was never a dull moment. Broughton had the assistance of a good breeze to commence with, and they very soon made a hot attack on the Warrington line, which Hallam and Fish ,:accounted for by successive tackles of Wilson and Hogg. Good forward play and judicious use of the touch-line changed the venue. Once within hail of the home quarters Warrington began to show their mettle. The three-quarters twice got away, only for)Dickenson to fail on one side and Fish to miss a good pass on the other. Then Wilson attempted to punt clear, but instead Dickenson secured at centre and simply romped away, giving the full back no chance to stop the try. Fish added a goal by an oblique shot against the breeze. Things hummed after this, but Warrington more then held their own, Mahoney twice getting away and menacing the home citadel. Play became still faster and the ball was repeatedly carried from end to end by combined efforts among the backs on each side. A few minutes from the interval the ball, quite unintentionally I am sure, came into the possession of Harry and Widdeson,and,:the right-wing pair by a workmanlike effort put on a try, Widdeson sprinting well for more than half the length of the field. Though W. James had an easier shot than Fish he failed to land a goal, and by his failure he lost the match. One would have thought the Rangers would have kept the right wing better employed after this but no, they went on working Wilson and Hogg to a standstill and left the other two starving for some- thing to do.

In the second half, Warrington completely changed their tactics. With the wind behind them they went in for defensive play, instead of going in for points as they might have done. Touch play and sure tackling may be effective, but a big risk is taken with a lead of only 2 points. The Rangers strove hard to score, and came within an ace of doing so on several occasions, whereas Warrington never attempted to attack. They were lucky to come off so well, and I think are to blame for slackening off after half-time. If they had doubled their score first it would have been excusable, but as things turned out, nothing but Hallam's wonderful steadiness and robust tackling saved the side more than once. The full back never played a finer game, especially considering the rough usage he had to submit to. He and Davies were both "knocked out "by the home forwards, and if referee Smith had been a bit sharper somebody would have received marching orders. However, "all's well that ends well," and the match ended well enough from a Warrington point of view.

By the way, history repeated itself in this match in a very remarkable way. Two seasons ago Warrington lost the match through a mis-kick of Wilson's which went right acroAs to Widdeson and gave him an easy try. On Saturday the Rangers lost the match for the very same reason. It was a mis-kick from Wilson which gave Dickenson possession at centre and resulted in the winning point. Warrington were very sore, I remember,on the first occasion to be:defeated by a point in such a way, hut the law of compensation operated very soothingly on Saturday.

The Rangers have their Captain largely to blame for the defeat. Wilson received nine out of ten passes from the scrummage, and was never allowed to go very far, whereas if he had seen that his fellow-centre was properly fed the game might hhve ended differently Widdesou was much more dangerous than Hogg, for he could outpace Forster, whereas the Scotchman was never equal to beating Fish. In fact " Jack " upset Wilson and Hogg so often that it is a wonder they did not get tired of trying to pass on his wing. He has rarely excelled his display on the defence,and made up for lack of opportunity to score. W. James, too, was poor,in fact both halves did nothing but sling the ball behind them, While the Warrington pair were al- ways trying to get" forrud." Davies was of little use after being hurt, but Mahoney at-rain played mo s promisingly and should make a class back. He is worth persevering with. In my opinion jie is the most likely recruit Warrington has signed on since the advent of Dickenson. I have already , alluded to most of the men on the winning side, but /I must not forget the forwards. They played well right through a very hard game and generally got the ball when it was badly needed. Cook; lam sorry to say,lias joined the Scotch Fusiliers—a distinct loss to the club. Thomas: and Hunt were both very prominent and merit special notice. •
The league table up to date is as follows _ : For. Against _ _ _ _ _ _ _

Warrington's position is virtually equal to second as they are only two points below the leaders, and the four clubs next above take priority of place by a fractional superiority in scoring average. Salford are still showing the way, and the club to give them a fright has yet to be fatind. Runcorn did almost as. well as Warrington, by winning at Swinton, while -Widnes are still in the dumps without a solitary victory.

. Warrington have another stiff engagement to-day, but as it is on the Wilderspool ground they should I enter upon it with confidence. Hunslet have generally given Warrington a handful, and so far this season , they have shown form which indicates that they will ! prove stern antagonists once more. Like Warrington they have won four matches out of five, but the two teams ought to change places in the table after to-day. • The home team will be the same as last week with the substitution of Morrison for Jolley in the forwards.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
Longford Depot Experiments.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednes- day afternoon, Mr. T. Halton presiding, There were also present:—Dr. Murray, Messrs. Brooks, Ball,Mather, Knowles, Forshaw, Houghton, with Dr. Sephton (medical officerof Health), Messrs. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), F. Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), and H. H. Burnage (assistant surveyor).

HOLLINS LANK, WINWICK The CLERK read a letter from Mr. Muspratt stating that at the last meeting of • the committee of visitors to Winwick Asylum he was instructed to ask when the improvement agreed to be made by the) Rural Council in Hollins lane would be completed. The committee were very anxious that the work should be carried through without furthe delay. He had replied stating that Mr. Newcombe hoped to proceed with the improvement shortly and al- though he could not give an approximate date for com- pletion he could assure the committee that when the work was commenced there would be no further delay. Mr. KNOWLES asked if the Asylum authorities paid one-third of the whole of the rates of Winwick.

Mr. S. SUTTON said they paid nearly that amount. Mr. KNOWLES said the authorities were very large ratepayers and it was time the Council did something to improve the road. The matter was referred to the roads committee and the clerk was instructed to write to the Superintendent of the asylum stating that the improvement would be placed in hand at once.

div.head: PENKETH _LIGHTING AND FOOTPATHS.
div.p: PENKETH _LIGHTING AND FOOTPATHS.

It was reported that at a meeting of Penketh Parish Council on Tuesday evening it was decided to make application to the District Council for two additional gas lamps to be erected—one in Cuerdley-road and one in Stocks-lane. It was also decided to have all the lamps in the township fitted with incandescent burners. The Council also resolved to ask the District Council to make and curb the footpath round the shop and property situated at the corner of Station and Chapel roads, in the occupation of Mr. Greenhalgh and others. Attention was drawn to the dangerous condition in which footpaths were being left after being taken up by the General Post Office contractors and the Council were asked to take such steps as would ensure the footpaths being properly repaired and cindered by the General Post Office after excavations. It was also re- quested that a certain•footpath be recindered. It was decided to agree to the proposals in regard to the lamps, and the other matter was referred to the Roads Committee.

LONGFORD DEPOT. The INSPECTOR reported that with reference to Long- ford depot he had taken observations during the month. On October Ist he visited the depot in company with the Medical Officer and found it fairly clean. There was a quantity of manure lying on the floor after being boiled. The nuisance still existed, but they were given to understand that further experiments would be carried out.

_ The CHAIRMAN said he attended the meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening and he was rather surprised at one or two remarks made. The Council, however intended to spend about £2,000 for extra plant, new pans, &c., so it looked as if they were moving in the right direction. Mr. KNOWLES: They talked like that many years ago. Continuing the CHAIRMAN said that one of the Councillors made a remark about refuse having been turned in great quantities into Sankey Brook for years. He was glad that had becn admitted in the Council Chamber as it showed that he was "on the right track" whenhe made some remarks a few months ago about sewage being turned into the brook. The work would be proceeded with at once, another engineer would be appointed, and expert advice obtained. The CLERK said a German expert had been consulted and the Council were about to adopt his system. Dr. SEPHTON said experiments were being made. He believed a certain amount of sewage was turned into Sankey Brook, but it was now proposed to put down bacteria filter beds near the works. Dr. Sephton explained the processes which it was intended to adopt, and said that if they were carried out the nuisance would be practically nil. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: APOLLO PRIZE MALE CHOIR
div.p: THE APOLLO PRIZE MALE CHOIR
Annual Concert.

With the advent of the winter musical season the Warrington Apollo Prize Male Choir has renewed its work with increased zest, and on Monday evening the 1 members gave further evidence of their ability to cater for the music-loving public by holding their third annual concert in the Parr Hall. A large audience assembled, although the better-priced seats were not as well patronized as one might reasonably have expected. The programme was one of more than ordinary interest and was sub- mitted in a way that earned theunqualifled approval of the audience. There was no lack of variety. At one moment the company might be listening to light,spark- ling opera music and at the next to the splendid chords of some stately chorus. Under the able conductorship of Mr. T. Brough the Prize Male Choir was keard to distinct advantage in the choruses "Hues of Day" (Jules Berleur) and "Pilgrims" (Parry) and the part songs" Spin, Spin "and "Wake, little Kate." The voices blended beautifully,and each piece was given with that careful attention to expression so essential to a successful interpretation. "Pilgrims" was rendered with particularly tine effect. Whilst the opening lines were solemn and subdued, the concluding passages, of a joyous and inspiring nature, brought out the full volume of tone. All the members of the choir, it is to be noted, paid attention to the conductor and Mr. Brough is to be congratulated upon the ability withwhich he piloted them through the intricacies of the various selections. The solos were admirably interpreted by Mr. J. Clayton and Mr. Percy George. The Apollo Prize Mixed Choir also appears to be making encouraging headway and added not a little to.the success of the entertainment. The choruses" Song of the vikings "(Eaton Faning) and "The storm" (Rowland 'loiters) were rendered with taste and precision. In the fast-named there was amain what might be termed a study in contrasts. Commencing with the supplicating cry of the voyagers on the storm-tossed vessel—" Miserere Domino" —it ends with the triumphant strains of "Gloria tibi Domine " as the ship lies safely at anchor in the bay. Mr. T. Brough again occupied the post of conductor and he and the members generally are to be congratulated upon the high degree of pro- ficiency attained. The selections .by the St. Helens Opera Company, under the conductorship of Mr. H. Berrey, formed an enjoyable feature. Most of them were of a light, sprightly description, and on the whore, were well presented. The soloists were Miss Griffiths, Miss A. Dennett, Miss Tabernacle, and Messrs. R. Atherton, W. Milne, J. Weddell, and R. Hamblett. Although choruses and part songs constituted the major portion of the programme there were some capital solos and duets. Miss Foster, who possesses a sweet voice of good compass, delighted the audience with an expressive rendering of "Dear Heart" (Mattel). In responding to an encore she sang the ever-popular "Scenes that are brightest "from "Methane." Messrs. H. Berrey and W. Milne scored a success with the duet "Our girls" and another pleasing duet was "The Ballad singers" by Messrs. H. Berrey and C. Rigby. Mr. Berrey had been announced to give a solo, but unfortunately he was seized with illness and to the regret of the audience, could not appear. Miss A. Dennett stepped into the breach and sang in a manner which earned high encomiums. 'A better humor- ist than Mr. Whit Cunliffe it would have been hard to find. Hilarity reigned supreme when he was on the platform, and again and again were encores accorded. Both as a mimic and vocalist Mr. Cunliffe excels, and he was distinctly happy in his choice of items. Efficient accompanists were found in Messrs. E. Wilkes, A.L.C.M., and A. Trow, who discharged their duties with taste and skill.

div.head: PROPOSED NEW STREET.
div.p: PROPOSED NEW STREET.
CARRIED BY THE CASTING VOTE OF
THE MAYOR.
Warm Discussion,

The subject of the proposed new street from Rylands- street to Sankey-street was again discussed at the meet- ing of the Warrington Town Council on Tuesday even- ing. A resolution was submitted by the General Pur- poses Committee as follows :—That the proposal con- tained in the following resolution of the Street Im- provement Committee be approved : A proposal from Mr. R. E. Garnett to add 20 feet in width co-extensive with his premises to the pro- posed passage behind the new premises in Bridge- street, and to give the scheduled property belong- ing to him, containing an area of 316 square yards, in exchange for the land in the Eagle and Child Yard, containing 531 square yards. i Alderman SUTTON said the simple explanation of the whole question was just this. They would be aware that a resolution was passed by the Council wherein the Corporation decided to form a passage, 10 feet wide from the east side of Trinity Church in Sankey-street to the back M the church, and 20 feet wide from this point to the Eagle and Child yard. for which they would be required to purchase two plots of land at a cost of £750. Mr. Garnett had since expressed his willingness Ito make a more important and more inviting proposal. In order to enable the Corporation to make a 40 feet street instead of a 20 feet passage, Mr. Garnett had offered to give them a2O feet footpath, equal to 371 square yards of land co-extensive withhis premises, and sell another additional width of 20 feet equal to another 371 square yards, including the buildings thereon' which he was told were now let at £2B per annum, at £3 per yard, which would be £1,113. Mr. Garnett also proposed to give the Corporation two plots of land,one containing 228 square yards, and Trinity-entry,which he claimed as his own property, subject to the right of road to the public which comprised 88 square yards, making a total of 316 square yards. These two plots Mr. Garnett would give in exchange for the plot of land behind the Royal Court Theatre, which land was dominated by lancient lights and through which Mr. Garnett had right of way. The result of such an arrangement which the Street Improvement Committee considered would ,be a great benefit to the town, and which Iby the resolution of the General Purposes Committee was approved, would be that the Corporation instead of getting a 20ft. passage as already agreed upon at a cost of £750 would secure a street 40 eet wide for £1,113, plus a ground rent of £lO, which part of the land was subject to, and at 28 years' purchase would be £23o,making at total of £1393. As a set off against this, the Corporation would be able to resell 217 square yards of land at, say £5 a yard, which would realise £1235. making a net total cost of .2158. In the event of the Corporation requiring the site of Trinity Church they would be enabled to carry a street 40 feet wide right through from Sankey- !street to Rylands-street. I Alderman HITTCIIINSON seconded.

Councillor PEMBERTON said he would like to ask the Town Clerk whether in the event of the proposal being carried out, it would be in accordance with tha bye-laws. He understood there would be no way out of the pro- posed new street as submitted, and according to the byelews no cul-de-sacs were allowed. The TOWN CLERK said that was so.
Councillor PEMBERTON observed that the scheme was therefore in contravention of the Council's own byelaws.

Alderman SUTTON: It has a passage at each end. Councillor PEMBERTON said he was astonished at Alderman Sutton bringing a proposition before the Councillwh/ch was in opposition to the byel2ws. The scheme had been before the Council on ( two previous occasions and it amounted to an insult to bring it forward again. (Hear, hear.) He was not in the best of health but he had come there on purpose to prevent what he called one of the greatest jobs that had ever been tried to be carried through in Warrington. He strongly objected to the practice of certaiE members of the Council to grossly mislead the Council when they had statements before them. This scheme had not the advantages that Alderman Sutton said it had. The benefit was all for one private person. There was no guerantee that the Corporation would get £5 a yard for a strip of land 20 feet wide. It was a clear mis-statement to say that the Council could get this street for £l5O and that the passage would cost £750. How could the street be brought through for that money? There were the shops of Chantry's and Benson's to be bought. Alderman SUTTON: I did not mentionthem.

Councillor PEMBERTION: You said when Trinity Church was pulled down the street could be carried through. It was as clear as daylight on the plan that it was intended to bring the street through the two shops he had mentioned. To purchase theta and also the land at the Rylands-street end would involve an expenditure of many thousands of pounds. If he were the owner of the land he would not hesitate to give £3,000 in addition to the land if the Corporation would do what was pro- posed. He wanted every thinking member of the Council to vote against the proposal on the ground that the cost was not fairly put before them. In public matters nothing ought to be hidden. He would beg of the Council to think well of this scheme before voting upon it. Councillor WILKINSON said any child in the fourth standard could understand the scheme if personal feel- ing was left out of the question. Councillor PEMBERTON : I must object to the words personal feeling. There can be no personal feeling in a matter of this sort.

Councillor WILKINSON (continuing) said the matter was so simple. If the Council constructed the passage it would be a passage for ever. The Corporation would have to buy a piece of land of Mr. Carter, whichseemed to have been forgotten by Alderman Sutton. If they took that into consideration, the passage would cost £1,200 Councillor LORD: Is Councillor Wilkinson seconding the amendment?

Councillor PEMBERTON : I move that it be rejected. Councillor WILKINSON: You did not move it before I got up. I take it Councillor Pemberton is not allowed to speak twice? The MAYOR: No Sir. Councillor PEMBERTON : Councillor Lord will move the amendment.

Councillor Wir.xiNsos (continuing) said some of the members were not looking ahead,they were always look- ing at the present. Warrington had been lost through men not looking ahead. (Laughter.) Instead of a passage costing .e 1,200 they had a scheme brought forward whereby for an exchange of land they got a 40ft. street. In addition the town would receive the benefit of an increased rateable value which would result from the buildings erected abutting the new street. It was quite true that the Corporation intended to carry the street through some day and the shops in Sankey-street wouldjbe wanted.MessrsCharles Broadbent and JohnPlatt advocated it many years ago, but owing to the interests of persons in adjoining streets the proposal was not agreed to. If the Corporation entered upon this scheme now,they could leave it to a future generation to carry the street through. Alderman BOLTON said he was under the impression that the Corporation had made a very good bargain, but the question arose was Mr. Garnett benefttting more than he was entitled to. He thought Mr. Garnett might have offered better terms, considering the improvement he got. The difficulty in his mind was whether Mr. Garnett would make the Corporation pay fancy prices for the land at the bottom of the proposed street. Per- haps some agreement might be come to on this point. Alderman BENNETT said the byelaws were made for the convenience of the Corporation and the advantage of the public, and not to stand in the way of a public improvement. Councillor Pemberton had characterized the scheme as a job. He would like to know what was the exact meaning of that expression.

Councillor PIOrBERTON: I-mean that if I had pro- posed this matter to the Corporation it would not have been accepted. It is cliquism to which I object. Alderman BENNETT said he thought Councillor Pember- ton meant that some members of the Council were in- terested in the scheme with Mr. Garnett. The cor- poration had no other intention than the general good of the town and he thought Councillor Pemberton ought to be a little more moderate in his language. As to the terms of the bargain he was not quite sure yhether Mr. Garnett was not having the best of the bargain, but the present terms were the best that the corporation could get and he thought it would be wise and well to close with them especially as the matter was barring the progress of other projects in Bridge street. Councillor LORD moved the following amendment : "That the minutes of the committee referring to the minute of the 28th September relating to the proposed new street behind the new premises in Bridge-street be not confirmed." He remarked that the scheme had been rejected on a previous occasion, byl7 votes to 7.
'Alderman Surrox said that was not so. Councillor LORD: I have it here in black and white in the Council proceedings. Alderman SUTTON: It was quite another scheme altogether. . . •

eo-uncillor LORD: It was a similar scheme and in the long run amounts to the same. You have admitted you will have to buy the two shops in Sankey-street. Alderman SUTTON: It does not include those at all

I Councillor LORD (continuing) said he thought the Corporation ought to get on with Bridge-street. They ought not to entertain proposals after proposals coming I from interested parties. The only return to the Cor- Iporation was an increased assessment of Mr. Garnett's property, amounting to £l4O. The Corporation was going to be run into an expenditure of 2,20,000. Councillor CRNIK seconded the amendment, and said ! if the matter was not a job he failed to understand ! what was. After being rejected by 17 votes to 7 the , scheme reappeared on the scene and was placed on the agenda for the General Purposes Committee under the heading "Bridge-street property." He failed to see how a street made from Rvlands-street to Sankey-street could be described as Bridge-street property. Alderman Sutton said the scheme would cost £l5O. Probably it Iwould do at the present time, but how much would it
cost before it was finished That was what they had to look at.

Alderman HUTCHINSON considered that the scheme would be a great boon to the town. They would never have the chance again. Alderman Musics pointed out that there was a car- riage way next to Chantry's shop, and he thought it ought to be part of the bargain, that the public could use that carriage way in order to get to the new street Councillor DODDS said he approached the subject without any prejudice but from what he had heard the thing seemed to have been done rather hurriedly. He thought when they ediscussed it two months ago they had ended it. He happened to see Mr. Garnett who told him that he was glad the Corporation had refused his offer because they would not have another opportunity, Now they were told he had made a better offer and if they put it off a bit further they might get further concessions and be able to arrange with the people at the top and bottom of the proposed street. (Hear, hear.) He suggested that it would be much wiser to defer the acceptance of this proposal until they were in aposition to deal with the whole of the land to put this street through. He supported the amendment.

Ald'erman Sur7rON said it was altogether absurd for members to keep on remarking that the matter was being pushed forward and that they had not had •an opportunity of discussing it. How many months did they want to consider it ? Councillor LORD: We want to settle it. Alderman SUTTON pointed out that the only alterna- tive was that they would have to make the narrow passage already agreed upon. In the scheme which was rejected the Council would have been obliged to pur- chase the shops in Sankey-street. but there was no such proposal now. Councillor LORD: What does Councillor Wilkinson say?

Alderman SUTTON: There is no proposal before us to buy the shops. What would the people say—(hear, hear)—what would the ratepayers in a few short years say if the Corporation refused this offer? They would' say that the members were blinded; that theycould not see the lengabof their noses ;and they let' the oppor- tunity pass. It would serve them right. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PEMBERTON, speakin,, in support of the amendment, ventured to suggest that no practical man who was laying out Warrington would MITA a main street 60 feet wide and within 35 yards of it, another street running parallel with it, 40 feet wide. The traffic from Sankey-street went down Bold-street and the traffic from the Central Station would always go- down Bridge-street. What would be opposite this new street ? Who wanted to go down Corporation-street? It was true that the matter had been considered by the General Purposes Committee but the members had not the slightest idea that the matter was coming forward. It was carried by the Mayor's casting vote. The MAYOR: I beg pardon. It was not the Mayor's casting yote._
Councillor PEMBERTON : I apologise. I was told the voting_ was 10-10
The-Mavoß : I voted once and that could not be called a casting vote.
Councillor c'EMBERTON contended that it would be a great mistake to go on with the scheme as it would cost £20,000.

Councillor WILKINSON hoped the people would not be misled by false statements. Even if the street was not made through they would get a 40 feet street in place of a narrow passage and at less cost. There were mem- bers of the Council who spent hundreds of hours for the good of the town to which they belonged, whilst there were other men going about the streets picking up bits of scandal, and that was all they did. (Hear, hear, and Laughter). _
Arderman /30LTON thought the matter ought to be adjourned until they had a definite understanding as to the right to use the cartway alluded to by Alderman Monks.

Alderman SUTTON: It belongs to Mr. Peter Garnett. A vote was then taken with the following results FOR THE AMENDMENT. AGAINST. Councillor Davies The Mayor 1t Burton Alderman Sutton „ Upson Jf Monks „ Brophy „ Smethurst Craik „ Bennett 9., lf Dodds .. Hutchinson Thornton Councillor Wilkinson. f? Pemberton 9, Tinnion lf Horrocks J, Sampson ~ Lord ~ Rogers ~ Brough tf John Evans The TOWN CLERK: There are eleven for and eleven against, _
-The MAYOR: I shall give my casting vote in favour of the committee.

div.head: Warrington Property Owners aud the Question,
div.p: Warrington Property Owners aud the Question,

At the annual meeting of the Warrington and District Proirrty Owners' Association on Wednesday evening. the newstreet question was discussed by Councillor Lord, Messrs. Gough, Hudson, England, Howard, and Shaw. Councillor Lord said he would move the rescind- ing of the resolution at the next Council meeting. The matter was finally referred to the Committee of the Association.

Cairo-street Chapel. Large congregations attended the harvest services' held in this place of worship on Sunday. The decor 3: tions were on a very extensive and artistic scale aucl were much admired. On Sunday morning the choir gave a creditable rendering of the anthem,"o Lord how manifold are Thy works,' Mr. Muir presiding at the' organ. Additional interest was lent to the proceedings by the presence of the newly-appointed minister, the Rev. Charles Harvey Cook, who will enter upon hie duties in November. He took for his text, the words: "Thus hath the Lord God showed unto me : and behold a basket of summer fruit. And he said, Amos' what seest thou? And I said, a basket of summer fruit. Then said the Lord unto me, the end is come upon my people of Israel; I will not again pass by them any" more"—Amos viii. 1, 2. The preacher, in the course of a carefully prepared address, pointed out that to religi- ous-minded men in all ages the harvest had been a time of joy and thanksgiving ; and so it ought to be. Allud- ing to the object for which the offertories of the day were to be devoted, namely, to the Warrington District Nursing Association Mr. Cook said he was pleased that the congregation had realized the need of sending help in the time of need to the association which would benefit by that festival. It was proper that they should' do so; it was a happy interpretation of what they felt,. The rev, gentleman again occupied the palpit in the evening when so many people were present" that they could not all be accommodated in the pews and it wag' found necessary to place chairs in the aisles. The service throughout was of an interesting and impressive character and much enjoyed.

ESTABLISHED 1870. TMUNICIPAL ELECTION. 1903. O THE ELECTORS OF FAIRFIELD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, I have been requested to become a candidate to re- present your Ward in the Town Council at the next Municipal Election—and after serious and thoughtful consideration I have consented and now beg respect- hilly to offer my services and submit your support and vote. I have had experience in Municipal work, having been a member of the tcwn council of St. Helens and served on the most important committees and only resigned that position a year after I came to reside in Warrington. lam not a member of any Political organization, nor am I a member of roar local Non-Trading Associa- tion, but I sin in full sympathy with them in their effort to purge the Town Council of all that is legally or morally wrong and would support them in their policy of Economy and Reform. In moving about your Ward I notize several matters waiting attention Most of your streets are insufficiently lighted, and many of your roads are in such a condition as to cause much annoyance to those people lwho have to use them, andi if selected would lose no time in bringing tha matter to the notice of the responsible committee. I have no axe to grind, and no personal ends to serve, bull would deem it an honour to serve you and do all that lies in my power to promote the welfare of my native town. It you honour me with your confidence I will en- deavour to do all I can to serve your interests to the beet of my ability. I remain Your Obedient Servant, JAMES POVEY. 11. Spriagfield-street, Warrington.

An inquest was conducted at the Police Station on Monday by Mr. Brighouse, coroner, touching the death of Martha Swanton, wife of Thomas Swanton, a general labourer; who lived at 7, Pilkington's-yard. The evidence showed that on September 15th deceased was in the act of reaching a hairpin from the mantelpiece when her clothing caught fire and she was so sadly burnt that she died on. October 2nd. She was at first taken to the Infirmary, but as there was no accommoda- tion there at the time the, injured woman was removed to her daughter's house at 38, Victoria-street, where she died. The Coroner said Dr. Leigh had sent him a note with reference to the deceased, who was 74 years of age. It appeared that the cause of death was old. age. Although death was accelerated by thelburns, they would not have hada fatal result in a younger person. The j cry returned a verdict of "Death from old age accelerated by burns." LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER the CLOCK, BRID GE-STREET.—Ad. Institute of Journalists.—Meeting at Widnes. A meeting of the members of the Warrington sub- district of the Liverpool district of the Institute of Journalists was held on Wednesday evening at the Town Hall, Widnes, by permission of the General Purposes Committee. The Chairman: of the 'sub-district (Mr. E. V. Walker) occupied the chair, and there . was a good attendance of Widnes journalists. The Chairman expressed Satisfaction at the good attendance of the local journalists, and alluded to the good results that might be obtained in various ways by the combina- tion of journalists. Mr. Isherwood also gave an in- teresting address on the work of the Institute, and quoted instances where journalists had obtained several important concessions in Warrington. As the result of the meeting, Messrs. J. Archer, H. Baker, P. A. G. W. Bailey, H. L. Williams, and J. Swale agreed to be nommated`for election as members and Messrs. H. Corrin. and Fryer as pupil associates. Votes of thanks to the Chairman for presiding, to the Mayor,.members of the General Purposes Committee, and the Deputy Town Clerk were cordially passed. FOR CLASS AND CHINA of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. The Polyglot Society. The opening meeting of the winter session was.held in the Old Academy, the Society's headquarters, on Wednesday evening. There was a large attendance of members and friends, with Mr. May, the president, in the chair. A charming and varied programme was opened with a violin solo by Miss Bouc'hier, accom- panied by Mrs. Holmes. Mr. May,in the course of his opening address, said that though the first meeting took the form of a social evening, a programme of serious work had been arranged for the winter. Each evening a paper in French and a paper in German would be given and discussed by the members of the respective sections and he hoped that the members woild work together to make this session even more successful than last year's. Mrs. Willett and Miss Bouchier, accompanied by Mrs. Holmes, delighted the company with violin duets, Miss Dreher gave a recitation in excellent German entitled " Herbstlied," Mr. Storey in French a recitation "La Grande Armee." ilerr Ockel gave an address in German on Dresden scenery copiously illustrated with .pictures. Mr. Gerard gave an amus- ing story of a Frenchman who went lion hunting and Mr. H. M. Ashton having read the ballad of" Schuit- zerl's Philosopede " wound up the programme with the" Frenchman's toast to the ladies. A hearty vote of thanks to the ladies for their kind assistance was proposed by Mr. Bunch, seconded by Mr. Kirk and carried unanimously by the members. Several new members were introduced and it is hoped that such a successful opening will lead to increased activity and usefulness during the -winter. On October 14th, an address will be given by Dr. Markel on " Salt and its formation." Intending members are cordially invited to write to the Secretaries, Messrs. Hulme and Haviour at the Old Academy. You CANNOT DO BETTER! Buy your boots and shoes at ALF. TAYLOR'S. Cheapest and best town. The Infirmary Concert. Warrington's concert season may be said to have commenced on Saturday evening when the annual concert promoted by the Workingmen's Committee in aid of the Infirmary and Dispensary was held in Parr Hall. Once more the appeal for help on behalf of a worthy institution has been willingly and generously responded to, the spacious hall being well filled in every part. It speaks volumes for the energy of the members of the committee-that they had succeeded in disposing of So many tickets and they are to be cordi- ally congratulated upon the gratifying measure of public Support which their efforts received. The concert was a "popular '.' one in the true sense of the word and the audience thoroughly •appreciated the admirable programme submitted. As, usual the mem- bers. of Mr. T. J. Down's orchestra gave their valued services and contributed in no small measure to the evening's enjoyment. Their playing was quite up to the high standard which we have become accustomed to , expect from this efficient orchestra.— if anything, they enhanced their reputation. Meyer- beer's majestic Coronation March was the opening item and served to demonstrate to the full the capabili- ties of the performers. The other iteins, which were all executed with marked taste and expression, were the valses "Ma Vie "• (Luinbye), selection of Scotch airs "The Thistle' (Myddleton) overture, "Hans Heiling " (Marschner), " Schluneme;lied " (Schumann), and gallop "A summer night in Denmark" (Lumbye). Mr. T. J. Down wielded the baton with his customary skill. The vocalists were Miss Blanche Cooper (soprano), Miss Nellie Anderton (contralto), and Mr. A. W. Proctor (baritone), and all found favour with the audience. Miss cooper possesses a pleasing, light voice,but her opening song Roses ih June "(German did not afford her much scope for the display of her nowers. She was heard to much better advantage in "A summer night" (Goring Thomas). Miss Nellie 'Anderton had the honour of a recall for her render- inn of "Goodbye " (Tosti) and responded:with "Allan Water." Her singing would have been much More acceptable had she infused more feeling and expression into it, but as it was the audience was undoubtedly pleased and applauded vigorously. Mr. A. w. Proctor Was in excellteit, voice, and sane; " Bedouin's love sang" (Pinsuti) in highly meritorious style: He responded to an encore with a spirited interpretation of The Yeoman's Wedding." Liter in the evening he gave "Only once more " (Moir) very creditably. The humorous element was entrusted to Mr. Arthur Bearle who created much merriment and was heartily r ecalled.
